articles.title: Abu Dhabi launches a wildlife rescue network
articles.body: A sea turtle in shallow water; a photograph accompanying the announcement of the Abu Dhabi Wildlife Response Network. The release of 76 turtles at Saadiyat Beach accompanies the network’s launch. The Environment Agency – Abu Dhabi (EAD) has launched the Abu Dhabi Wildlife Response Network to coordinate reports, interventions and animal care with partners and the community. Its announcement was published on 17 October 2026. The launch was accompanied by the release of 76 hawksbill and green sea turtles at Saadiyat Beach following treatment and rehabilitation, according to EAD. The agency said its joint efforts with partners had returned more than 1,500 turtles to Abu Dhabi’s waters over several years. From reporting to rehabilitation Cases are recorded and assessed before a specialist team intervenes, stabilising the animal if necessary and transferring it for veterinary care. Release follows recovery, while animals needing further attention remain in care. Experience predating the network Field work has an earlier history: the joint rescue programme with The National Aquarium began in August 2020. In 2023, EAD explained that some released turtles carried tracking devices, while a rehabilitation area in the waters around Louvre Abu Dhabi provided care before release. Protecting animals and their habitat EAD lists abandoned fishing nets, marine debris, pollution and coastal development among the threats to green turtles, alongside the importance of avoiding boat strikes. Protecting waters and beaches therefore remains complementary to animal rescue. At Saadiyat, the Emirates Nature-WWF guide asks visitors to keep a safe distance from marine wildlife and avoid feeding it. It lists 800-555 for reporting sightings, strandings and pollution, and response@ead.gov.ae as the rescue network’s email address. articles.title: Air Rifles
articles.body: Spring / gas-ram air rifles: cheaper guns, cheaper pellets. With cartridge prices rising, air rifles are among the first practical alternatives — cheaper guns, cheaper pellets. This opener covers spring / gas-ram designs, how they work, and why they demand respect. After our discussion of rising cartridge prices and available alternatives, it is worth noting that one of the first practical options is hunting with air rifles — for their relative affordability and that of their pellets. We begin with air rifles in their many types, shapes, and sizes: what they share, what sets each type apart, and how the firing system shapes performance. In a series of articles we will cover each type, its weak points, and the advantages and drawbacks of each design. The best-known air-rifle type is the spring / gas-ram airgun. What made it so widespread is availability and an acceptable price, putting it within everyone’s reach; most hunters owned one at the start of their path. How the rifle works — brief overview: Opening the barrel (“break barrel”) or using a tool or handle under the barrel (“underlever”). In both types above, the purpose of the handle or barrel action is to compress the spring or piston so that air is compressed in the storage chamber inside the rifle body. When the trigger is pressed, the spring or piston is released, and with it the compressed air in the reservoir, driving the projectile. The pellet leaves the barrel with a spiral (rifled) spin. When the trigger is pressed, the spring or piston is released. Many believe that a piston- or spring-powered air rifle is inaccurate. That is wrong: there are very accurate rifles, but one must always choose high-quality guns. Among the drawbacks of this system is that the shooter must practise thoroughly because of barrel vibration; that vibration varies and affects accuracy depending on how the rifle is held and handled. The rifle is very sensitive to hold and practice — the only way to reach satisfactory accuracy. It is worth noting that air rifles have hunting limitations; chief among them is that take is on perched birds, with its own challenges — challenges that add an extra pleasure to the hunt. Air-rifle pellets remain relatively affordable. Will we see a rush toward air rifles in the near future? Will the scene shift from 12-gauge and .410 shotguns to air guns? Next season will tell us everything. We stress: air rifles are very dangerous. Everyone must be responsible and treat them as firearms — they must never be underestimated.

articles.title: Sparrowhawk Hidden in a Backpack: Two Detained in Akkar Raptor-Poaching Operation
articles.body: From the anti-poaching operation in Akkar. Field monitoring by CABS with MECSHAP and Lebanese security forces led to weapon seizures and documentation of gunfire directed at four honey buzzards. In the highlands of Akkar, crossed by migrating birds of prey, one unusual detail stood out during an anti-poaching operation: a sparrowhawk inside the backpack of a man stopped by Lebanese security forces. According to the Committee Against Bird Slaughter (CABS), its team had been monitoring a mountain location in Akkar known for the illegal shooting of raptors, working with the Middle East Center for Sustainable Hunting and Anti-Poaching (MECSHAP) and the police. CABS said officers detained two men at the site. One had the sparrowhawk in his backpack; the other was intercepted while walking towards his vehicle. According to the organisation, the second man had evaded arrest at the same location the previous autumn. The injured sparrowhawk in a backpack in Akkar. Photo: APU The two men were taken to a police station, their weapons were confiscated and criminal proceedings were initiated, the organisation reported. The field operation did not end with those two men. CABS said its observers also documented two other individuals shooting at honey buzzards, two birds each. The team tracked both men to their homes and handed information and evidence to the police for follow-up action. The operation is part of the work of the joint Anti-Poaching Unit (APU, MECSHAP–CABS), in coordination with Lebanon's Internal Security Forces, to protect migrating birds and tackle illegal hunting of protected species. The Akkar case illustrates the value of field monitoring, evidence gathering and cooperation between specialist teams and the security authorities in protecting migratory raptors. Source: CABS

articles.title: Alexandra of CABS: our fight is against illegal hunting
articles.body: Interview: Shireen Bou Rafoul Alexandra watches birds during fieldwork in Lebanon. From watching migration routes to documenting offences, CABS volunteer Alexandra discusses her field experience in Lebanon and Europe, and the patience, risks and cooperation involved in protecting birds. In this interview, she explains why she distinguishes responsible hunters from people who break the law. Alexandra, please introduce yourself and tell us how your work protecting birds and volunteering with CABS began. I’m Alexandra, I’m 33, and I have been volunteering with CABS for more than three years. I studied conservation biology in Vienna, where I explored species protection in depth and developed a particular love of birds. In my main job, I work with BirdLife Austria on combating the illegal persecution of birds of prey in Austria, so I am involved professionally as well as through volunteering. You are German, live in Austria and take part in field operations in different countries. What keeps you going? My strongest motivation is to do my part to stop people destroying nature. I believe we should stand up for the things that matter to us. Of course, this work can sometimes be very frustrating and exhausting, but I draw strength from the people fighting alongside me. Celebrating small and large victories together, and giving each other courage and support, is something beautiful. What is your role within CABS, and what are your main responsibilities during field campaigns? As a volunteer field activist, my main task is to monitor hunting areas, identify and document illegal hunting, and gather strong evidence, such as photographs and videos, that can be handed to the competent authorities. The material we collect is also used in our international awareness campaigns and media activities. Alexandra documents observations with a camera during fieldwork in Lebanon. What does monitoring and documenting hunting offences actually involve on the ground? It means staying alert all the time. It takes patience, calm and perhaps a little stubbornness. Giving up quickly is not an option. You also need a high tolerance for frustration. You spend a lot of time sitting, watching and waiting; then events can suddenly move very fast, and you have to be ready to act. You have taken part in field operations in Lebanon. What impressed or surprised you most about hunting and bird migration there? Bird migration here is truly astonishing. Because of Lebanon’s unique position between the sea and the mountains, it is a very important bottleneck for migrating birds. For example, almost all the world’s lesser spotted eagles pass through Lebanon. You can also see an impressive number of species in concentrations rarely encountered elsewhere. It is a remarkable natural spectacle. At the same time, I have never seen so many birds of prey being shot at or targeted. That contrast is very difficult to comprehend. From your experience in different countries, what are the main differences between Lebanon and Europe when it comes to illegal hunting? Compared with Austria or Germany, the motives for killing birds are very different. In Austria, some people shoot or poison birds of prey because they see them as pests or competitors for hares and pheasants. Here, migrating birds are shot as a hobby or for food. The second difference is the enormous number of birds killed illegally: it is on an entirely different scale. Have you ever faced difficult or dangerous situations during fieldwork? How did you handle them? Not in Lebanon, but in northern Italy someone once pointed a hunting gun at me. It was my first field operation, and of course I was frightened. Fortunately, nothing happened, and my colleague was very supportive and helped me get through it. For a moment, I thought: “What the hell am I doing here?” Just twenty minutes later, we found illegal trapping nets, and I realised again that it was all worthwhile. How important is cooperation between international organisations, local teams and security forces to achieving real results against illegal hunting? Cooperation with the police is essential. Without it, we do not have a real chance of tackling poaching. The same applies to cooperation within the team between Lebanese and international members. CABS brings decades of experience and expertise in combating poaching, which is essential to working effectively. But the Lebanese part of the team is equally important: its members understand local conditions and work on the ground all year round. Only by working together can we achieve real results. If you could specialise more deeply in one area of combating poaching, what would it be, and why? Combating poaching is not just about birds; it covers other groups of animals too. I already work in a very specialised field: the illegal killing of birds, particularly birds of prey. I do not think further specialisation would be useful, because having varied skills also gives us many advantages in this work. Alexandra during an activity in Austria.Photo: BirdLife Away from work, what are your hobbies and interests? Which activities best reflect your personality? I have played volleyball since I was nine. I love spending time in nature, whether hiking, gathering mushrooms or watching birds. I also really enjoy growing my own vegetables. Some people think combating illegal hunting means opposing hunters. How do you explain the distinction between a responsible hunter and illegal hunting? First, the key issue is the law: that is the main distinction. A responsible hunter hunts within the law and respects hunting seasons, protected species and permitted quotas. Illegal hunting means ignoring all of that: shooting protected species, hunting during closed seasons and using prohibited methods. Our fight is not against hunters themselves, but against people who break the law and threaten wildlife. After your experience in Lebanon, what message would you like to give hunters, young people and everyone interested in protecting birds and nature? Bird migration is one of nature’s greatest wonders, and Lebanon lies at the heart of that route. I would ask hunters to see these birds not as targets, but as precious living beings crossing their skies. To young people, I say: go outside, look up at the sky and help protect nature. The more people know and love these birds, the better their chances of surviving and completing their journey. Related reporting

articles.title: From the Atlas Foothills to the Red Sea Coast… The Arab Hunting Season Enters Autumn 2026
articles.body: A group of hunters and their dogs advancing on a dirt track through Atlas scrub — a Maghreb field scene from Morocco’s foothills.حجل أطلس / Hajal Atlas Guns return to some open country and stay silent in others… Nine Arab states meet the autumn migration with nine different hunting maps With the first shift in the late-summer air, a scene every Arab hunter knows begins to form. From the Atlas foothills in Morocco and Algeria, through Tunisia’s woodlands, Libya’s coasts, and Egypt’s marshes, then along the great eastern flyway through Lebanon, Syria, and Jordan, out to the deserts of Saudi Arabia and the Red Sea shore, birds move south—and with them moves the memory of a whole season of waiting. This is migration autumn. It is not, necessarily, hunting autumn everywhere. As October 2026 begins, the Arab hunting map looks like a mosaic of systems, dates, and limits: Saudi Arabia entered its season at the start of September; Jordan opened defined seasons for named species; Morocco and Tunisia opened their seasons on 4 October, while Algeria set 10 October as the official opening date under each wilaya’s approved hunting plan; in Lebanon, wild hunting remains closed because no official open-season decision has been issued. And in Libya, autumn itself brought the opposite kind of decree in parts of the southeast: protect migrants and ban hunting them. So the journey from the Atlas to the Red Sea is not only a journey between countries. It is a journey between wholly different ways of handling hunting, migration, and wildlife. Morocco: the first Sunday in October returns hunters to the field On the Atlas slopes, among forests and plains that shaped one of North Africa’s deepest hunting cultures, the season has begun. Morocco’s 2026–2027 hunting season opened nationwide on Sunday, 4 October 2026, the date set by the Higher Council for Hunting. The decision followed an assessment of the 2025–2026 season and the state of the national game stock, within a policy that ties continued hunting to managing species and habitats. According to the National Agency for Water and Forests (ANEF) report published on 6 October, the first day’s national average bag was 1.91 partridges per hunter, with reinforced monitoring, awareness and guidance across hunting areas. Morocco is not a small hunting market. Last season, more than 65,000 hunters practised in open and leased domains, plus about five thousand in tourist hunting. That figure explains part of the scene that returns with every opening: hunting associations, hounds, partridge, leased and prepared land, and a standing tourist-hunting sector that receives shooters from abroad. But 4 October does not make every bird fair game. The annual decision sets species, periods, and bags; turtle dove stays outside the general opening and keeps its own seasonal calendar. From here the journey turns east. Hunter and pointing dog in Atlas scrub — shotgun on the shoulder, cartridge belt, mountain woodland.حجل أطلس / Hajal Atlas Algeria: a national opening on 10 October, implementation under each wilaya’s plan The Directorate General of Forests announced the official opening of the 2026–2027 hunting season from Saturday, 10 October 2026, under each wilaya’s approved hunting plan, in a statement reported by the Algerian Press Service (APS) on 30 September. The statement requires compliance with the hunting areas defined in the plan, excluding fire-affected areas, and with the permitted species, hunting periods and quotas. For the hunter, knowing the national opening date is not enough; the questions remain: In which wilaya? For which quarry? Within which areas, periods and quotas? From northern forests to the high plateaus, the local decision becomes part of the hunter’s kit—alongside gun and dog. That a species may be hunted in one place does not make it lawful somewhere else. Tunisia: also 4 October… but on a densely detailed calendar Across the Algerian border, the picture is clearer. Tunisia’s Ministry of Agriculture, Water Resources and Fisheries issued its decision regulating the 2026–2027 season, published in the Official Gazette. On 4 October 2026, hunting of hare, partridge, resident quail, rock dove, and sandgrouse (“kudra”) opened and runs to 6 December, limited to Sundays, public holidays, and official leave days. Waterbirds keep another clock. Woodpigeon and a wide set of waterfowl do not open until 22 November 2026, running to 28 March 2027. The list includes ducks, teal, geese, coot and others, with special rules for waterbird hunting on “the pass.” This detail states a principle that repeats across the Arab map: migration does not open the season; the legal decision does. The sky may fill with birds long before the law allows a single shot. Migration is not a hunting permit A sky full of birds does not make a shot legal. A season opens by official decision—species, place, time, bag—not by the migration calendar alone. Two hunters on a Moroccan slope aiming shotguns amid green brush under a clear sky.حجل أطلس / Hajal Atlas Libya: autumn arrives this time with a protection order Farther east, the scene grows more complex. In Libya—where desert, wetlands, and coastal corridors form parts of the Europe–Africa flyways—September 2026 brought news unlike the usual season openings. On 20 September, the Libyan Authority for Heritage and Wildlife announced a ban on hunting migratory birds in several southeastern areas after declines in numbers and hunting practices described as wrongful and abusive. The measure covered Jalu, Awjila and Jikhra (Ijkhira) and other zones out to Tazirbu and Kufra, protecting the natural corridors linked to them, for two consecutive migration seasons (passage and return). So while Moroccan and Tunisian hunters returned to the field on 4 October, a hunter in parts of Libya faces a different sign: birds pass here, but passage is not permission. It is one of the sharpest paradoxes of the Arab 2026 season. Egypt: when quail reach the coast Then the road reaches Egypt. Here autumn is visible on the Mediterranean shore, in the Delta, and on the northern lakes. Quail, garganey and other migratory birds make Egypt one of the known stops on the Eurasia–Africa flyway. In September 2026, the 2026–2027 bird-hunting season had already opened within the legal hunting frame—including wild quail, garganey, and other species expressly authorized under the governing ministerial decree. Turtle dove is not listed here among the expressly authorized species. The message that accompanied the start was plain: opening the season is not opening hunting without limits. Some species are allowed, others protected; practice is regulated; the stated aim is to keep hunting possible without turning the yearly migration into depletion. Egypt especially shows how hard that balance is. Its position makes it a vast geographic bridge for migrants—from the Mediterranean coast and Lake Bardawil to the Delta, Fayoum, and beyond. Here the line between the lawful hunter and random shooting is more than wording; it is the difference between a season that can return and a resource that can vanish. Lebanon: the birds arrived… but the season did not open A Lebanese hunter with a shotgun on a mountain ridge under the autumn sky. From Egypt to the eastern Mediterranean, we reach the most sensitive case. Lebanon sits on one of the region’s major bird-migration corridors. In autumn large numbers of migrants cross its skies. But as of 29 September 2026, no official decision has opened the 2026–2027 wild-hunting season. Wild hunting therefore remains prohibited until the legal decision that opens the season is issued. This is not theory. On 14 September the Internal Security Forces announced the arrest of three people in Danniyeh as part of efforts against abusive wild hunting and for protecting migratory birds. Lebanon’s terrestrial hunting law No. 580 of 2004 provides that opening and closing the season, and the quarry list, fall to the Minister of Environment on a proposal from the Higher Council for Hunting; the season does not open automatically with the arrival of autumn. So a Lebanese hunter may see autumn flocks over mountains and valleys, yet quarry overhead does not make a season. The law does. Syria: birds return before the regulatory picture is complete Northward, migrants cross Syrian land—from the coast to inland plains and wetlands. Scattered field reports point to ongoing terrestrial hunting in some areas, alongside crackdowns on illegal hunting elsewhere, without that translating into a clear published national calendar for autumn 2026–2027. As of late September 2026, the published regulatory picture remains incomplete: no recent, reliable central decision has set a national Syrian calendar for autumn 2026–2027 with the clarity available for Morocco, Tunisia, or Saudi Arabia. Hunting on the ground is one thing; a published legal season with limits, species, and dates is another. What has not been published officially stays outside the confirmed calendar map. Jordan: ten birds per outing… and partridge stays closed In Jordan the precise numbers return. On 18 September 2026 an autumn season opened for defined pigeon species, running to 29 November, on Fridays and Sundays only, in permitted areas west of the Hejaz railway. The Wildlife Protection Committee set a ceiling of 10 pigeons of the allowed species per licensed hunter per outing, excluding the European turtle dove (Streptopelia turtur), known locally as al-hamam al-raqti, according to Jordanian reporting of the RSCN announcement on 17 September. Most important: opening pigeons did not become a general open season. The committee kept partridge and sand partridge closed. Call devices and nets are banned, night hunting is banned, and a licence plus compliance with permitted zones are required. Jordan: open by species, not by blank season Pigeons: 18 Sep–29 Nov · Fri & Sun · west of Hejaz railway · max 10/outing (European turtle dove excluded). Partridge & sand partridge closed. ʿUṣfūr al-tīn & al-farr: 15 Aug–31 Oct · 15 each/outing. Callers, nets, night hunting banned. Jordan had also opened an autumn season for the birds known locally as ʿuṣfūr al-tīn (Eurasian blackcap, Sylvia atricapilla—«fig sparrow» in Levant hunting speech) and al-farr (local name; scientific identity not locked in official English wording) from 15 August through 31 October 2026, at 15 birds of each species per licensed hunter per outing in defined areas. It is a model of opening by species, period, bag, and place—not an unbounded “season is open.” Saudi Arabia: from 1 September… a sixth season into midwinter At the eastern end of the journey, the map reaches the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. Here the season began ahead of most countries we have passed. The National Center for Wildlife Development officially announced the sustainable hunting season 2026–2027 starting 1 September 2026 and running to 31 January 2027. The present season is the sixth since the regulatory experiment began in 2021. Permitted species rose to 30, with the national bag up 11% and licences up 34%, according to the Center. In the autumn window, from September through the end of November, the list includes species such as common quail, common partridge, sand partridge, and a range of pigeons, doves, and sandgrouse, among others; some species are taken with falcons. But the Saudi picture differs sharply from the classic Arab image of a hunter with a shotgun. The current system allows licensed non-powder hunting guns powered by gas or spring pressure, plus falconry under its rules, and bans pellet guns, nets, and unauthorised attraction or calling devices. The hunter also needs a permit through the “Fitri” platform. The spatial limit is striking too: hunting is barred inside reserves, major projects, populated areas and other defined zones, and along the Kingdom’s coasts to a depth of 20 kilometres inland. Saudi: “Fitri” permit + 20 km coastal ban Sixth season (1 Sep 2026–31 Jan 2027) · 30 species · via Fitri. Licensed non-powder guns (gas/spring) + falconry under rules; pellet guns, nets, unauthorised callers banned. No hunting in reserves, populated zones, or along coasts 20 km inland. Here, at the Red Sea, the journey ends. One sky… nine different seasons From the Atlas to the Red Sea, birds do not know the borders people drew. The quail leaving the northern Mediterranean carries no passport. Pigeons, ducks, and passage birds do not know whether the sky below is Moroccan, Tunisian, Egyptian, or Jordanian. But the hunter knows—or must. Autumn 2026 shows a clear shift in what an “Arab season” means. The question is no longer only “Has hunting started?” but what may be taken, where, when, by what means, and in what number. Morocco and Tunisia opened their seasons on 4 October. Saudi Arabia entered on 1 September under a system of licences, bags, and species. Jordan opened some species and closed others. Egypt met migration season within legally regulated hunting. Algeria set Saturday, 10 October as the official opening date, with implementation governed by each wilaya’s approved hunting plan. In parts of Libya, the season arrived as protection and prohibition. In Lebanon, through the end of September, the season had not opened at all. As for Syria, the published regulatory picture remains less clear as of late September, with no confirmed national calendar in the available official sources. Nine countries, then—and nine hunting maps under one autumn sky. Perhaps the most important change a hunter should read in 2026–2027 is this: the survival of hunting no longer hinges only on quarry being present, but on hunters and authorities together keeping that quarry present for the season after. A lawful shot is not merely a shot fired inside the season dates. It is a shot that knows species, bag, place, and time. From Morocco’s Atlas foothills to Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea approaches, the future of Arab hunting looks set to be decided at those four edges.
articles.excerpt: Nine Arab hunting maps for autumn 2026: Morocco and Tunisia open 4 October; Saudi season since 1 September; Jordan by bags; Lebanon still closed; Libya protection order.

articles.title: Arabian Saluki Center marks 25 years of preserving the falconer’s companion
articles.body: The Arabian Saluki Center building in Abu Dhabi. Founded in Abu Dhabi in 2001, the center combines Saluki care and training with the preservation of native Arabian bloodlines. Abu Dhabi’s Arabian Saluki Center is marking its 25th anniversary in 2026. Established in 2001 as a project of the Emirates Falconers’ Club, it has combined the preservation of hunting heritage with the development of care, training and native Arabian bloodline conservation. Over a quarter of a century, its work has expanded from boarding and daily care to breeding programs, bloodline documentation and veterinary services, alongside guidance for breeders and owners on care and responsible ownership. Training is a central part of this work. According to the club’s report, the center has running areas attached to its kennels and an outdoor training ground covering more than 1,000 square meters. Its programs include fitness, swimming, behavior, obedience and sprint racing, as well as preparation for shows and beauty competitions. One milestone has been its organization of the Arabian Saluki Beauty Contest at the Abu Dhabi International Hunting and Equestrian Exhibition since 2004. These activities continue with the 2026–2027 Arabian Saluki Championship in Al Ain and Al Dhafra, with competition expected to begin this November. The center also provides veterinary examinations and consultations, vaccinations and microchipping, together with travel and transport guidance. These practical services connect the preservation of the falconer’s companion with the needs of breeders and dogs today. Source: Emirates Falconers’ Club. articles.title: Arabian Saluki Championship starts in November with three distances and five season titles
articles.body: Salukis racing on a sandy track; a photograph supplied with the club’s press material. The Emirates Falconers’ Club and Abu Dhabi’s Arabian Saluki Centre will hold the inaugural season in Al Ain and Al Dhafra from November 2026 to April 2027. The Emirates Falconers’ Club and the Arabian Saluki Centre in Abu Dhabi will organise the first Arabian Saluki Championship in Al Ain and Al Dhafra from November 2026 to April 2027, aiming to develop this heritage sport and preserve its ties to hunting culture and desert life. The championship brings together speed, distance and endurance races in a season built around registration, classification and cumulative points. Handlers with Salukis in a photograph supplied with the club’s press material. Three distances for males and females Competitions comprise 1,000-metre sprints, 1,500-metre middle-distance races and 2,000-metre endurance races, with male and female categories. The season includes preliminary rounds, semi-finals and finals, with points accumulated across rounds to determine the category champions. Five seasonal titles will be awarded: Speed Champion, Distance Champion, Endurance Champion, Arabian Saluki Champion and Best Breeder. The programme also includes cash prizes, an Arabian Saluki beauty competition, or mazayen, and a simulated hunting competition using a mechanical lure. A registry of bloodlines, owners and breeders The club says the championship will establish the first official Arabian Saluki registry in the UAE and the Gulf region, documenting bloodlines, owners and breeders and issuing annual registration and classification certificates. The system will allow each Saluki’s performance to be tracked and assessed throughout the season rather than through a single race result. The organisers’ vision also includes a scientific database to study genetic and physical capabilities, programmes to improve bloodlines, training and assessment, and broader participation by owners, breeders and enthusiasts. Source: Emirates Falconers’ Club. Photographs: Emirates Falconers’ Club.
articles.excerpt: The Emirates Falconers’ Club and Abu Dhabi’s Arabian Saluki Centre will hold the inaugural season in Al Ain and Al Dhafra from November 2026 to April 2027.

articles.title: Asian Houbara — Chlamydotis macqueenii
articles.body: Asian houbaraPhoto: Kudaibergen Amirekul — Wikimedia Commons — CC BY-SA 4.0. Asian houbara (MacQueen’s bustard) — Chlamydotis macqueenii Range: A sleek desert bird of the bustard family. Its range runs from east of Sinai across Iran and Central Asia to the Gobi Desert in Mongolia; northern populations are partial migrants wintering south toward Pakistan, western India, and parts of the Arabian Peninsula. In the Levant it was historically wider in dry steppe; today it is rare or only a vagrant in the Lebanese context compared with soaring migrants. This entry locks Chlamydotis macqueenii only. The African houbara Chlamydotis undulata—North Africa and the Canary Islands—is a separate species elevated in 2003, paler, with different crest feathers in display and a Maghrebi range, not Asian–Levantine; it must not be mixed with the species treated here. Life cycle and habitat: The male performs a striking visual display: inflating neck feathers and folding the head into a “ruff,” then running in lines or circles around shrubs. Mating is polygynous on the male’s side; the female alone tends the nest. She usually lays 2–4 eggs in an open scrape; incubation lasts about 23 days. Precocial chicks follow the mother. It prefers arid desert and steppe with sparse shrub cover; the diet mixes seeds, berries, and insects, and it can forgo free water when food moisture suffices. Lifestyle: Wary, relying on camouflage and crouching low when approached. When pursued it rises and spirals upward. Sensitive to nesting disturbance by people and livestock. Migration routes avoid the highest mountain chains, as satellite tracking has shown; breeding timing links to local temperatures that trigger spring departure. Asian houbaraPhoto: Harsha Jayaramaiah — Wikimedia Commons — CC BY-SA 4.0. Hunting status: Across Arab countries, Asian houbara is generally protected and hunting is tightly restricted; the species is globally threatened. In Lebanon, Wild Hunting Law No. 580/2004 limits hunting to quarry species set by the minister; everything else is protected year-round; houbara is not among the permitted quarry in the absence of a current open-season decision. Documented exceptions only within licensed falconry frameworks: in Qatar, Ministerial Decision No. 7 of 2026 lists houbara among species that may be taken with falcons only during a set period (1 September 2026 – 15 February 2027), and bans call-playback devices (Ministry of Environment and Climate Change via Qatar News Agency). In Abu Dhabi, within licensed traditional falconry under Executive Council Decision 5/2021 and Environment Agency – Abu Dhabi notices, houbara may be taken by licensed falconers in defined seasons—without implying that all hunting pathways in the emirate are limited to houbara alone. Conservation status: Globally Vulnerable (VU) with the International Union for Conservation of Nature (BirdLife assessment 2021), owing to declines tied to hunting and habitat degradation. Listed on CITES Appendix I and CMS Appendix II. Captive-breeding and release programs form part of the conservation response across parts of the range. Traits: The male’s display is documented courtship, not invented folklore: neck plumes folded over the head, measured pacing, and a soft breathing sound audible only at close range. Doing without free water is a true desert adaptation. An icon of falconry heritage and of conservation duty alike.

articles.title: As Autumn Migration Begins… Field Action to Protect Bird Flyways over Lebanon
articles.body: Photo: Fouad Itani As Lebanon enters the autumn bird migration season, the Middle East Center for Sustainable Hunting and Anti-Poaching (MECSHAP) is intensifying its field efforts through the Anti-Poaching Unit (APU) and a network of sustainable hunters and collaborators, to monitor violations and help protect migratory birds as they cross Lebanese territory. This action takes on special importance given Lebanon’s location on one of the foremost bird migration flyways between Europe, Asia, and Africa. Autumn migration usually begins in late August and extends to mid-November, with dense movement of birds heading south toward the African continent. Work during the season focuses on following sensitive points along migration lines, monitoring, documenting, and reporting cases of illegal hunting, alongside coordination with the competent security and judicial agencies and cooperation with local and international bodies concerned with bird protection and anti-poaching. This approach stems from a vision that sees the responsible hunter as a partner in protecting nature and the sustainability of hunting, not an adversary to them. That vision has accompanied the center’s path since it grew from within the sustainable hunters’ community, and developed with the launch of the Anti-Poaching Unit in 2018 as a specialized field arm for monitoring, documentation, and intervention, in cooperation with official institutions and specialized partners. The unit has continued its field operations during the current year. In June 2026, members of the Anti-Poaching Unit and CABS carried out a joint patrol in the Baalbek–Hermel area, during which protected wild birds that had been held were received and returned to their natural habitats after their legal status was clarified. (Details of the joint APU and CABS operation in Baalbek–Hermel — linked on the AR page.) Protection efforts give special importance to birds of prey, protected and threatened species, and large birds that cross Lebanon during migration. Documented incidents during last spring’s migration again highlighted the risks these birds face, including the death of a large pelican after it was shot on Amchit beach while passing within a migrating flock. (Incident of the migrating pelican on Amchit beach — linked on the AR page.) The importance of protecting these birds is not limited to Lebanon alone. Birds that cross its skies link, on their journey, multiple continents and countries, making the safety of migration flyways a responsibility beyond local borders, and placing cooperation among sustainable hunters, official bodies, local communities, and specialized organizations at the heart of any effective protection of biodiversity. With the launch of autumn migration 2026, Sayd opens with this follow-up the first files of the new season—to track bird movement over Lebanon, the risks and violations they face, and protection and monitoring efforts—in parallel with following the file of regulating the hunting season and the role of the responsible hunter in protecting the sustainability of their hobby and the nature in which they practice it. Lebanon is a corridor for migratory birds… and protecting that corridor is a shared responsibility.

articles.title: With Autumn Migration… How Does the World Protect Birds and Regulate Hunting?
articles.body: Prepared by Sayd | 8 September 2026 Birds that cross the sky carry a story longer than the distance we see. Behind every journey are breeding areas, rest and feeding stops, and places where they spend the winter. What happens at one of those stops can affect an entire journey spanning countries and continents. With the autumn migration season, recent international news and reports offer a picture of the challenges these journeys face, and of the tools used to protect them: scientific research, habitat conservation, hunting regulation, and people’s participation in monitoring. More than half of migratory species are declining On 28 July, the British Trust for Ornithology (BTO) presented results of a global review published in the journal Nature Reviews Biodiversity, with researchers from international institutions including Georgetown University and the Smithsonian Institution. The review finds that 51% of migratory bird species worldwide are declining in numbers. That percentage concerns species that are declining; it does not mean half of all bird numbers have disappeared. Pressures include habitat loss, climate change and extreme weather, pesticides, disease, and collisions with buildings and structures. Researchers therefore call for protection that takes account of the bird’s full life cycle and links efforts among the countries it crosses. Source: BTO and the scientific review; results presented 28 July. In Albania… flamingos at the heart of an environmental case Little Egret over Narta Lagoon, Albania — archival photo, 2015.Photo: Pasztilla (Attila Terbócs) / Wikimedia Commons — CC BY-SA 4.0. The image is for site identification and does not document current development works. In a report published by BirdLife International on 7 September, attention returned to protests protecting the Vjosa–Narta area in Albania, after a hundred days of actions known as the “flamingo protests.” According to the organization, the coastal area hosts more than two hundred bird species and lies on a migration route between Africa and Europe. The protests concern works and development projects inside a protected area and the risks they pose to wetlands. BirdLife says the channel linking Narta Lagoon to the sea was closed during the works and then reopened, warning of the effect of disrupting water flow on the lagoon’s balance and birds’ food. The case reveals a basic side of protection: the bird needs a place fit for life when it lands. Source: BirdLife, 7 September 2026. From Croatia to Egypt… interconnected stopovers Ferruginous Duck in Aswan, Egypt — archival photo, 2010. terolinjama / iNaturalist, via Wikimedia Commons — CC0. In a piece published on 26 August, BirdLife chose the Ferruginous Duck (English name as given in the source) to illustrate the importance of connectivity among migration stopovers. It notes that the species is classified as Near Threatened, and that its survival depends on the integrity of wetlands separated by vast distances. The piece highlights the Pokuplje basin in Croatia and Lake Nasser in Egypt as important sites for this species and other waterbirds. It also presents a three-year initiative, supported by a grant of £7.5 million, to protect and restore sites on the African–Eurasian flyway. The lesson of this journey is that protecting one site gains greater value when connected to protecting the other sites the bird needs. Source: BirdLife, 26 August 2026. Regulated hunting… quotas monitored and decisions reviewed On the hunting file, the European Federation for Hunting and Conservation (FACE), which represents hunters’ associations, published its 2026 report on the European Turtle Dove on 18 July. The federation presents the experience of adaptive harvest management: setting quotas, recording birds taken, tracking when the allowed ceiling is reached, and closing the season when it is reached. According to its assessment, turtle dove numbers continue to rise on the western flyway, while the situation remains less positive on the central–eastern flyway. These are results presented by a hunters’ federation and should be read in their specific context; they do not mean every bird species has recovered, nor do they provide a basis for generalizing hunting to other regions. But they put a practical question before the debate: how do we link permission to hunt to data on bird numbers and their capacity to recover, and to a real capacity to monitor? Source: FACE, July 2026 report. What do we take away at Sayd? These developments push us to see the season as an epistemic responsibility as well. Correct species identification, documenting sightings, protecting rest places, and respecting the law are elements that can bring together the responsible hunter, the birdwatcher, the photographer, and the researcher. In our view, success in managing the season is measured by the clarity of its rules, the quality of its information, the effectiveness of their application, and by birds remaining able to continue their journey and return in coming years.

articles.title: The Barn Owl
articles.body: Barn Owl (Tyto alba). The Barn Owl (Tyto alba) — also called the barn or loft owl — is a common resident breeder across Lebanon’s coast, mountains, and Beqaa Plain: a silent nocturnal hunter of rodents, and a species still threatened by habitat loss, pesticides, and illegal killing. The Barn Owl — also known as the loft or barn owl, and in English as the barn owl (Tyto alba) — is a common resident and breeder in Lebanon, found on the coast, in the mountains, and across the Beqaa Plain. It can adapt to a wide range of habitats, from farmland and pastures to forests and residential areas. Let us get to know it better… The Barn Owl is a pale, medium-sized owl with a distinctive heart-shaped face and dark eyes, lacking the barring and streaks found in many other owls. The upperparts are creamy grey; the underparts are white, sometimes yellowish. In flight it shows slender wings and body, with white underwings. Its heart-shaped facial discs help funnel sound to its ears. This unique facial feature lets it locate prey in total darkness by relying on acute hearing. Uneven ear openings allow it to pinpoint the direction of sound with remarkable precision — including prey under vegetation or snow. The Barn Owl is an exceptional nocturnal hunter that primarily takes small mammals such as mice and voles in complete silence. Specialised wing feathers reduce turbulence, allowing it to approach prey without the usual whistling sound associated with flying birds. It earned its name because it often roosts and nests in barns, abandoned buildings, and tree cavities. It does not build nests; instead it lays eggs on a bed of regurgitated pellets and prey remains. Barn Owls regurgitate indigestible parts of their prey — bones and fur — as pellets. Scientists often use these pellets to study the owl’s diet and the local ecosystem. For centuries the Barn Owl has been part of human folklore and symbolism. In some cultures it is seen as a symbol of wisdom and protection; in others it is linked to omens, superstition, and bad luck. Despite its adaptability and wide distribution, Barn Owl populations face threats including habitat loss, pesticides, and illegal hunting. Barn Owls are truly remarkable creatures that capture the imagination with their unique adaptations and mysterious behaviour — of lasting interest to bird enthusiasts and researchers alike. articles.title: Barn Swallow in the Arab world: autumn wings between passage and residency
articles.body: Barn Swallow Birds skim a field, turn sharply above a pond and rise towards a wire where others are gathering. In autumn, Barn Swallows seem to draw a line between villages, water and distant skies. Yet the scene does not mean that every swallow in the Arab world is passing through: the species includes local breeders, passage migrants, winter visitors and resident populations. Identification card Arabic names: السنونو الشائع; خطاف الحظائر English name: Barn Swallow French name: Hirondelle rustique Scientific name: Hirundo rustica Family: Hirundinidae Length: approximately 17–19 cm, with variation in the outer tail streamers Habitat: fields, pasture and open country near water and buildings Arab-world occurrence: breeding, passage and winter occurrence vary; Egypt has a resident population Global conservation status: Least Concern (LC) One species, different seasonal lives Across the Maghreb, swallows pass through open landscapes and wetlands, and breed locally in parts of the region. Research on Morocco's Ma'amora bird community documents Barn Swallow as both a breeding summer visitor and passage migrant. An agricultural landscape can be more than a stopover: it may also be where birds begin life before joining a later journey. In the Levant, Lebanon's checklist records breeding, widespread passage and less frequent winter occurrence. The OSME regional list identifies breeding populations of the subspecies transitiva in the Levant and the resident Egyptian savignii. A winter swallow in Egypt should therefore not automatically be described as a European bird that migrated late. In Arabia, seasonal passage is prominent, with documented winter occurrence in Oman and rare breeding recorded at some Arabian sites. Saudi observations identify September–October and March–May as clear passage periods. These situations differ between countries and sites: scarce nesting in one area does not mean that the species breeds nowhere in the Arab world. Autumn has more than one timetable The Eurasian-African Migration Atlas describes Middle Eastern autumn passage from late August to early November, peaking in early October. This summarises studied populations rather than setting a timetable for every village flock. African winter destinations also differ with breeding origin: not all birds follow the same route or finish in the same place. Birds may gather on wires or at roosts before dispersing above fields and water. Recording group size, observation time, direction and feeding behaviour is more useful than assuming that every flock is a new migration wave. European roost studies show that these gatherings also form part of the period when birds build energy reserves before travelling. Reading a bird in flight Long pointed wings, a forked tail, glossy dark-blue upperparts in suitable light, and a rusty forehead and throat are helpful features. The rump stays dark, useful when comparing it with white-rumped martins. But light and distance change the impression: throat and back colours can disappear, leaving an apparently dark bird. Juveniles are less glossy, with paler throats and shorter outer tail feathers. Females tend to have shorter streamers than males, but overlap prevents confident sexing from every photograph. A short tail alone is insufficient for identification or ageing: consider wing shape, face, rump and tail together. Underpart colour also varies geographically, from pale to warm or rusty, with reddish tones prominent in some eastern Mediterranean and Egyptian populations. Belly colour alone should not establish sex, and a photograph from another continent should not be treated as a template for every regional bird. Insects in the air, mud in the nest Barn Swallows catch insects in flight above fields, pasture and water. Their use of insect-rich places makes habitat quality important: a large agricultural area is not necessarily a good feeding area if prey is scarce. The nest is an open mud cup in a sheltered position, often inside or beneath an accessible building. BTO data give a typical clutch of four to five eggs, incubated mainly by the female. Timing depends on population and climate; a European calendar does not establish the nesting season in Egypt or the Levant. Where a nest is occupied, leave entrances and access space undisturbed. Protecting a familiar neighbour Least Concern is a global category, not a statement that all populations are stable. Monitoring programmes document declines in parts of the range, while habitat change, insect availability and nest sites are important conservation issues. A decline measured in Europe or North America cannot be assigned to an Arab country without local data. Watch flocks from a distance and do not approach a roost to force birds into flight for a photograph. Leave occupied nests in peace and avoid blocking entrances while birds are present. Hunting and protection rules should be checked locally with the competent authority. Giving swallows room to feed, continue their journey or return to a nest is a practical way to preserve this shared landscape. articles.title: Birds in Bags… From an Akkar Sparrowhawk to Forged Trafficking Papers
articles.body: A sparrowhawk inside a backpack during an anti-poaching operation in Akkar, October 2026. In the highlands of Akkar, a backpack held an unexpected cargo: a sparrowhawk. One of two men detained by security forces was carrying the bird inside his bag during a field operation against the hunting of birds of prey, announced by the Committee Against Bird Slaughter, CABS, on 6 October 2026. The incident took place in a mountainous area of Akkar, following surveillance by CABS in cooperation with the Middle East Centre for Sustainable Hunting and Anti-Poaching, MECSHAP, and the security forces. According to the organisation, both men were taken to the police station, their weapons were confiscated and legal proceedings were initiated against them. The backpack is the detail that stays with the reader: a bird of prey, whose domain should be the sky, concealed among belongings carried on someone’s back. The published information does not establish that the Akkar incident was part of cross-border trade. It does, however, open a window onto other, separate cases in which concealing a bird is the beginning of the story, followed by an attempt to conceal its origins. In Spain… A Backpack Becomes Part of a Court Case On 14 October, SEO/BirdLife announced that it had joined criminal proceedings as a private prosecutor before Investigating Court No. 11 in Málaga, in the case arising from Operation Bétula. The investigation concerns suspected theft of raptor chicks from their nests, trafficking and forged documentation. Its participation marks a new legal development in a case whose underlying events took place months earlier. The operation was announced on 20 July 2026. According to the published account, two sparrowhawk chicks without identification rings were found inside a backpack in a car near Alhaurín el Grande, together with ten metal rings. The investigation examined whether wild-caught birds were being presented as captive-bred. Here, the backpack is no longer the only object under scrutiny. A ring attached to a bird’s leg and the document accompanying it are supposed to help establish its identity and origin. If they are used to misrepresent that origin, the appearance of legality itself becomes part of the case. The inquiry included checks on documents associated with CITES, the convention regulating international trade in endangered species, and the collection of samples for genetic tests to verify parentage. Collecting samples does not mean that test results have been issued, just as an investigation is not a conviction. There was another chapter in the two chicks’ story: coverage of the operation reported that the Guardia Civil’s mountain rescue team returned them to their nest. Questions about the origins of other birds and their accompanying documents remained before investigators. Goldfinches Bound for Oran About a month before the legal development in Málaga, a different case emerged at the Spanish port of Alicante. On 11 September 2026, details were published of the seizure of 1,500 goldfinches inside a car preparing to board a ferry to Oran, Algeria. According to information attributed to the Guardia Civil, the birds were packed into thirty boxes in severely overcrowded conditions, without the required documents. That large number conceals a loss that matters just as much: the reports said that 90 birds were found dead, another 90 needed care and 1,320 were released. Ninety goldfinches had paid the price before the sea crossing even began. In Akkar, a bird inside a backpack; in Alicante, hundreds of birds inside a car. The circumstances and numbers differ, but turning a living creature into concealed cargo puts it at risk before it reaches any market. Another Bag at Baghdad Airport Earlier in the year, on 2 January 2026, Video News Agency carried a statement from Iraq’s General Customs Authority about a live falcon discovered concealed in an Iraqi passenger’s bag at Baghdad International Airport’s Babylon arrivals hall. The passenger had arrived from the United Arab Emirates. The report referred to a single falcon and did not identify its species. That detail was absent from the information released about the seizure. These sources provide no evidence that the three cases were the work of a single network. What links them in this account is the method of concealment, and the questions each raises about the bird’s origins, its papers and the legality of possessing or transporting it. Earlier Cases Along the Same Route Goldfinch seizures are not new to Alicante’s port. SEO/BirdLife has cited the seizure of 83 goldfinches there in June 2025, also bound for Algeria. Earlier still, in 2022, around 2,400 goldfinches intended to be smuggled to Algeria were seized in Oujda, Morocco, according to the organisation’s account. These older incidents help explain why goldfinches recur in discussions of trade across the Mediterranean and within North Africa, without making every seizure evidence of an organised connection to those that preceded it. Tunisia: Seeking a Response Across Borders Against this backdrop, Tunisia is hosting an international meeting from 16 to 18 October 2026 to combat the illegal hunting, capture and trade of wild birds. According to an announcement by the Association Les Amis des Oiseaux, reported by Tunisian National Radio, the meeting brings together ten partners from eight Mediterranean countries. The programme focuses on sharing experience and improving monitoring, documentation and cooperation, particularly between North Africa and the Balkans. The Association Les Amis des Oiseaux and its partners are involved in organising the meeting, alongside institutions working to protect birds and natural habitats. The meeting’s importance becomes clear when these cases are considered together: field surveillance stops an offence, an inspection prevents a shipment from leaving, and an investigation looks beyond a ring or a document. Each step has a role, but protecting a bird does not end when it is taken out of a bag. A backpack may be opened in Akkar, a car at a Spanish port or luggage at Baghdad airport. The question remains open: when will bird smuggling and the illegal trade in birds end? Sources: CABS · SEO/BirdLife · Bétula · Málaga Hoy · Diario de Alicante · SEO/BirdLife · 1,500 · Video News Agency · Radio Nationale Tunisienne. Photo: Anti-Poaching Unit (APU).

articles.title: Black Redstart in the Arab world between local residence and autumn migration
articles.body: Black Redstart A rusty tail quivers above a rock or old wall, followed by a short flight to the ground and a return to the perch. This movement may draw attention to a Black Redstart before its colours become clear. Its Arab-world distribution stretches from Morocco to the Levant and the Arabian Peninsula, but its relationship with these regions varies: some populations breed locally, while others pass through or spend the winter away from their nesting areas. Species profile Arabic names: الحميراء السوداء; also الحميراء الدبساء English name: Black Redstart French name: Rougequeue noir Scientific name: Phoenicurus ochruros Family: Old World flycatchers and chats, Muscicapidae Length: approximately 14–15 cm Range: extensive parts of Europe, Asia and North Africa, with geographically and seasonally varied occurrence in the Arab world Main Arab examples: Morocco, the Levant, Egypt and countries of the Gulf and Arabian Peninsula Residency and migration: resident breeder in some areas; passage migrant or winter visitor in others Global conservation status: Least Concern (LC) Legal status: determined by the country and its applicable rules and decisions; global conservation status does not confer hunting permission From Morocco to the Arabian Peninsula Morocco supports local breeding populations of Black Redstart, with some mountain birds moving to lower elevations in winter. Morocco and Algeria also receive birds from Europe. Local birds may therefore occur alongside migrants in the same season; seeing this species in winter does not mean that every individual has travelled from a distant country. In the eastern Arab region, the picture differs between countries and among populations within a country. Lebanon's bird guide records resident breeders alongside passage migrants and winter visitors. Syria also has resident and passage populations, whereas passage and non-breeding occurrence are prominent in Jordan. Migrants also reach Egypt. On the Arabian Peninsula, passage and winter occurrence are especially clear in examples such as Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. The species has the same recorded status in King Salman bin Abdulaziz Royal Nature Reserve in northern Saudi Arabia, while Oman is included in its passage and non-breeding range. What autumn means for this bird Autumn can bring two overlapping movements: arrivals from breeding areas and the descent of some local mountain birds. European ringing data show movement towards wintering grounds beginning in September, with arrivals continuing through October and November. This describes the studied populations; it is not one arrival calendar for the whole Arab world. A local comparison illustrates the difference. Lebanon's usual autumn passage runs from mid-October to early December. In the UAE, regular occurrence is concentrated between late October and March, with records outside that window. October may therefore be an active passage month at one site and the lead-in to a more conspicuous season at another. An observation becomes more useful when its date, location, elevation and habitat are recorded, rather than simply announcing that a “winter bird” has arrived. Plumage alone does not reveal an individual's country of origin or entire route. A ringing record linked to a documented subsequent encounter can establish some points in an individual’s movement; reconstructing its route requires suitable tracking data. One rusty tail, several appearances The rusty tail is useful but insufficient: Common Redstart, Phoenicurus phoenicurus, shares that feature. Females and young birds may look grey-brown, unlike the dark adult male repeatedly illustrated in guides. Look at the face, breast, underparts and wing as well as the tail. Male Black Redstarts also vary among populations. Western birds may be charcoal-coloured with a pale wing panel, while eastern populations can have more conspicuously rusty underparts. This matters when comparing an Arab-world bird with a single European photograph. A male's lack of a prominent white forehead, together with black extending onto the lower breast in some forms, helps distinguish it from Common Redstart. Females require closer assessment of several features. From rocks to villages and towns Black Redstarts are strongly associated with rocky ground and sparsely vegetated slopes. Walls, ledges and roofs offer some of the same features: an elevated lookout, sheltered spaces for hiding or nesting, and open ground for finding prey. Birds may therefore occur near buildings without depending on food supplied by people. Watch the movement between perch and ground: a short pause, a dash after small prey, then a return to a higher position. This behaviour reveals the importance of a small patch combining food and shelter, whether at a mountain's foot or beside a building. In towns, sealing cavities during renovation can remove nesting places used by the species. Small prey and a sheltered nest Insects and other small invertebrates form the basis of its diet, collected from the ground or during short sallies. It may also eat small fruits. The bird belongs to a food web linking plants, invertebrates and birds. It builds a nest from plant material in a protected place, such as a rock crevice or a gap in a building. A typical clutch contains four to six eggs, incubated by the female. Nesting dates depend on location and population. A bird seen beside a house in autumn is not necessarily preparing to breed there. Conservation and responsible observation Least Concern describes global extinction risk. It does not establish that every local population is doing well, or determine hunting law in any country. Legal status should be checked with the competent national authority, including protected-area rules and seasonal decisions. A game list or legal exception from one Arab country cannot simply be applied in another. Leave enough space for the bird to continue feeding, and avoid following it to a nest or disturbing it for a closer photograph. Record behaviour and habitat, with a clear side-on image if possible. Such details can turn a brief tail movement into a useful observation of birds across the Arab world's different environments. Photo credit: Greg Schechter — Wikimedia Commons — CC BY 2.0.

articles.title: Austria takes team gold at Cairo’s 300m Rifle World Championship
articles.body: Three rifle shooters take aim from the standing position on a shooting range. Austria leads the men’s prone team event on 18 October, a day after Finland took individual gold and Norway won the team title in three positions. Austria won the men’s 300m prone team gold on Sunday, 18 October 2026, at the World Championship being held at Egypt International Olympic City in the New Administrative Capital. The team scored 1,782 points with 91 inner tens, ahead of Switzerland and Poland. Alexander Schmirl scored 595, Patrick Diem 595 and Andreas Thum 592. Switzerland finished second with 1,780 points and 95 inner tens, and Poland third with 1,777 and 83 inner tens. Egypt placed eighth with 1,719 points and 46 inner tens. Finnish and Norwegian gold in three positions Finland’s Aleksi Leppa had won the men’s individual 300m rifle three positions title on 17 October with 591 points and 29 inner tens. Poland’s Maciej Kowalewicz matched his points total but recorded 22 inner tens to take silver, while Norway’s Jon-Hermann Hegg earned bronze with 589 points and 23 inner tens. In the three positions team event, Norway led with 1,760 points, followed by Austria on 1,753 and Switzerland on 1,751. Egypt finished sixth with 1,673 points. A separate event on Cairo’s calendar The championship runs from 15 to 20 October, bringing together 57 athletes from 19 countries. The programme for 19 October includes the men’s individual prone event and the open standard rifle event. This championship is a separate competition from the Rifle/Pistol World Cup hosted by Cairo earlier in the same month. articles.title: Cairo Shooting World Cup: gold for Privratsky and Teh Xiu Yi
articles.body: Men’s air-rifle competition at the Cairo Shooting World Cup, 12 October 2026. Source: ISSF 12 October results: the Czech wins men’s air rifle and the Singaporean takes women’s 25m pistol gold, with competition continuing until 15 October. Czechia’s Jiri Privratsky and Singapore’s Teh Xiu Yi won Monday’s two titles on 12 October 2026 at the ISSF Rifle and Pistol World Cup at Egypt International Olympic City in Cairo. The event runs from 8 to 16 October. Men’s air rifle gold for Czechia In the men’s 10m air rifle final, Privratsky scored 251.3 points to finish 1.1 ahead of Sweden’s Marcus Madsen, who took silver with 250.2. France’s Dimitri Dutendas earned bronze with 229.9, according to the International Shooting Sport Federation. Singapore wins the women’s pistol title In the women’s 25m pistol final, Teh Xiu Yi secured gold with 38 hits, ahead of France’s Heloise Fourre on 37. Bulgaria’s Miroslava Mincheva claimed bronze with 32 hits. Arab participation ahead of Doha The competition brings together 385 athletes from 51 countries, according to the ISSF. The final entry list includes athletes from Egypt, Oman, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Libya and Yemen. The programme covers air rifle and air pistol, three-position rifle, sport pistol, rapid-fire pistol and mixed-team events. Competition began on 10 October and continues until 15 October. Tuesday’s programme, on 13 October, includes the women’s 50m rifle three positions final, with the remaining finals taking place over the following two days. Cairo remains a preparation stop before the World Championships in Doha, from 1 to 14 November, where the first shooting quota places for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics will be awarded. No Olympic quota places are awarded at the Cairo World Cup. The city will also host the 300m Rifle World Championship from 15 to 20 October. articles.title: How cities reshape bird diversity, and why winter reveals the difference
articles.body: Seagulls in front of Galata Tower and Istanbul’s buildings, 17 March 2015. Illustrative photograph. Photo: MehmetBurakCoban, via Wikimedia Commons. Original image, unchanged. · CC BY-SA 4.0 A Nature Cities study drawing on around 17 million records across 452 North American cities shows how urban bird diversity varies with season and climate. Cities are more than buildings interrupting a natural landscape: they may also reshape the distribution of bird diversity. A study published in Nature Cities on 19 October 2026 analysed around 17 million eBird records, comparing 452 North American cities with their surrounding areas. The team examined species richness rather than simply the number of individual birds, distinguishing native from non-native species and comparing seasons. The north–south difference in native bird diversity was more pronounced in winter, but cities weakened that difference relative to surrounding areas. Great white pelicans above the American University of Beirut campus, 17 September 2018. Illustrative video frame. Footage: Bassem (باسم), via Wikimedia Commons. Still frame extracted at 60 seconds, unretouched. · CC BY-SA 4.0 Season and climate change the picture Another contrast emerged: higher human population density was generally associated with fewer native bird species, but the direction of that relationship reversed under cold conditions. For non-native species, the relationship between diversity and latitude was weak or absent across seasons. The findings highlight the importance of considering season and climate together when studying birds and cities: the distribution of species diversity across cities varies with climatic and seasonal conditions. Sources: Nature Cities study, published 19 October 2026

articles.title: Common Chiffchaff in the Arab World
articles.body: Common Chiffchaff From the Maghreb to Egypt, the Levant and the Arabian Peninsula, the Common Chiffchaff occurs on migration and in winter, with breeding documented in some areas. This small bird reveals how migration calendars differ, and identifying it requires attention to detail rather than a search for striking colours. Identification card Arabic names: الشفشافة الشائعة and النقشارة الشائعة English name: Common Chiffchaff French name: Pouillot véloce Scientific name: Phylloscopus collybita Family: Phylloscopidae, the leaf-warblers Type: a small passerine feeding mainly on invertebrates Arab-world range: examples include Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Egypt, Palestine, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Oman; occurrence varies by country, habitat and season Approximate measurements: length 11 centimetres; wingspan 18 centimetres; weight 8 grams Seasonal status in the region: passage migrant and winter visitor across extensive areas, with summer breeding documented locally, including in Lebanon Global conservation status: Least Concern (LC) Hunting law: check each country’s current laws and decisions; the global conservation category is not a hunting permit In October, a slight movement inside a shrub or among garden branches deserves a second look. The Common Chiffchaff is one of those birds that may pass a watcher without attracting attention through its colours. Its body is small and its plumage echoes the shades of leaves and shadows, but anyone patient enough to follow it can learn to read a bird through its movements, shape and voice together. In the Arab world, an autumn sighting may mark the beginning of a winter stay or a stop along a migration route; the month alone cannot reveal the bird’s destination or origin. How can we identify it? The upperparts are predominantly olive-brown, while the underparts look pale and may show a yellowish wash. A rather subdued pale eyebrow runs above the eye, and the legs are usually dark. Chiffchaffs move actively among branches, with a repeated tail movement that helps draw attention to them. Males and females look alike, so plumage colour alone cannot determine the bird’s sex. The most notable confusion species is the Willow Warbler, Phylloscopus trochilus. The chiffchaff has relatively shorter wings, and the tips of its flight feathers usually project a shorter distance beyond the tertials on the folded wing. Leg colour is a useful clue, but it is not a decisive test on its own. It is better to combine several features and record what was clearly seen rather than fill in details by guessing. If doubt remains, a clear side-on photograph and a note of the voice can help with a later identification review. The chiffchaff is famous for a repeated, rhythmic song echoed by its English name, but an autumn watcher should not rely on hearing that song. The bird may give short calls or remain silent. Distinguishing calls from song, while examining the wing and face, makes an observation more accurate. Distribution across the Arab world The Maghreb forms part of this species’ passage and wintering range. In Morocco, a field study published in 2024 on two High Atlas valleys lists it as a passage migrant and winter visitor. In Algeria, a study of the Algiers Sahel published that same year records it as a wintering bird. In Tunisia, a study of Dyr El Kef published in 2025 likewise lists wintering and passage status. The chiffchaff’s presence extends eastwards to Egypt and the Levant. In Egypt, an environmental study in the Nile Delta region records passage and wintering status. In Palestine, it is known as a common migrant and winter visitor. Lebanon adds a different situation: alongside passage and wintering, its 2026 bird guide confirms summer breeding. A single country may therefore hold breeding birds, passage migrants and winter visitors, with different periods of arrival and residence. On the Arabian Peninsula, Saudi references describe the chiffchaff as a widespread passage migrant and winter visitor, including in the southwestern highlands, and do not record it breeding in the Kingdom. In Oman, too, it is listed as a passage migrant and winter visitor. What does its presence in October mean? Ringing and recovery data brought together by the Eurasian-African Bird Migration Atlas show autumn movements towards North Africa and the Near East, with arrivals appearing in October and more records in November. In the UAE, the February 2026 checklist describes a very common migrant and winter visitor from late October to early April. October should therefore not be treated as a single arrival date across the Arab world. Passage may already be underway at one site while the usual winter season starts later at another. A watcher can be more accurate by linking an observation to its place and date, then comparing it with local records. Habitats and food Chiffchaffs inhabit a variety of wooded and shrubby settings, from forests and their edges to gardens, orchards and vegetation near wetlands. Suitable habitat combines opportunities to find food with branches, leaves and shrubs that provide cover. Small green spaces can therefore be worth watching alongside larger natural habitats. They pick off insects and their larvae, spiders and other small invertebrates, and can catch some prey in flight. This diet places them within the web of relationships linking plants, invertebrates and birds. Watching them search among leaves makes the role of a shrub or green margin clearer: it provides both food and cover. This highlights the importance of maintaining a diversity of native plants and limiting the use of pesticides that reduce the resources available to insect-eating birds. From the nest to autumn migration The species breeds across extensive parts of Europe and Asia, and many populations head south during the cold season. The female builds a domed nest close to the ground or low down in dense vegetation. A clutch usually contains five or six eggs, and incubation lasts around 13–14 days. Autumn offers an opportunity to watch the bird searching for food away from the nest. It is best to stay on paths, allow it to approach as part of its natural movements, and avoid chasing it through shrubs for a photograph. Recording the date, location, habitat and behaviour can make a brief sighting more useful, even if the bird’s identity remains uncertain. Conservation and legal status Globally, the Common Chiffchaff is classified as Least Concern (LC). This assesses the species’ extinction risk worldwide; it does not guarantee the health of every local population. Protecting woodland, shrubs and wetland margins, and reducing pesticide use and disturbance, remain useful ways to safeguard the places where the bird finds food and cover. There is no single hunting rule that can be attributed to the entire Arab world. Determining the legal position requires identifying the country and checking the legislation and decisions in force on the date of the activity, including rules for protected areas, seasons and permitted species. An LC category does not make hunting permissible. Watching this small movement among the leaves and recording it without chasing or disturbing the bird can deepen our understanding of the nature shared by the region’s countries.
