articles.title: Common Greenshank: a shallow-water visitor to the Arab world
articles.body: Common Greenshank From coasts to inland pools, this migrant combines greenish legs with a bill that turns slightly upwards. Name and classification The Common Greenshank, Tringa nebularia, is a wader in the family Scolopacidae and order Charadriiformes. Its French name is Chevalier aboyeur. It is distinct from the Green Sandpiper, Tringa ochropus: similar common names do not denote the same species. Identification Its long legs are grey-green or olive, and its relatively robust bill turns slightly upwards towards the tip. Winter birds are grey above and white below, with light streaking on the head and neck. Breeding plumage has stronger contrast and darker markings; juveniles show conspicuous pale edges to their back feathers. Leg colour alone is insufficient. Marsh Sandpiper, Tringa stagnatilis, is smaller and more delicately built, with a thinner, straighter bill. Green Sandpiper is shorter and more strongly contrasting, dark above and white below. The sexes look similar, and a general photograph does not reliably establish sex. Habitat, food and behaviour It uses mudflats, estuaries, lakes and shallow pools, including some artificial wetlands. It takes invertebrates from water and mud and may chase small fish through the shallows. It feeds alone or in small gatherings and can be active by day or night. Its ringing call is often delivered as a sequence of notes. Life cycle and breeding It breeds in northern Eurasia where boggy ground and marshes adjoin open woodland or open country. It nests on the ground, usually laying three to four eggs. Chicks can move and seek food early, while still receiving parental protection and care. After breeding, birds move towards passage and wintering areas; some non-breeding individuals remain south of the breeding range in summer. Arab distribution and autumn relevance Autumn is a useful time to look for migrants arriving at Arab wetlands or continuing farther south. Wetland references document passage and winter occurrence in Lebanon, while Libyan winter counts establish its presence at coastal and inland sites. It is a regular passage migrant and winter visitor in Oman. Field studies also document winter occurrence at Moroccan wetlands, while Banc d’Arguin reports record wintering and passage in Mauritania. Egyptian Environmental Affairs Agency reports include it among birds recorded at wetlands. These are local examples, not a map of equal abundance across countries. In the UAE, records are most numerous between August and April along coasts and at wetlands; a few non-breeding birds may remain in summer. Abundance and migration timing differ across the Gulf, the Levant and North Africa. One country’s observation period must not become a timetable for the entire region. Summer presence alone does not prove breeding. Ecology and conservation Migration depends on a connected network of feeding and resting sites; protecting the coast does not replace conserving inland pools and marshes. Globally the species is Least Concern (LC), but the UAE national assessment conducted in 2019 and published in 2021 classified it as Near Threatened (NT): these assessments cover different geographic scales. Coastal land-use change, pollution and disturbance can reduce habitat quality. Watching from a distance, without chasing birds or repeatedly flushing them, allows their behaviour to be observed with less interference. References Sources: IUCN and BirdLife International; UAE National Red List of Birds; British Trust for Ornithology; Palm Islands reserve management plan; Atlas of Wintering Waterbirds of Libya; Oman bird list. articles.title: Common Kestrel — Falco tinnunculus
articles.body: Common kestrelPhoto: Alexis Lours — Wikimedia Commons — CC BY 4.0. Common kestrel — Falco tinnunculus Range: A familiar small falcon over fields and city edges across Eurasia and Africa. Resident or partial migrant according to latitude. In Lebanon and the Levant it appears as a local resident, a passage migrant, and a winter visitor depending on area and elevation. It is recognised by its hovering while searching for prey, relatively long tail, and marked face. Adult males usually show a grey head and tail, with black spots on the back and wing coverts; females and juveniles are more heavily rufous-barred above. The adult male’s spotted back and black claws, when clearly visible, help distinguish it from the lesser kestrel Falco naumanni (Arabic: العُوَيْسِق), whose adult male has an unspotted back and pale claws. Separating females and juveniles of the two species requires careful assessment of several plumage and structural features. Life cycle and habitat: Breeding begins in spring; the pair defends a hunting territory. The female typically lays 4–6 eggs; incubation lasts about a month, mostly by the female while the male supplies prey. Nestlings remain several weeks before first flight. It nests in rock cavities, buildings, and old nests of other birds. It hunts over open ground—fields, pastures, fallow land, road edges, and urban fringes that offer high lookout points. Main prey is small rodents, with large insects, lizards, and nestling birds when rodents are scarce. Lifestyle: Its signature behaviour is windhovering: rapid wingbeats and a fanned tail against the breeze while scanning the ground, then a controlled drop onto prey. Diurnal hunting by sight. Solitary or in pairs when breeding; it adapts well to people wherever nest cavities and open hunting space remain. Dark facial markings and moustaches reduce glare—an adaptive detail shared with other falcons. Common kestrelPhoto: © Giles Laurent, gileslaurent.com — Wikimedia Commons — License CC BY-SA 4.0. Hunting status: Across Arab countries, birds of prey are generally protected and may not be hunted as quarry. In Lebanon, Wild Hunting Law No. 580/2004 limits hunting to quarry species set by the minister; everything else—including all birds of prey—is protected year-round and may not be hunted; the common kestrel is not among the permitted quarry. Despite legal protection, it still faces illegal shooting in some seasons and along some flyways. Conservation status: Globally Least Concern with the International Union for Conservation of Nature, despite local declines in some intensively farmed regions. Locally it may be affected by pesticides and loss of nest sites. Traits: Its hover is a visual scanning technique that gauges distance before the stoop, not a show. A living bridge between field and city, and an indicator of rodent abundance where it is regularly seen.

articles.title: Study: common loons choose breeding lakes that resemble where they hatched
articles.body: A common loon in breeding plumage in Minocqua, Wisconsin, July 2011. An illustrative photograph of the species examined in the study. Data from northern Wisconsin link breeding-territory choice to shoreline development on natal lakes, while revealing a different nest response close to hatching. A bird’s first lake may leave a lasting mark on its choice of the next. That is what a new study of common loons (Gavia immer) in northern Wisconsin suggests: the birds settled to breed in territories resembling their natal lakes in their level of shoreline development. The study was published in Behavioral Ecology on 17 October 2026 as an accepted manuscript, before final copyediting and typesetting. Its authors are Emily Renkey, Katie Adler and Daniel Blumstein of the University of California, Los Angeles, and Walter Piper of Chapman University. The first lake as a reference point The researchers drew on a marked population in a long-term study in northern Wisconsin between 1992 and 2023 to investigate links between shoreline development and human activity, breeding-territory choice and nest-defense behavior. Similarity in shoreline development was one of the striking findings. The researchers interpreted this pattern as an indication of natal habitat imprinting: features of the early environment becoming a reference for later breeding-habitat selection. This means choosing a similar environment, rather than necessarily returning to the same lake. Closer to hatching, less likely to leave In another part of the study, the team found no effect of shoreline development on the distance at which a loon left its nest as humans approached. Incubating birds were, however, less likely to leave the nest late in the incubation period. The researchers view this response as consistent with greater investment in protecting a breeding attempt as hatching approaches. The finding concerns nest-leaving behavior under the study conditions; it does not establish that development or human approaches are harmless to the birds. Are the birds responding to people or to food? The match between natal and breeding lakes does not establish exactly which features the birds recognize. The researchers suggest another possibility: common loons may be seeking lakes with familiar fish-species communities, rather than being attracted by the level of human activity itself. This remains a possible explanation, not a cause demonstrated by the findings. The distinction matters: a bird choosing a lake with familiar features does not mean it prefers buildings or is immune to their effects. Choosing a habitat does not guarantee its safety For conservation context, New Hampshire’s Loon Preservation Committee explains that development along lake shores and islands has reduced nesting habitat on many lakes. People approaching nests can also cause incubating birds to enter the water, leaving their eggs exposed to predators, heat or cold. The Wisconsin study adds a behavioral perspective: the environment in which a bird grew up may influence its later choices, even when that environment includes a human presence. But the research concerns a particular species in a particular region. It is not sufficient to extend the finding to other birds or to wetlands in the Arab region. articles.title: Common Quail — Coturnix coturnix
articles.body: Common quailPhoto: Dûrzan Cîrano — Wikimedia Commons — CC BY-SA 4.0. Range: A small ground bird of the pheasant family, heard more often than seen. It breeds across Europe, North Africa, and western Asia, and winters in sub-Saharan Africa and parts of southern Asia. Lebanon and the Levant form a key autumn and spring passage corridor; it hides in cereal fields, pastures, and dense grass, and rarely flies except in short low bursts before dropping back into cover. Life cycle and habitat: Males usually reach breeding grounds ahead of females. The female scrapes a shallow nest on the ground, lined with a little plant material, and typically lays between 8 and 13 eggs, incubating them alone for about 17–20 days. The chicks are precocial: they leave the nest soon after hatching and feed themselves, with the mother brooding them in the first weeks. Plumage is nearly complete by about day 19. It prefers open habitats with enough grass cover to hide in, and avoids dense forest; its diet is grass seeds, fallen grain, and insects and their larvae. Lifestyle: Secretive and terrestrial; it creeps more than it flies. The male’s short, repeated call is heard at dawn and dusk—and sometimes at night—while the bird itself stays hidden among the stalks. Much of the migration is nocturnal. Its wings are relatively longer than those of many ground gamebirds, matching a true long-distance migrant rather than a local wanderer. Outside the breeding season it may gather in small groups on passage or in winter. It should not be confused with the Japanese quail Coturnix japonica despite superficial likeness; each has a distinct call and core range. Common quailPhoto: LuisNDamas — Wikimedia Commons — CC BY-SA 4.0. Hunting status: Across Arab countries, hunting common quail is generally prohibited unless a specific state issues an official seasonal decree that expressly lists it. In Lebanon, Wild Hunting Law No. 580/2004 limits hunting to quarry species set by the minister; everything else is protected year-round; common quail is not among the permitted quarry in the absence of a current open-season decision. Conservation status: Globally Least Concern with the International Union for Conservation of Nature. In Europe it is assessed regionally nearer Near Threatened because of declines linked to intensive farming and hunting on flyways—a regional context, not a substitute for the global listing. Traits: A bird “heard, not seen”: the male announces himself with a short call while remaining hidden. A familiar marker of Levantine fields in migration season, and sensitive to how seasons and farmland habitats are managed.

articles.title: Common Redshank: red legs beside winter wetlands
articles.body: Common Redshank Red legs and a white trailing edge to the wing identify a wader that reaches many Arab wetlands on migration and in winter. Name and classification Common Redshank, Tringa totanus, belongs to the family Scolopacidae and order Charadriiformes. Its French name is Chevalier gambette. Associated with shallow water, it is distinct from Spotted Redshank, Tringa erythropus, which can look similar outside the breeding season. Identification and age differences Adults have red or orange-red legs and a red base to the bill, with a dark tip. The upperparts are grey-brown, more strongly marked in breeding plumage; winter plumage is plainer and less patterned. In flight, a broad white trailing edge to the wing is an important feature, beyond leg colour alone. Juveniles have pale, spotted feather edges, and their legs may be less red than those of adults. The sexes look similar. Spotted Redshank has a longer, finer bill and lacks the same broad white wing edge. Identification therefore combines bill shape, wing pattern and body structure rather than a single feature. Feeding habitat and alarm behaviour It uses estuaries, saltmarshes, mudflats, lake edges and wet grasslands. It picks small invertebrates from the mud surface or probes the substrate with its bill. Coastal feeding opportunities change as mud is exposed and water recedes; safe resting places are needed when feeding grounds are flooded. It is a vocal bird and may give clear whistles when disturbed. Outside the breeding season it can occur with other waders; breeding pairs defend the area around their nests and may join in warning of danger. Breeding and life cycle It breeds across extensive parts of Eurasia, not only near the sea: waterlogged grasslands and marshes are important nesting habitats. The ground nest is concealed among vegetation, and a clutch usually contains four eggs. Chicks leave the nest and begin taking food early, but need parental protection and vegetation in which to hide. After breeding, birds move towards stopover and wintering sites; routes and distances differ between populations. Some non-breeding birds may remain in wintering areas during summer, so a summer sighting does not automatically indicate a nest. Arab distribution and seasonality Lebanese references document passage and winter occurrence, while references for Qatar and Oman describe regular passage and winter visitors. The UAE national Red List documents a non-breeding population; Iraqi and Egyptian wetland references also record the species. In North Africa it occurs among wintering wetland birds, including at Libyan sites, but the regional waterbird identification guide also reports local breeding in Tunisia and Libya. Its Arab occurrence must therefore not be described as exclusively wintering. Autumn brings renewed interest to water margins and tidal areas as migrants arrive, without implying one arrival date or equal abundance in every country. Ecological role and conservation It links mud-dwelling invertebrates to avian predators and depends on wetlands suitable for feeding, breeding and resting. Its global Least Concern (LC) classification does not rule out local or regional declines. Wet-grassland drainage, coastal alteration, pollution and disturbance are pressures worth monitoring. Protecting wintering sites must be accompanied by protection of breeding habitats along its migratory range. articles.title: Common Sandpiper in the Arab world: a traveller along the water’s edge
articles.body: Common Sandpiper On a riverside stone or the edge of a pond, a brown-and-white bird takes short steps and teeters before continuing to feed. It may look solitary, well away from large wader flocks. Yet the Common Sandpiper belongs to a broad network of waterways and migration stopovers stretching across the Arab world. Identification card Arabic names: الطيطوي الشائع; الطيطوي الاعتيادي English name: Common Sandpiper French name: Chevalier guignette Scientific name: Actitis hypoleucos Family: Scolopacidae Length: approximately 19–21 cm Habitat: freshwater and saltwater margins, muddy and rocky banks, lakeshores and canals Arab-world occurrence: passage migrant and winter visitor in varying numbers; a summer sighting alone does not establish breeding Global conservation status: Least Concern (LC) Where it occurs in the Arab world National studies in Morocco document wintering birds on both Atlantic and Mediterranean coasts and at inland waters. Tracking of some Scottish breeders has also revealed Moroccan staging sites on journeys to and from West Africa. The country can therefore serve two different purposes: a stopover for some individuals and a wintering area for others. In Lebanon, a wader study published in the Lebanese Science Journal describes a common passage migrant and scarce winter visitor, recorded throughout the year at inland waters, along the coast and on islands. Year-round records do not establish nesting at all those sites: non-breeding birds may remain away from breeding areas. In Saudi Arabia, Common Sandpipers occur on passage and in winter, including inland. Observations also show variation within the country: passage is prominent in the Eastern Province, while smaller numbers winter along its coast and pools. A waterbird is not necessarily confined to the sea or to large marshes. A migration that starts before autumn feels close Post-breeding movement in European populations begins in July, with adults generally preceding juveniles. Many birds reach African wintering areas by October. Riyadh-region records place the main autumn passage between July and late October, with spring movement from March to May. Timing and numbers vary by site, population and year. The first birds may consequently appear in late summer, before the weather suggests autumn. Repeated sightings of one sandpiper do not prove that the same individual has remained: different birds may use the same suitable patch. Dates, counts and behaviour help turn impressions into seasonal observations that can be compared. A white wedge in front of the wing Grey-brown upperparts contrast with a white belly and a white projection rising between the side of the breast and the folded wing. This is particularly useful when comparing it with Green or Wood Sandpipers, which lack the same white shoulder wedge. Its tail extends beyond the folded wings, and the legs look short beside those of many other waders. A white wing-bar shows in flight, often low over water with distinctive flicking wingbeats. There is no reason to flush the bird to see it. Head-bobbing and teetering are frequent while it walks, and may intensify when a person approaches. If it stops feeding and continually watches you, step back. The sexes look similar overall. Feather-edge details differ between juveniles and adults, but ageing requires a clear view and assessable plumage. The strength of a brown tone, or apparent size in an unscaled photograph, cannot establish age or sex confidently. What the bank provides It feeds on aquatic and terrestrial insects and larvae, worms, small crustaceans and molluscs, picking food from the ground and water's edge. It may use a canal bank or small pond that people barely notice. The value lies in food, water and accessible margins, rather than the size or fame of the landscape. It breeds mainly across Europe and Asia, placing the nest near water in concealing vegetation. BTO data give a typical clutch of four eggs, incubated by both sexes. These are facts about the species' biology, not evidence of breeding at an Arab site without a documented nest or confirmed breeding behaviour. Keeping quiet margins available The global category remains Least Concern, but feeding and resting sites matter to successful migration. Loss or pollution of natural banks, and repeated disturbance, can reduce the usefulness of a place that looks small on a map. Watch from a distance. Avoid walking directly towards the bird along a narrow bank or trapping it between yourself and the water. Do not catch it for identification. Check legal status with the competent authority in each country: neither its name nor its conservation category authorises hunting. A clear side-on photograph with a date and location is more useful than a flight image obtained by disturbance. articles.title: Common Shelduck: A Protected Waterbird and Rare Migrant in Lebanon
articles.body: Common Shelduck (Tadorna tadorna). The Common Shelduck (Tadorna tadorna) is a scarce migrant and winter visitor to Lebanon’s wetlands, coasts, and islands — a protected Anatidae species that must never be treated as game. The Common Shelduck (Tadorna tadorna; English: Common Shelduck) is known as a scarce migrant and wintering waterbird on wetlands, coasts, and islands in Lebanon. It belongs to the duck family Anatidae and is distinguished by its large size and well-balanced plumage of white, black, and chestnut-red. The male has a black head and neck with a glossy green sheen and a chestnut breast; the female is similar but with duller tones and a less prominent bill. The Common Shelduck inhabits coastal areas, saline lakes, marshes, and ponds, preferring shallow muddy or sandy waters that suit its foraging. It is widespread across Europe and Asia and migrates to the Mediterranean and North Africa in winter. Its breeding season begins in late spring and early summer. The female nests in ground burrows or rock crevices, often reusing abandoned burrows of other animals such as rabbits. She lays 8 to 12 eggs; incubation lasts 28 to 30 days. After hatching, she leads the young to water to teach them how to find food. The Common Shelduck probes mud and sand with its flattened bill. The Common Shelduck feeds on molluscs, crustaceans, worms, aquatic insects, aquatic plants, and algae, probing mud and sand with its flattened bill. It also plays an important ecological role by helping control crustacean and mollusc numbers and by improving water quality through stirring and aerating the substrate. The species faces multiple threats, chiefly habitat destruction from urban expansion and coastal development, plus environmental pollution that degrades water quality and the plants it depends on. Illegal hunting is a further threat, alongside climate change that may alter its range and feeding areas. The Common Shelduck is internationally protected under the Agreement on the Conservation of African-Eurasian Migratory Waterbirds (AEWA). It is not among the species permitted for hunting — a fact that calls for stronger protection of the bird and of its natural habitats so it can remain in the wild.

articles.title: Eurasian Teal: a small duck linking Arab wetlands with northern flyways
articles.body: Eurasian Teal At the edge of shallow water, a teal can look like a small duck among larger flocks. A male’s chestnut head and green face patch reveal a bird connecting northern breeding grounds with Arab winter wetlands. October highlights the value of quiet pools and stopovers, but migration, residence and breeding must remain distinct. Identity and taxonomic scope Arabic name: الحذفة الشتوية, documented in The Birds of Saudi Arabia. The species is Anas crecca, family Anatidae, order Anseriformes. AviList v2026 calls the broader species Green-winged Teal and includes the American carolinensis as a subspecies. This account centres on the Eurasian form Anas crecca crecca, also called Eurasian or Common Teal; its French name is Sarcelle d’hiver. Different English names therefore do not denote two separate species in this treatment. [1] [2] [8] Recognition A brightly plumaged male has a chestnut head with a broad green eye patch, spotted breast, grey flanks and a yellow rear patch bordered by dark markings. Females are mottled brown; both sexes show a green wing speculum. Brown plumage alone cannot identify a female among similar ducks. [6] Age, sex and lookalikes The Eurasian form measures about 34–38 cm. Outside bright plumage, males may resemble females. Accurate ageing uses wing and tail feather details and wear, not body size alone. Small size and the speculum pattern help distinguish females from other brown ducks, but distant photographs or concealed wings may prevent reliable identification. Criteria developed for birds handled during ringing cannot simply be applied to a fleeting photograph. [7] Garganey Spatula querquedula warrants comparison: it is slightly larger, and its brightly plumaged male has a broad white eyebrow rather than the teal’s green face patch. [13] October, migration and Arab distribution Saudi references describe common passage in February–March and September–October, common winter presence in November–February, irregular summer occurrence and no breeding in the book’s account. The UAE’s 2026 checklist lists the Eurasian form as a common to very common migrant and winter visitor. These are national status descriptions, not counts for autumn 2026. [2] [4] Lebanon’s 2020 checklist treats it as a former breeder, with passage in March–early May and mid-August–late November, and winter presence chiefly in Beqaa wetlands during December–March. Pairs seen in May in earlier years were not accepted as evidence of renewed breeding. Tunisian surveys in December 2020–January 2021 documented winter occurrence; the study appeared in 2024 and is not a new count. [3] [5] Farther west, Danish ringing recoveries document birds reaching Morocco in winter. Egypt’s historical Ramsar information sheet for Lake Burullus also records wintering teal. These examples span the Maghreb, Egypt, the Levant and the Gulf; they are neither an exhaustive country list nor grounds for assigning every Arab population to one route. [9] [10] In Egypt, a BirdLife report published in February 2025 identifies Lake Nasser as a teal stopover and wintering site. In Iraq’s Central Marsh, the October 2013–June 2014 survey recorded teal in December–March, not among observed breeders; this is not a current census. [11] [12] Habitat, food and behaviour It uses shallow, vegetation-rich wetlands, including small pools, lakes and saline lagoons. Plant material and invertebrates are taken at the surface or by dipping and upending. The Saudi account describes much feeding at night, with daytime activity too: a resting daytime flock does not mean that a wetland has little feeding value. [2] Life cycle and reproduction BTO gives a typical single brood, 8–11 eggs and female incubation lasting about 21–23 days. Chicks hatch downy and mobile. These are reference biological values, not a uniform Arab nesting calendar. Breeding is followed by movements towards post-breeding and winter sites; ringing shows that some birds stop for weeks while others move on quickly. A duck remaining in summer is not proof of a nest or successful hatching. [8] [9] Ecological importance and conservation The need to feed and rest at several sites makes a connected wetland network more valuable than protection of one pool alone. The Tunisian study describes habitat pressures including pollution, urban expansion and illegal hunting. Such general pressures cannot be converted into a species-specific loss estimate without relevant data. [5] BTO reports Least Concern, LC, for Eurasian Teal; this reference is not a new assessment of the species under its expanded taxonomic scope in AviList 2026. A taxonomic change is not, by itself, evidence of a population increase or decline. [1] [8] Responsible observation Watch from a stationary position at a distance that does not flush the flock, and record date, location and plumage. Reliable identification takes priority over naming every bird: where diagnostic features are hidden, an unresolved small-duck record is preferable to a false species record. This account does not authorise hunting; legal status is separate from abundance and conservation category. articles.title: Dubai Safari Park opens its eighth season with wildlife tours and bird shows
articles.body: Lions in the Explorer Safari area. A first-ever opening week runs until 18 October, with a children’s camp across a park whose six zones are home to more than 3,000 animals. Dubai Safari Park reopened on 12 October 2026, launching its eighth season with a week of family activities alongside safari tours, bird and raptor shows, and experiences introducing visitors to wildlife. The park is holding an opening week for the first time, according to the announcement carried by the Emirates News Agency. Running until 18 October, the programme includes the Little Explorers’ Base Camp, with painting, arts and crafts, animal-model colouring and group games, as well as a stage show performed four times a day and two roaming parades. For bird enthusiasts, the programme includes Birds Kingdom and Birds of Prey presentations, while Echoes of the Wild introduces visitors to animal behaviour and adaptations. These activities combine observation with awareness of the importance of habitats and wildlife conservation. A macaw encounter in the African Village. Safari tours offer views of lions, giraffes, rhinos and other animals in spaces designed to reflect their habitats. Admission includes the Arabian Desert Safari, while the Explorer Safari Tour is available as part of an upgraded package. An Explorer Safari tour passes giraffes. Located in Al Warqa 5 in Dubai, the park covers 119 hectares across six zones and houses more than 3,000 animals from around 300 species, according to its figures. It welcomes visitors daily from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m., with the last admission at 5 p.m. Photos: Dubai Safari Park – archive. Emirates News Agency · Opening-week programme – Dubai Safari Park

articles.title: Dunlin: a small wader linking the north to Arab shores
articles.body: Dunlin Its plumage changes from a black summer belly to winter grey, while its journeys connect northern breeding habitats with passage and wintering coasts. Name and classification Dunlin, Calidris alpina, is a small wader in the family Scolopacidae and order Charadriiformes. Its French name is Bécasseau variable. Arabic references use both al-durayja al-albiyya and al-durayja al-mutaghayyira; these alternative names do not denote different species. Plumage, age and similar species It has a black bill curving slightly downwards and dark legs. Breeding plumage includes a black belly patch and reddish-brown patterned upperparts; in winter, the back is grey and the belly white. Birds arriving in autumn may retain some summer feathers, so individuals need not look identical. Juveniles show stronger patterning and pale edges to their back feathers, with dark spotting below. The sexes look similar and bill length varies, so a general photograph does not establish sex. Curlew Sandpiper, Calidris ferruginea, usually has longer legs and a longer bill; Sanderling, Calidris alba, is paler in winter and shorter-billed. These features must be considered together because age and moult complicate comparisons. Food and the tidal rhythm It takes worms, molluscs, crustaceans, insects and other invertebrates by picking or probing wet mud and sand. Coastal feeding areas change with the tides; when water covers the mudflats, birds gather at nearby roosts. Its close-knit flocks are striking: as they turn, they appear alternately dark and pale. Small groups also occur beside inland lakes and pools during passage. Large numbers at one site do not establish that the species is secure throughout its range. Life cycle and breeding Breeding areas lie mainly in northern, Arctic and sub-Arctic regions, including tundra, grasslands and wet peatlands. The nest is on the ground and a clutch usually contains four eggs. Chicks can move and seek food early but still need care and protection while growing. After breeding, populations leave for wintering areas along different routes. Ringing data show that some European breeders reach North Africa, whereas other populations travel elsewhere. Dunlins in Arab countries do not all originate in one country or follow a single route. Arab distribution and seasonal relevance Its Arab range extends from Mauritania and the Maghreb to Egypt, the Levant, Iraq, the Gulf and the Arabian Peninsula, with local differences in abundance and occurrence. Banc d’Arguin in Mauritania is particularly important as a wintering area for some northern populations. Libyan winter surveys document coastal distribution and use of some inland wetlands. In Lebanon it is recorded as a passage migrant and winter visitor; in Oman it is a regular wader during passage and winter. Autumn is therefore a useful season to look along coasts and pools. An out-of-season bird does not by itself establish residence or breeding, and inclusion on a national list does not mean regular numbers occur at every site in that country. Ecology and conservation The IUCN global assessment of 2024 classified Dunlin as Near Threatened (NT), with an overall declining trend. This supersedes references still displaying its former Least Concern category. Its future depends on northern breeding habitats and on passage and wintering sites together. Loss of mudflats, wetland degradation and disturbance affect opportunities to feed and rest. Observers can help by recording species, location and date while avoiding intrusion into roosts or repeatedly forcing birds to fly. articles.title: Egypt: New Hunting Rules and Field Action as Autumn Migration Begins
articles.body: A field researcher removes a bird from illegal nets. Egypt’s Ministry of Local Development and Environment announced a new decision regulating hunting, as the Environmental Affairs Agency began monitoring with the start of the autumn migration season. At Burullus Protected Area, about 200 migratory birds were released and roughly 750 metres of illegal nets were removed. The ministry is also holding a community dialogue with NGOs and specialists to shape clearer rules specifically for hunting migratory birds. A team to tackle illegal bird hunting The Egyptian team to combat excessive and illegal bird hunting was launched at the Journalists’ Syndicate on 30 September 2026, on the initiative of Nature Conservation Egypt, in cooperation with the Association of Environmental and Development Writers. Al-Ahram reported Mahmoud Bakr’s description of it as a voluntary coordination platform involving government and parliamentary representatives, researchers, civil society and the media. According to Press Street, the team supports the national 2026–2030 roadmap through five committees: legislation, policies, enforcement and compliance; research and monitoring; economic alternatives and ecotourism; funding, institutional empowerment and capacity building; and awareness, media, ethical and cultural values. Al-Watan reported Khaled El-Noubi’s announcement of preparations for an “Invitation to a Code of Honour” initiative during the current hunting season in Matrouh, El-Dabaa and Ras El-Hekma, on the northwestern coast. It seeks voluntary agreements with hunters and local community leaders to curb excessive hunting.

articles.title: Egypt–UAE cooperation to protect houbara and strengthen Omayed Reserve
articles.body: African houbara (Chlamydotis undulata) in Algeria, 2 October 2020. A planned scientific study will support management and habitat conservation in Matrouh, building on cooperation that included African houbara reintroduction in 2022. Egypt and the United Arab Emirates have discussed strengthening cooperation to protect African houbara and improve the management of Omayed Reserve in Matrouh Governorate, through a scientific assessment of the reserve’s ecological characteristics and natural habitats and more coordinated biodiversity protection measures. According to a statement published by Egypt’s Ministry of Local Development and Environment on 18 October 2026, discussions with the UAE-based International Fund for Houbara Conservation covered support for the reserve, protection of its resources and the use of specialist scientific expertise in wildlife management. A scientific assessment of habitats The latest step includes a directive to establish a scientific committee bringing together experts from outside the ministry and representatives of the protected areas sector. The committee will study Omayed’s ecological features, assess its biodiversity and propose appropriate measures to protect its natural resources and habitats. The work focuses on the needs of the reserve and the birds that depend on it, alongside environmental safeguards suited to its characteristics and the long-term health of its ecosystems. The statement did not specify a completion date for the study. Building on the 2022 reintroduction The cooperation builds on an earlier initiative at Omayed on 18 June 2022, when 2,000 African houbara were released and reintroduced. DNA and molecular biology analyses preceded the operation, with results compared against reference samples to confirm that the birds belonged to the local lineage present, or historically present, in Egypt. The cooperation framework also covered joint research and activities to restore and conserve houbara, the exchange of expertise and the development of national wildlife management capacity. It included exploring projects that could deliver economic and social benefits to communities around species conservation areas. A reserve with varied habitats UNESCO has listed Omayed as a biosphere reserve since 1981. The reserve represents part of Egypt’s Mediterranean coastal desert and contains coastal dunes, inland ridges, saline and non-saline depressions, and an inland plateau. According to UNESCO, environmental pressures in the area include land degradation, habitat fragmentation, overgrazing and biodiversity loss. The reserve also has an important role in long-term ecological monitoring, improved rangeland and ecotourism management, and linking nature conservation with sustainable local livelihoods. articles.title: Eurasian Coot: resident and migrant flocks meet in Arab wetlands
articles.body: Eurasian Coot From a distance it looks like an unassuming dark waterbird. Closer views reveal two prominent features: a white bill and a white shield on the forehead. The Eurasian Coot combines diving skills with life in winter flocks. Yet not every coot seen in October is a new arrival: at some Arab wetlands, resident breeding birds meet visitors from colder regions. Identification card Arabic name: الغرّة الأوراسية; the Saudi bird reference uses غراء أوراسية. English: Eurasian Coot; French: Foulque macroule. Scientific name: Fulica atra, family Rallidae, order Gruiformes. Despite sharing the water with ducks, it is not a duck. Global conservation status: Least Concern (LC), which does not mean every local population is stable. The scientific name follows AviList v2026; regional references document differing patterns of occurrence between countries. [1] [2] [7] Why watch it in autumn? European ringing data show autumn movements beginning in late August and strengthening from mid-September, with returns to distant wintering sites during October. They also document connections between south-western Europe and North Africa. These are observed migration patterns, not a common arrival calendar for all Arab coots: the species includes both resident and migratory populations. [11] An Arab map of residence, passage and wintering Lebanon’s 2020 checklist describes the coot as a resident breeder at inland wetlands, and very common on passage and in winter, mainly from September to late May. Seeing a bird in autumn therefore does not establish that it is a migrant; nor does a winter flock show that all its members breed at that site. [3] In Morocco, a study of Daya Takaddoum in the Bouregreg valley documented breeding in 2018 and 2019, and increasing numbers with the arrival of winter visitors. This is local field evidence, not a current nationwide count. Tunisian winter surveys conducted in 2020–2021 and published in 2024 also recorded the species, underlining the seasonal importance of wetlands. [4] [6] Saudi Arabia’s bird reference classifies it as a rare breeding resident and an uncommon winter visitor, occurring in winter from October to March. The Emirates Bird Records Committee checklist, updated in February 2026, calls it a locally common migrant and winter visitor, with resident breeding populations at particular sites, including Al Warsan Lakes and Al Wathba Wetland Reserve. Such differences rule out treating one country’s status as that of the entire Gulf. [2] [5] In Egypt, the Lake Burullus Key Biodiversity Area account, whose latest listed assessment is from 2016, includes coots among wintering waterbirds. This is reference evidence of the site’s winter importance, not a recent count. [12] In Iraq’s Central Marsh, a study published in 2017 recorded coots as winter visitors from November to March during surveys conducted from October 2013 to June 2014. It did not record them in the breeding season within the study area; this does not establish an absence of breeding throughout Iraq. [13] Recognising age and distinguishing similar species Adult coots have charcoal-grey bodies, blacker heads and white bills and frontal shields. Their long toes carry separate skin lobes that aid swimming, unlike the continuous webbing familiar in ducks. To take off, they run across the water before gaining height. [8] The sexes look similar: black plumage alone does not identify an individual’s sex. Juveniles are paler, with greyish white on the face, fore-neck and breast, and a frontal shield that is not yet fully developed. The Red-knobbed Coot Fulica cristata is particularly similar. Red knobs above the shield help identify breeding adults, but their apparent absence in a distant photograph is not enough to exclude that species. [9] Adult Common Moorhens Gallinula chloropus, by contrast, have a red frontal shield. Combine head, bill and body shape rather than calling every dark waterbird a coot. [8] Food, habitat and behaviour Coots use lakes, ponds and slow-flowing waterways, including urban waters. They eat aquatic plants and seeds, as well as molluscs, insects and larvae, diving for food or grazing close to the bank. Their presence in a treatment pond does not make its water drinkable, and bird abundance alone is not a water-quality test. [10] Life cycle: from nest to flock Both partners build a nest of plant material near aquatic cover, share incubation and care for the young, and defend the surrounding territory. Breeding-season disputes between neighbours can be fierce, unlike the winter gatherings that bring many individuals together. [2] [8] BTO data give a typical clutch of 5–7 eggs, incubation of about 21–24 days and flight capability at roughly 55–60 days. The downy young can move early but remain dependent on parental care. These are reference values, not fixed numbers or durations for every Arab nest; a European nesting calendar cannot simply be transferred to a different climate. [7] Its value, and what needs protecting Following coots helps reveal how a lake is used throughout the year: where flocks feed, and where vegetation suitable for nesting remains. The Daya Takaddoum study highlights wetland habitat change under urban pressure. Protecting the place, not just the bird, preserves opportunities to feed, breed and rest. [4] Watch from the bank without repeatedly forcing birds to flee, and do not approach nests or chicks for a better photograph. Record the date, site, count and behaviour, distinguishing a sighting from breeding evidence. Global Least Concern status neither automatically permits hunting nor replaces local regulations. articles.title: Eurasian Wigeon: a grazing duck connecting northern Eurasia with Arab wetland winters
articles.body: Eurasian Wigeon When a group of ducks leaves the water to graze on short grass, Eurasian Wigeon may be among them. A brightly plumaged male combines a pale forehead with a chestnut head and grey body, but the forehead is not its only identifying feature. This migratory duck links Eurasian breeding areas with wintering sites, including Arab wetlands whose value changes with water, food and freedom from disturbance. Identity card Arabic: الصواي الأوراسي; also الصواية English: Eurasian Wigeon French: Canard siffleur Scientific name: Mareca penelope; older sources use Anas penelope Order and family: Anseriformes; Anatidae Length: approximately 42–52 cm Habitat: lakes, marshes, wet grassland, sheltered bays and coastal lagoons Arab-world status: chiefly passage migrant and winter visitor; abundance varies among countries Global conservation category: Least Concern (LC); scientific name and taxonomy follow AviList v2026 [1] Why watch for it in late October? This period combines continuing autumn movements with the first settlement of some ducks at wintering sites. In Saudi Arabia: passage in October–November, wintering in November–March, and no breeding. These are regional dates, not a calendar to apply uniformly from Morocco to Oman. In practice, record repeated presence, flock size and behaviour rather than assuming that the first sighting marks the completion of winter arrivals. [8] From the Maghreb to the eastern Arab world and the Gulf In Tunisia, a winter 2020–2021 survey, published in 2024, confirms its presence. In Egypt, BirdLife and its partner Nature Conservation Egypt identify Lake Nasser among its stopover and wintering sites. These examples do not describe its entire Arab range, but provide specific evidence rather than suggesting a uniform distribution across a broad map. [11] [12] In Palestine, the Wildlife Society describes it as locally common in winter and on passage. “Locally” matters: it does not mean common at every site. In the UAE: uncommon to fairly common on passage and in winter, with some summering individuals. Summer presence does not automatically establish breeding. [10] [9] Presence within a country must also be distinguished from the role of a particular site: a bird may use one lake to rest, another to feed, or stop for a few days before continuing its journey. Country lists cannot replace dated site records, and a single observation cannot establish peak timing or a long-term population trend. How can it be distinguished from similar ducks? A male in bright plumage has a chestnut head, a pale forehead stripe, a pinkish breast, a grey body and a dark rear. A large white wing patch may be visible. The bill is short, blue-grey and black-tipped, and the head is rounded: useful structural clues when colours are unclear. [2] Females are brown or grey-brown, young birds resemble them, and males in eclipse plumage become less striking. A white belly may show in flight, but is not a sufficient standalone feature. American Wigeon, especially females, and hybrids can cause confusion. If the combination of features is unclear, leaving identification unresolved is more accurate than forcing a name onto a distant photograph. [3] [6] A duck that grazes and feeds near the surface The diet is predominantly plant-based, including leaves, stems, seeds and other plant parts. Wigeon graze on land and take food at or just below the water surface, sometimes benefiting from plants brought up by other waterbirds. Invertebrates also contribute, particularly during growth and breeding. Feeding can occur by day or night, and groups resting or moving together may include other duck species. [4] [6] Life cycle: northern breeding and mobile winter quarters The breeding range lies in northern Eurasia near freshwater, including boreal woodland and tundra-edge habitats. The female selects a ground site concealed by vegetation, builds a down-lined nest, incubates and cares for the ducklings. This nesting description should not be transferred to an Arab wintering site as though the birds seen there normally breed at that location. [4] A typical clutch contains 8–9 eggs, with natural variation, and incubation takes about 24–25 days. Ducklings leave early and feed themselves under the female’s care, flying at roughly 40–45 days. Breeding is followed by moult and renewed plumage; replacement of the wing feathers brings a temporary flightless period before seasonal movements resume. [5] Value, conservation and careful observation Comparing Wigeon with Shoveler and Pintail shows that ducks sharing a wetland do not all feed in the same way. Maintaining a variety of water depths, vegetation and quiet margins therefore retains feeding and resting options. A site’s value is not only the number of birds present, but also whether they can use it without repeated disturbance. The global category is Least Concern, but local monitoring and protection against habitat loss and degradation remain necessary. Watch from a distance; do not chase birds to expose a wing patch or obtain a closer photograph. Record what you actually observed, including limits to identification confidence. Hunting permission is a separate matter governed by applicable local rules, not a species name or one day’s abundance. articles.title: The European Bee-eater
articles.body: European Bee-eater With its chestnut back, yellow throat and turquoise breast, the European Bee-eater is a striking sight in the skies across much of the Arab world. Its flocks may pass through one country on migration, while other populations remain to breed in another. Seeing the bird, or simply describing it as “migratory”, is therefore not enough to understand the nature of its presence in a particular place. Species profile Arabic name: الوروار الأوروبي English name: European Bee-eater French name: Guêpier d’Europe Scientific name: Merops apiaster Family: bee-eaters, Meropidae Order: Coraciiformes Seasonal status in the Arab world: a passage migrant across wide areas and a summer breeder in parts of North Africa, the Mashriq and the Arabian Peninsula; its status varies locally Global conservation status: Least Concern, LC, according to BirdLife’s 2024 assessment Legal hunting status: determined by each country’s laws and the regulations in force; global conservation status does not establish whether hunting is permitted How to distinguish it from other bee-eaters The adult combines a chestnut head and back with a yellow throat, separated by a black line from the blue-green underparts. Other features include its long, slightly curved bill, the dark stripe through the eye and the two elongated central tail feathers. Juveniles look greener and lack the same tail extensions, so identification should draw on more than one feature. The general name “bee-eater” covers several species in the region. The Blue-cheeked Bee-eater Merops persicus is predominantly green, with a blue tinge on the face. The region also has smaller, mainly green species, including the African Green Bee-eater Merops viridissimus and the Arabian Green Bee-eater Merops cyanophrys. Modern checklists recognise these as separate species following the split of the former Green Bee-eater group. Scientific names remain an important reference when Arabic names differ between guides and countries. Where it occurs in the Arab world In Morocco, the European Bee-eater occurs both on passage and as a seasonal breeder, with occasional winter records noted in the national checklist. A field study published in 2023 documented breeding colonies near Meknes. In Tunisia, too, it is a migratory breeder and passage migrant, although its colonies are not evenly distributed among sites. In Egypt, ringing studies confirm its passage in spring and autumn. In Lebanon, it is a common passage migrant, and there are summer observations, but local breeding remains unconfirmed. The situation differs in Iraq, where it is listed as a summer breeding visitor and passage migrant. Its connection with the Arabian Peninsula extends beyond flying over it: Oman’s official checklist lists it as a summer breeding visitor and passage migrant, describing it as uncommon. Migration and wintering follow different regional calendars This species links breeding areas in North Africa, Europe and Asia with wintering areas in Africa. Tracking and ringing data show that European populations take different routes to western, eastern and southern Africa. Passage dates in one country cannot be applied to all Arab countries. In Lebanon, for example, the scientific checklist places spring passage between early April and early June, and autumn passage between mid-August and early November, with September and October particularly prominent in autumn. The occasional winter records from Morocco do not make the species a regular winter visitor throughout the Arab world. Recording the location, date and behaviour helps distinguish a passing flock from a feeding stopover or a sustained presence that warrants further observation. The diet of an aerial hunter The European Bee-eater catches flying insects, including bees, wasps and other prey. It may return to a perch to handle its prey before swallowing it. Despite its name, its diet is not limited to honey bees, and the proportion of bees in its diet varies between sites and seasons. A field study near apiaries in Murcia, Spain, found that honey bee consumption differed between sites and stages of the breeding season. It is therefore inappropriate to assume that every flock causes the same losses, or that predation on bees automatically strengthens the colony. A more accurate understanding starts with establishing when the birds are present, what food is available and the conditions at the apiary, rather than turning an ecological relationship into a single, fixed judgement. Nesting in the soil The bee-eater excavates a tunnel in suitable soil, often in an earth cliff or bank, ending in a nest chamber. Nests may be close together in a colony. This explains the importance of undisturbed earthen slopes in breeding areas, alongside open habitats rich in insects. Observers do not need to approach the tunnel entrance to confirm the bird’s presence. Watching from a distance allows adults to continue entering and leaving normally, while avoiding disturbance to nests or leaving them exposed. Preserving natural earth cliffs is just as important as protecting the birds themselves. Conservation begins with accurate knowledge The species’ global classification as Least Concern does not necessarily reflect the condition of every local population, nor does it grant permission to hunt it. Hunting and protected-area rules must be checked for the country and date concerned. Understanding the bird in the field begins with identifying the species correctly, understanding why it is present in that season and place, and allowing it to feed and breed without pursuit or disturbance.

articles.title: European warning: 11–36 million birds illegally killed or captured annually in the Mediterranean
articles.body: Illegal bird nets in Lebanon’s Bekaa, 1 October 2026 — Sayd archive / Adonis Elkhateeb, Editor-in-Chief. An estimated 11 to 36 million birds are illegally killed or captured annually across the Mediterranean, according to a 2016 scientific study whose findings were highlighted again by conservation organisations on 10 October 2026. This figure featured in a warning issued by Tour du Valat, EuroNatur and BirdLife International on 10 October 2026, World Migratory Bird Day, calling for more effective protection along migration routes. According to the warning, 83% of the 46 assessed countries have yet to take sufficient measures to meet the commitment to halve illegal killing and capture by 2030. The organisations called for closing legal gaps, strengthening field monitoring and awareness, and wider cooperation between public authorities, hunters and conservation groups. Lebanon on the migration route In Lebanon's Bekaa Valley, Sayd Magazine's archive documents the removal of nets used for trapping birds, an example of the risks migratory species face along the route. Countering indiscriminate trapping is compatible with safeguarding responsible and lawful hunting within applicable seasons and regulations. An international project for the Egyptian vulture Egyptian vulture — Charles J. Sharp / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0). Also on 10 October, the Bulgarian Society for the Protection of Birds announced the LIFE EV Safe Return project, bringing together 15 organisations and institutions from Europe, the Middle East and Africa. Running until 2031, it aims to improve the prospects of the Egyptian vulture, a migratory raptor travelling over 5,000 kilometres between the Balkans and its wintering areas in Africa. The project addresses poison baits, illegal hunting and electrocution on unsafe power infrastructure. Both initiatives highlight the need for coordinated cross-border protection, from nesting areas to stopover sites and wintering grounds.
articles.excerpt: European warning: 11–36 million migratory birds illegally killed or captured yearly in the Mediterranean; 83% of 46 countries lack sufficient measures.

articles.title: Field balance: Beretta A400 Xtreme Plus or Benelli SBE 3? Gas versus inertia
articles.body: Beretta A400 Xtreme Plus in the field: an empty hull ejects on the shot. Editorial photo. Ask a hunter at first light on the firing line what shotgun they swear by, and the debate may never end. Narrow it to Italy’s two leading semi-auto schools, and the contest usually returns to the same pair: the Beretta A400 Xtreme Plus and the Benelli Super Black Eagle 3 (SBE 3). Both guns — most often in 12-gauge with a 3½-inch (89 mm) chamber — are mature designs with long field pedigrees. The real difference does not show on climate-controlled shelves; it shows in wadis, on coastal sand, and in cold spray. Gas breath versus inertia Beretta A400 Xtreme Plus. Manufacturer-style photo (Beretta). Beretta A400 (Blink) gas system: Powder gas drives the bolt back, ejects the hull, and chambers the next round. With Kick-Off in the stock, felt recoil is typically softer. On fast flocks — rock dove or turtle dove — that helps keep the muzzle on the line for a second and third shot, and shoulders notice it after a long day. Benelli Super Black Eagle 3 (SBE 3). Manufacturer-style photo (Benelli USA). Benelli SBE 3 (Inertia Driven): No gas pistons and far less carbon packing in gas tubes. A spring in the bolt group uses recoil motion to cycle the action. The forend is slimmer, the gun is often lighter, and pointability on snap shots is a clear strength. Reliability in dirt is the other headline: light mud or sand can often be brushed off so you are back shooting without a full strip-down — a trait coastal and marsh hunters value. Which way does the scale tip? If your days are long on foot and you want a lighter gun with simpler cleanup, many hunters lean to the Benelli SBE 3. If you sit fixed blinds, shoot heavier loads, and want clearer recoil absorption with a quicker second and third bird, the Beretta A400 Xtreme Plus makes a strong field case. There is no absolute winner — only the system that matches your ground, your shoulder, and how you hunt.
articles.excerpt: A calm field comparison of the Beretta A400 Xtreme Plus and Benelli SBE 3 — Blink gas versus Inertia Driven, and which school fits which hunt.

articles.title: “From the Poem to the Maqnas”: A Migration Journey in Arab Memory
articles.body: Each autumn, as the air shifts and birds begin their passage over the region’s skies, an old feeling comes back. The maqnas—the traditional hunt outing, with its waiting and its quiet—is more than a day in the open country. It is a cultural word that has long lived in language and in image. Let us follow the bird on a reverse migration, from our present into heritage. In classical Arabic literature, hunting scenes were never idle decoration; they tested a poet’s power of sight. Those images took shape in the Abbasid age in what are known as tardiyyat—Abbasid hunting poems. One opening by Abu Nuwas is enough to show how he saw the scene: he sets out before the clear brightness of morning, before the dark hens begin to cluck, while night is still wrapped in its own hide—pitch-black, as if its dye had not yet been stripped away. Here the hunt is not cast as an act but as a pure visual moment: night withdrawing, the horse rising. Abu Nuwas then turns to the tools of the chase—the horse that carries him, and a hound whose household lives by the animal’s labor, whose deep-set jaws and long cheek mean gazelles meet only hardship in the drive. Beside falcon and hound, the Arabs also hunted with cheetahs—a practice that left its mark in descriptions of the leap and the strike. Today a magazine reader may never go out into the open country, and may settle for an image on a screen or a poem in an old book. Even so, the feeling stays near: a yearly rhythm that binds Arab memory to the paths of birds over desert and plain. Classical poetry did not invent that feeling; it gave it a high language, and so it became a store we return to whenever the sky begins to move. In that sense, maqnas grows wider than the outing itself. It may mean a family inheritance told at leisure, a literary image learned at school, or the distance that opens between “season news” and “reading heritage.” Contemporary readers bring scientific pictures of migration routes, and that gives the old text a second life. The poem that described the hawk or the horse celebrated precision and attention—the qualities that give a relationship with nature its depth. Arab hunting verse was not always a cry in the wild; often it was directed silence: waiting, watching, a slow account of detail. Autumn, with its migrants, gives that silence a natural stage—flocks passing, colors shifting, distances that remind us wildlife is larger than the moment of capture. From poem to maqnas, from the tardiyya to the sense of migrants in the sky, one cultural thread runs on. In the Arab imagination the hunt was always larger than a passing act; it was a way of looking, a rhythm, and one of literature’s frontiers in facing the world. When the flocks pass overhead, that old rhythm still sounds in memory—like a journey that never quite ends.

articles.title: George Taza: We Must All Take Part in Protecting Fish Stocks
articles.body: George Taza, head of the Lebanese Fishermen page. An interview with George Taza, head of the “Lebanese Fishermen” page — on illegal methods at sea, weak enforcement, women anglers, and a shared duty to protect fish stocks. The sea has its own world! Underwater we enjoy watching marine creatures, coral, and caves; on the surface we enjoy the calm of the horizon, relax under the sun, converse with moonlight, and dance to the sound of the waves… That is how George Taza — head of the “Lebanese Fishermen / الصياد اللبناني” page — sees it. From the conversation: I began this hobby on my first outing with my father in 1999. Hunters face many problems, including illegal, abusive fishing — putting poison in bread and throwing it to catch fish, blasting, or dredging — all violations with severe consequences for fish stocks. Disrespect for marine fishing laws stems from lack of accountability, absence of monitoring, and scarce awareness programmes from the relevant ministry. The state as a whole has a duty to monitor and to stop dumping waste into the sea, because it is a livelihood for many fishermen. Fishing is both a hobby and a livelihood, always in need of development. Every fisherman’s experience helps raise the level of the craft. “The sea is treacherous” — but in our lexicon it means fishing and passion; that does not cancel the need for caution and safety. The landfill project over the seal cave in Amchit was stopped by a decision of the Ministry of Environment after complaints from environmental activists and after our rapid mobilisation and posting of photos on social media. Young women compete with men in sea fishing; they have patience and composure. Often, when you reel in the line, a large fish comes to seize the one already hooked and pulls the line loaded with hooks; a fish fighting for its life can also injure you — these are among fishing’s risks. We laugh a lot when a fish slips off the hook inside the boat between our feet — and when fish leap at night as the boat moves and land aboard. The sea’s bounty is great; we must all take part in protecting fish stocks and respecting the law. What is needed: awareness in schools; monitoring fish markets; media awareness programmes; more visits to ports; and follow-up on fishermen’s problems so they become partners in conserving fish stocks.

articles.title: Tempted delivers Godolphin’s first Everest victory as attention turns to her next start
articles.body: Tempted leads a group of horses during The Everest at Randwick. The Australian filly reverses the 2025 result against Ka Ying Rising, with Flemington and Randwick among the options being considered. Tempted gave Godolphin its first Everest victory when she won the 1,200-metre sprint at Australia’s Randwick racecourse on Saturday, 17 October 2026. The four-year-old filly beat Ka Ying Rising, reversing the result of their meeting in the 2025 edition. Ridden by Chad Schofield and trained by Ciaron Maher, she defeated a rival who arrived with 21 consecutive victories. The result added one of Australia’s leading sprint titles to Godolphin’s record. Six wins in 2026 Bred by Godolphin in Australia, Tempted now has ten wins from 15 starts. The daughter of Street Boss and Calliope has won all six of her starts in 2026, including the Group One Surround Stakes and Everest. Two options for the next start Her next race has not been decided. In an interview published by Racing.com on 18 October, Godolphin Australia Racing and Bloodstock Manager Jason Walsh said the team was considering the 1,200-metre Champions Sprint at Flemington on 7 November. The 1,300-metre Russell Balding Stakes at Randwick on 31 October remains another option. The decision will depend on Tempted’s recovery and her trainer’s assessment. Experience on Flemington’s straight course could help inform plans for future campaigns, but any next destination remains a possibility until a decision is announced.
