articles.title: Neighbours in Poland, migration routes 3,750 kilometres apart
articles.body: Andrey Gulivanov / Wikimedia Commons They leave from almost the same area and head for Africa, but their routes are less alike than we might expect. Five male European honey-buzzards breed at sites no more than 60 kilometres apart, yet their migration routes diverge until they are separated by 3,750 kilometres. The contrast emerged from a study published in the Journal of Ornithology, after researchers tracked the birds in northeastern Poland between 2018 and 2024. They used four migration corridors: Gibraltar, the Apennines in Italy, the Balkans and the Bosporus. Mirski et al. / Journal of Ornithology, 2026 More strikingly, their wintering areas were much closer together than their routes, with no more than 575 kilometres between them. Neighbours at departure, widely separated paths across continents, then relatively close destinations. The same bird can change its route The differences were not only between birds. Some individuals changed their routes from year to year, taking detours around obstacles such as mountains, seas and deserts. Mirski et al. / Journal of Ornithology, 2026 Variation in migration timing was most apparent during the spring return, with clear differences in arrival dates at the breeding grounds. The researchers see the results as evidence of flexibility and individuality in route choice. The small sample of five males documents this flexibility among the tracked birds and opens the way to studying it on a larger scale. Why is the shortest route not always the best? Earlier research helps explain some of the reasons for detours in this species. In an independent study tracking 62 journeys by 12 adult birds, researchers found that seasonal detours through West Africa allow the birds to take advantage of favourable winds, reducing the energy cost of crossing the Sahara. The shortest distance on a map is not necessarily the least costly in the air. The European honey-buzzard, whose scientific name is Pernis apivorus, is a broad-winged, long-tailed raptor that spends the winter in tropical Africa. It searches bees’ and wasps’ nests for larvae, and large numbers may gather during autumn migration before crossing the Mediterranean. Yet behind a flock that seems to be heading in one direction, tracking devices reveal different stories: each bird has its own route, and that route may change from one journey to the next. Sources: Mirski, Komar and Tumiel study in the Journal of Ornithology; Independent research on wind effects in the Journal of Animal Ecology; Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB)
articles.excerpt: Five male European honey-buzzards breed close together in Poland, then take four migration corridors to Africa.

articles.title: How Can Farmers Protect Migratory Birds This Autumn?
articles.body: In these very weeks, flocks of white storks (Ciconia ciconia) and herons cross the skies of the Bekaa on their way south, while the olive harvest peaks in the mountains and along the coast — from Lebanon to Syria and Jordan. The two events are not as separate as they may seem. The agricultural calendar that governs our harvest season overlaps in time with the biological calendar followed by millions of migratory birds along the eastern Mediterranean flyway. Our olive harvest: an existing strength worth keeping Unlike some southern European countries where olive growing has shifted to intensive systems with large suction and shaking machines that work at night under floodlights — a practice official bodies there have documented as killing millions of migratory birds sleeping in the trees each year, prompting bans in some regions — harvesting in Lebanon, Syria, and Jordan remains largely manual or done with a handheld comb/shaker, and usually by day within family or community labour. That in itself is a real environmental strength our farmers deserve credit for, not only warnings drawn from others’ mistakes. Keeping this pattern — daytime picking, without turning to suction machines or strong night lighting if operations expand later — is enough to spare Lebanon the fate that hit intensive European olive estates. One practical detail still deserves attention: nets spread under the trees to gather fallen fruit, if left stretched on the ground all night without being lifted or checked in the morning, can hinder birds that feed on the ground near trunks or use neighbouring grassy patches to rest. Lifting or folding the nets at the end of each workday, instead of leaving them out between picking sessions, is a simple step that costs almost no extra time. Grain fields: a refuelling stop that needs no complex intervention Unlike the spring breeding season, when birds focus on the nest and longer-term food, their autumn needs are simpler and more urgent: quick energy, water, and a safe place to rest before continuing. Wheat and barley fields harvested in summer provide that service for free if the farmer leaves them without immediate ploughing for a few weeks, so flocks can use spilled grain as fuel for mountain bottlenecks. A small, low-edged water pond in a corner of the land is also enough to draw noticeable numbers of birds exhausted by the journey. Timing rodenticide in orchards In olive and fruit orchards, some farmers use rodent poisons around trunks or storage sheds. The problem is that raptors such as the common kestrel (Falco tinnunculus) and owls, which feed specifically on these rodents and form a free natural defence line against them, suffer secondary poisoning when they eat a poisoned rodent. Better to avoid these pesticides or cut them back during the peak of passage itself, and rely on resident and passing raptors as the alternative control tool. Living hedgerows: shelter that costs nothing Native shrubs along field edges, instead of wire or metal fencing, give passing flocks safe rest points from wind and predators, plus wild fruit that adds another energy source at this exact time of year. The greatest danger remains the gun, not the plough However careful farming practices become, the first danger to these flocks has nothing to do with agriculture at all: indiscriminate shooting by irresponsible individuals at entire flocks in passage — a practice specialist organisations document every year, and one that sometimes turns into mass slaughter of fully protected species, unrelated to any legally permitted quarry. That is precisely the focus of the current autumn campaign run by the APU unit of MECSHAP in cooperation with CABS, which we recently announced in Sayd to protect migration corridors this season. Alongside that direct threat sits a different kind of environmental harm: military operations in southern Lebanon in recent years left wide destruction of forests and farmland — Lebanese official estimates speak of some 16,000 hectares burned, including thousands of dunams of age-old olive trees, and more than a fifth of the south’s agricultural and woodland area — and the south itself sits on one of the most important flyways millions of birds use between Europe and Africa twice a year. Losing plant cover and natural stopover points there deepens the fragility of flocks already worn down by thousands of kilometres of flight. A shared duty: the farmer’s field and the sustainable hunter’s gun The farmer who waits a few weeks before ploughing, and the sustainable hunter who tells lawful quarry from a protected passing flock, serve the same goal from two places: a living environment able to renew itself season after season. Neither has to sacrifice their interest for the other — only some awareness of when and how farm work is done, so that autumn shifts from a season of risk for birds into a safe passage worthy of Lebanon and the Levant’s long history as a natural corridor for their migration.
articles.excerpt: As the olive harvest peaks and white storks cross the Bekaa, simple farm steps can protect migratory birds on the eastern Mediterranean flyway.

articles.title: Seven Migratory Birds Extinct or Presumed Extinct in 150 Years
articles.body: The last photo of the Slender-billed Curlew taken by Chris Gomersall at Merja Zerga, Morocco on 2 February 1995. An environmental investigation into seven migratory bird species that are extinct or presumed extinct, drawing on BirdLife International data. On 2 February 1995, Chris Gomersall photographed a Slender-billed Curlew (Numenius tenuirostris) at Merja Zerga, Morocco — the last photo of the species. No one knew then that history would record that sighting as the last confirmed appearance on Earth of the bird. Today, with the release of BirdLife’s State of the World’s Birds report, doubt has hardened into a bleak certainty: its extinction has been formally declared, placing it among seven migratory bird species that have become extinct or are presumed extinct over the past 150 years. Not all seven are classified as confirmed extinctions. The report shows that a migration route is not an imaginary line on a map but a “tightly linked chain”: break one link — whether a breeding bog in Siberia or a feeding bay in the Mediterranean — and the whole life cycle of the species collapses. Case files: seven extinct or presumed extinct species A review of the organisation’s historical records shows that six of these birds were lost in the Americas, while the latest and most shocking loss fell on the Eurasian–African mainland: 1. Slender-billed Curlew — the latest casualty Date of fall: Formally declared extinct in the organisation’s latest assessments (after decades of absence since 1995). Extinction scenario: Its extinction is the first of its kind for a bird on the Eurasian–African mainland in modern history. The puzzle of its disappearance exposes weak protection of long-haul flyways; despite exhaustive tracking attempts, its flocks faded as peatlands and wetlands in its likely breeding grounds were drained, tidal flats it used to rest on around the Mediterranean were destroyed, and indiscriminate hunting pressed along its migration line. 2. Passenger Pigeon — from billions to zero Martha, a passenger pigeon — the last of her species — died at the Cincinnati Zoo on 1 September 1914, age 29. Her body was donated to the Smithsonian Institution. Mounted with the notation: “MARTHA, last of her species, died at 1 p.m., 1 September 1914, age 29, in the Cincinnati Zoological Garden. EXTINCT.” Date of fall: September 1914 (with the death of the female “Martha” in her cage at Cincinnati Zoo). Extinction scenario: The twentieth century’s most infamous environmental crime. It once filled North American skies with flocks that blocked the sun and were counted in the billions, then faced industrial commercial hunting to sell as cheap meat, alongside the felling of the deciduous forests whose mast it fed on — breaking its mass-breeding system and wiping it out in a few decades. (Ectopistes migratorius) 3. Eskimo Curlew — sport shooting at stopovers Esquimaux Curlew (Eskimo Curlew), Plate 208 — John James Audubon’s Birds of America. Courtesy of the John James Audubon Center at Mill Grove, Montgomery County Audubon Collection, and Zebra Publishing. Date of fall: Listed as Critically Endangered and Possibly Extinct (last decisive documentation 1963). Extinction scenario: It flew a punishing route from arctic tundra toward South America. The bird was drained during exhausted stopovers on the American Great Plains, where hunters targeted it by the millions for food markets, as prairie steppe was turned into farmland that upended its diet. (Numenius borealis) 4. Labrador Duck — fatal dietary specialisation Pied Duck (Labrador Duck), Plate 332 — John James Audubon’s Birds of America (male adult and female). Courtesy of the John James Audubon Center at Mill Grove, Montgomery County Audubon Collection, and Zebra Publishing. Date of fall: 1878 (the first of the seven to vanish in this era). Extinction scenario: A unique sea duck with a lined bill built for picking small molluscs and crustaceans on North American coasts. The feather and egg trade, pollution of river mouths, and the decline of molluscs under settler activity finished off numbers that were already fragile. (Camptorhynchus labradorius) 5. Bachman’s Warbler — axe victims in winter and summer A male Bachman’s Warbler, in one of the last photographs taken of this species.Photo: Jerry A. Payne, USDA Agricultural Research Service, Bugwood.org (1958). Date of fall: Late 1980s (last documented sighting 1988). Extinction scenario: A small songbird migrating between southern U.S. swamps and Cuban forests. It faced a death sentence from both ends: drainage of swamp forests in its northern home, and conversion of Cuban winter woods into sugarcane estates, leaving it nowhere to shelter on either half of its journey. (Vermivora bachmanii) 6. Jamaican Petrel — traps of invasive animals Jamaican Petrel, adult — illustration by Joseph Smit, 1866 (Proceedings of the Zoological Society of London). Date of fall: 1879 (listed Critically Endangered and strongly Possibly Extinct). Extinction scenario: A seabird that nested in ground burrows in Jamaica’s highlands. The disaster was not at sea but on its return to land: colonists introduced mongoose and rats to control rodents, and they preyed on this bird’s eggs and helpless chicks in their earth nests. (Pterodroma caribbaea) 7. Guadalupe Storm-petrel — islands turned into graves Oceanodroma macrodactyla — male Guadalupe petrel (mount, FMNH 33449, Field Museum of Natural History, Chicago).Photo: James St. John (CC BY 2.0). Date of fall: Around 1912. Extinction scenario: It inhabited Guadalupe Island off Mexico. Goats brought by people destroyed the thin plant cover that sheltered its nesting burrows, while feral cats left on the island finished off adults and chicks until total extinction. (Hydrobates macrodactylus)

articles.title: Macho hunting… when some look for their manhood among bird carcasses!
articles.body: Photos received by the Anti-Poaching Unit team, October 2026. Among the strangest sights we see on social media are photographs of people standing proudly in front of dozens of dead birds, lining them up on cars or spreading them across the ground, holding their shotguns with triumphant expressions, as though they had returned from a historic battle in which they had achieved a great victory! More amusing still, some of them use their companions’ game, or pool the take of several hunters, and sometimes even borrow birds from other people’s refrigerators to complete the picture of heroism they seek! It seems that, for some, heroism can now be borrowed, and even stored in refrigerators! But what kind of heroism is this? And what kind of manhood needs dozens of carcasses to prove its existence? Hunting is a sport of courage, patience, skill and challenge, founded on knowledge of nature and respect for it, and on an ethical code that makes hunters responsible for their actions. Sustainable hunting is a culture that protects wildlife and ensures that the sport continues for future generations. A professional hunter is known for his experience, conduct and respect for nature. He knows his worth well and does not need to display bird carcasses to convince others of his skill. Adonis Alkhateeb, Editor-in-Chief, during an anti-poaching field activity in Lebanon, October 2026. As for our friend who needs this spectacle to feel important, perhaps he is trying to make up for a status he lacks, or gain admiration he cannot earn through a genuine achievement. Let us imagine for a moment that the bird carries a shotgun, just like the hunter who fires at it. Would we see the same display? Would our friend stand with his chest puffed out before an opponent equally capable of fighting back? It is very easy to manufacture heroism when the other side is unable to defend itself! Sadly, these displays damage the reputation of respectable hunters and turn a time-honoured sport into scenes of killing and boasting, degrading life and dismissing the values of compassion affirmed by ethics and religious teachings. Even Lebanese Law No. 580/2004, in Article 8, expressly prohibits displaying hunted game outside cars and on public roads. What a disgrace! Birds that have travelled thousands of kilometres and overcome storms and dangers during migration end their lives as part of an absurd spectacle, while the man behind it waits for a few likes and comments! More ironic still, some even boast about game they did not hunt! Gentlemen, hunting is about ethics and responsibility, and respect for one’s quarry is part of a hunter’s self-respect. And anyone who convinces others that he is strong, brave and important should ask himself how real that strength and courage are. Manhood is not measured by the number of birds we kill, and a hunter’s worth shows in his ethics and respect for life. As for anyone searching for his manhood among bird carcasses, he would do better to look for it somewhere else!

articles.title: Hunting Tourism in the Arab Gulf Countries
articles.body: In a three-part investigation, Sayd explores hunting tourism programmes across the Arab world, from traditional hunting trips to accommodation, guiding services and local products. We begin in the Gulf, then move to the Maghreb, and conclude with Egypt, Iraq and Jordan, exploring how these experiences connect with tourism and local development. Source: Abu Dhabi Media Office Camps in northern Saudi Arabia, falcons and Saluki hounds in Al Dhafra, hunting linked to a resort in Al Ain, and game from Qatari farms. Behind these trips are accommodation, guiding, transport and breeding services, while the knowledge and crafts of desert communities become part of a tourism offering with its own visitors and bookings. At Saudi Arabia’s Al Shamal Reserve, a group of hunting enthusiasts can choose a camp for twelve people, with six sleeping tents, a traditional woven tent and a dining tent. Larger groups can book a camp for thirty-one guests, with fifteen sleeping tents, a main suite, a kitchen and outdoor seating areas. A guide specialising in the environment and hunting accompanies the guests. These are the details of a trip built around traditional hunting: where does the visitor stay, who accompanies them, and how do they spend their time in the desert? The Saudi experience, alongside Al Marzoom and Barari in the UAE and Al Jnoub Reserve in Qatar, reveals different sides of a market that combines hunting with hospitality and gives desert heritage a place in tourism programmes. Northern Saudi Arabia: a camp, a guide and products from the local community Established in 2022, Al Shamal Sustainable Hunting Reserve covers around two thousand square kilometres within the Imam Turki bin Abdullah Royal Reserve. Its experiences range from hunting houbara bustards with falcons to hunting gazelles with Saluki hounds or designated firearms, and Arabian oryx with firearms, according to the reserve’s rules and the type of programme. The hunter is a guest… and a customer for the artisan At Saudi Arabia’s Al Shamal Reserve, home-based producers display their crafts and products for hunting visitors. Accommodation ranges from camps to an eco-lodge offering bedrooms, a majlis reception room, a kitchen and outdoor seating areas. This variety makes it possible to arrange a trip for a group of friends or choose a more private stay, while keeping the day’s hunting and hospitality services at the same destination. Source: Al Shamal Sustainable Hunting Reserve Behind the game is a process that begins before the visitor arrives. The authority has explained that the programme relies on breeding game and preparing it to adapt to the natural environment before release, with hunting limited to specified numbers. Through this approach, breeding and field management become part of running the destination, alongside the camps and guest accompaniment. Source: Imam Turki bin Abdullah Royal Reserve Development Authority The local community has a direct place in the experience. The reserve has set aside an area where home-based producers display traditional products and handicrafts. This space connects visitors with local people, allowing them to discover and buy what they make. Across the wider royal reserve, the authority also trains local residents in ecotourism guiding, falcon handling and honey production, and supports artisans and small-business owners. The Darb Zubaydah Winter Festival provides temporary jobs and opportunities for home-based producers to take part. This setting places the hunting trip within a broader tourism activity connecting the desert with heritage and local markets. Source: Saudi Press Agency Source: Saudi Press Agency Al Marzoom: the falcon leads the journey in Al Dhafra In Abu Dhabi’s Al Dhafra region, Al Marzoom Reserve retains the rhythm of traditional hunting. Visitors are divided into groups accompanied by experienced field guides, and hunt with falcons and Saluki hounds, without firearms. The game includes houbara bustards, hares and antelopes, while travel within the reserve and overnight stays in its camps complete the experience. Hunting… without a bullet! At Al Marzoom in Abu Dhabi, hunting is with falcons and Saluki hounds, not guns. Here, the guide is part of the trip’s value: knowing the place, accompanying the group and guiding it through an experience different from a wildlife-watching tour. Overnight options range from the Royal Camp and Elite Camp to the Individuals Camp, while the desert setting allows visitors to discover its plants and wildlife. Since opening in 2015, the reserve has welcomed falconry enthusiasts and tourists from Arab countries and beyond. The details of hospitality add a social dimension to the hunt. Falconers can take their game away or cook it at the campsite, and activities at the destination include camel riding, guided tours and traditional cooking. The experience thus extends beyond the hunting hours to time spent in camp and with companions. Al Marzoom also features in Sayd’s early archives: the magazine covered its opening in November 2015, then documented its reception of falconers from Saudi Arabia and Qatar in February 2017 as part of an experience-exchange programme. This history highlights the destination’s role in bringing hunting enthusiasts from the region’s countries together around a shared experience. Barari in Al Ain: hunting enters the resort world In Remah, Al Ain, Barari Hunting, associated with Telal Resort, offers a model combining hunting experiences with desert accommodation facilities. The operator offers three types of game: Arabian oryx, sand gazelle and the mountain gazelle known as damani. For international bookings and enquiries, it lists agents in Spain and Romania, alongside direct contact with its team in the UAE. Not everyone on the trip is a hunter! At Telal in Al Ain, companions can enjoy horse riding, camel riding and safaris alongside the hunting programme. In an interview with Khaleej Times published in September 2026, Barari’s hunting manager, Saif Al Saleh, explained that the operator provides firearms, vehicles and professional supervision, and that participants do not bring their own weapons. He said the game intended for this experience is captive-bred and hunted under the supervision of the Environment Agency – Abu Dhabi. In this model, equipment and accompaniment are services supplied by the operator itself. Telal Resort, meanwhile, offers accommodation and activities including camel and horse riding and desert safaris. These options give companions a programme of their own, allowing one visit to bring together people who have come to hunt and others who have chosen to stay and explore the desert. Source: Telal Resort Al Ain The link between hunting and hospitality also appears in the project’s investment structure. Alpha Dhabi Group’s 2025 financial statements list Telal Resort among the companies of Mawarid Holding Investment, with its stated activities combining hotel and resort management with the operation of sport-hunting reserves. It is a clear illustration of hunting experiences becoming part of the tourism and accommodation business. Qatar: a journey connecting camp and farm In southern Qatar, Al Jnoub Reserve combines traditional hunting with camping across terrain ranging from sand to rock and vegetation. The model’s distinctive feature begins with the source of its game: it is bred on Qatari farms, numbered and released under the reserve management’s inspection. The Ministry of Environment and Climate Change explains that this approach aims to ease pressure on wild game and allow its numbers to increase. The game’s journey begins on the farm At Qatar’s Al Jnoub Reserve, local farms breed game that is numbered and released under the reserve’s supervision. The reserve offers a large camp with a majlis, four sleeping tents and a kitchen, and a smaller one with a majlis, two sleeping tents and a kitchen. Its services include vehicles equipped for hunting, while the game list includes hares, houbara bustards, stone-curlews and antelopes. Source: Qatar’s Ministry of Environment and Climate Change The programme is booked through the reserve’s app, and hunting methods are limited to falcons and hunting dogs. Operational details include the provision of water, fuel, daily cleaning services and transport of visitors’ belongings to the camps, with shops at the main headquarters. Private cars are not allowed into the reserve, and movement and hunting arrangements are subject to its management’s instructions. Source: Qatar’s Ministry of Environment and Climate Change These details show how work is distributed around a single trip: a farm breeds the game, a team prepares the camp, a service transports belongings, and workers handle cleaning and supplies. In this local network, the pursuit of traditional hunting meets services that visitors need throughout their stay. Where does the value of the trip go? From Al Shamal to Al Dhafra, Al Ain and southern Qatar, some operational elements are similar, while the character of each experience differs. Falcons and hunting dogs are central to Al Marzoom and Al Jnoub; hunting methods are more varied at Al Shamal; and the Barari model adds outfitted hunting services to a resort stay. These differences allow hunters to choose between a heritage-centred trip, a group stay in camp and an experience combining hunting with hotel services. The value of the trip is spread across accommodation, transport, specialist guiding, meals and camp equipment, alongside game breeding and the management of releases. The involvement of home-based producers at Al Shamal adds a channel linking visitor spending with local crafts and products. A destination’s opportunities grow when companions also find things to do. Camel and horse rides, nature exploration and desert stays add other activities to the trip, allowing family members or friends with different interests to take part. This is where organising the whole programme matters: hunting attracts enthusiasts, while hospitality makes the destination suitable for a stay that others can share with them. These Gulf experiences show the practical elements of hunting tourism: an identified location, an operator responsible for services, specified game and hunting methods, and accommodation linked to the programme. At their heart remain people with expertise, from guides and falconers to breeding and hospitality workers and artisans. Through them, the details of the trip become work, and heritage finds a place in the local economy. Sources: Saudi Press Agency, Imam Turki bin Abdullah Royal Reserve Development Authority, Abu Dhabi Media Office, UAE Ministry of Climate Change and Environment, Qatar’s Ministry of Environment and Climate Change, the operators, and Sayd’s archives. articles.title: Hunting Tourism in the Maghreb
articles.body: A hunter at El Koudia in Morocco, as identified by the organiser. From European travel agencies to lodges, guides and local teams: how do hunting trips generate services and income in Morocco and Tunisia, and what does Algeria need to broaden its appeal as a hunting-tourism destination? A trip may begin in an office in Paris or London, but that office cannot deliver a day’s hunting on its own. Behind it are a driver welcoming the group, a lodge preparing rooms, a guide who knows the terrain and a team handling meals and work in the field. Across the Maghreb, these services come together in packages marketed by European and local agencies to enthusiasts who visit for a few days and spend on much more than game. After exploring the Gulf, Sayd turns in this second instalment to a different market: proximity to Europe, programmes for partridge, small game and wild boar, and businesses providing local organisation. Morocco and Tunisia offer commercial examples and statistics that reveal the outlines of this activity, while Algeria raises the question of how hunting regulation can translate into a complete tourism product. A hunting dog carrying game, from DHD-Laïka’s small-game programme in Morocco. Morocco: from three days in the field to a stay in Marrakech According to figures from Morocco’s National Agency for Water and Forests reported by 2M, hunting tourism welcomed around 5,000 visiting hunters during the 2025–2026 season, and the sector comprises 146 specialist companies. This is a base of visitors and organisers extending beyond isolated individual trips. The offers show how European demand reaches Moroccan terrain. French agency DHD-Laïka advertises a programme between Rabat and Tangier with three hunting days and four nights, starting at €2,750 per hunter for groups of five or more. It includes flights from Paris, excluding airport taxes, accommodation, meals, transfers, guides, porters and permits. The package spans international travel and services at the destination; its entire price does not flow into the local economy. In a different model aimed at private groups, Britain’s William Powell Sporting markets El Koudia in the Jbilet hills near Marrakech: two days for eight hunters at an advertised team price of €40,400. Field staff, hospitality, transfers, permits and the equipment specified in the offer are included; hotel accommodation is not. Marrakech also offers non-hunting companions places to stay, sights to visit and shopping, extending the trip beyond time spent hunting. Yet the two products are not the same experience. At El Koudia, the marketer explains that reared birds are released before the season. This differs from a programme based on wild game. Each model requires management and environmental monitoring; neither bird density nor a high price establishes sustainability. The Moroccan organiser also has a place in the legal framework. Hunting-tourism rules link the reception of non-resident visiting hunters to an authorised organiser and require staffing, an investment project and a leased hunting area. The local partner is therefore more than a sales intermediary: it carries responsibilities for managing both the trip and the area. Two hunters in the field during a Tunisian wild-boar drive, as described by DHD-Laïka. more than the price of game Rooms and meals, transport and guiding, field work and fees: these are the services within a hunting trip. Local communities’ share depends on wages, purchases and local contracts, not the package price alone. Hunters and a camera crew after a hunt, with two wild boars; from Chasse Sanglier Tunisie. Tunisia: a clear French market—and teams from villages In Tunisia, the figures provide a tangible picture of visitors and public revenue. The National Report on the State of the Environment and Sustainable Development for 2022 records 606 visiting hunters in the 2021–2022 season, including 532 French nationals. Treasury receipts from hunting tourism reached 300,233 Tunisian dinars. This is a historical total of fees and public revenue associated with the activity, not visitors’ total spending or organisers’ profits. France remains visible in the marketing. DHD-Laïka advertises a wild-boar programme with five hunting days and six nights for €2,390 per person in groups of ten to twelve. It describes employing a team of fifteen to twenty beaters from villages, alongside hotels, transport and local organisation. These services create opportunities for seasonal work in villages, tied to trip dates rather than necessarily providing permanent, year-round jobs. Within Tunisia, Desert Rose offers programmes in Spanish, providing another channel to European customers. The advantage is not simply language: a local agency brings knowledge of the region together with accommodation, transport and group reception. Tunisian regulations give this role practical substance. Hunting tourism is organised by Tunisian travel agencies and hotel establishments under rules that include accompaniment by a guide, insurance and obtaining hunting permits in advance. When a responsible organiser oversees the trip, monitoring participants and game becomes part of the service rather than something left to the visitor. Treasury revenue, not turnover 300,233 Tunisian dinars: Treasury receipts from hunting tourism in the 2021–2022 season, according to the national environment report. The figure does not automatically include spending on hotels, transport and meals, nor establish that all of it was earmarked for nature conservation. Algeria: regulation alone does not create a destination Algerian legislation explicitly addresses hunting tourism, linking it to a tourism agency and specific conditions, including areas where game is artificially bred. The Directorate-General of Forests announced the opening of the 2026–2027 hunting season for 10 October, as reported by Algeria Press Service. Opening the general season, however, is different from making a fully compliant programme available to foreign hunting tourists. Developing this activity into a broader tourism product requires bringing together the elements of the trip: an agency to receive visitors, a suitable hunting area, accommodation, transport, guiding and a clearly defined programme that can be marketed and booked. The Moroccan and Tunisian examples show that geography alone is not enough. What visitors buy is an organised trip from arrival to departure. Mauritania: an opportunity raised in development plans In Mauritania, the operational assessment of the tourism strategy, prepared in 2017 with support from the United Nations Development Programme and published by the ministry, considered the potential revival of hunting tourism under strict, enforced regulation and coordination between the tourism and environment sectors. This approach puts management before expansion. It is a historical planning proposal, not an announcement of a hunting programme operating today. From seasonal income to a lasting resource The Maghreb’s examples show where value can arise: in lodges and hotels, through drivers, guides, cooks and field workers, and in fees collected by the state. Companions and other tourism activities can broaden spending rather than confining a visit to a single day’s hunting. Turning an opportunity into development, however, takes more than increasing visitor numbers. Contracts, wages and local purchasing determine what remains in the area, while training, safety and predictable seasons influence the quality and continuity of work. Game and habitats, meanwhile, require scientific monitoring, quotas and enforcement: pressure on the natural resource can undermine the very activity on which livelihoods depend. Calling a trip “sustainable” in an advertisement is therefore not enough. The test is whether it combines legal, accountable activity with services that benefit local people and management that safeguards the resource for future seasons. At that intersection, hunting tourism becomes more than a brief visit: an opportunity for a local economy that deserves careful organisation, measurement and protection. Sources: Morocco’s National Agency for Water and Forests, as reported by 2M; Tunisia’s National Report on the State of the Environment and Sustainable Development for 2022; legislation governing hunting tourism in Morocco, Tunisia and Algeria; Algeria Press Service; the 2017 assessment of Mauritania’s tourism strategy; published offers from organisers. The prices cited come from commercial offers checked on 23 October 2026, not market averages or confirmation of booking availability. From the series: Hunting Tourism in the Arab Gulf Countries. Next instalment: Hunting Tourism in Egypt, Iraq and Jordan. Photo sources: William Powell Sporting, DHD-Laïka, Chasse Sanglier Tunisie

articles.title: Illegal Hunting Destroys the Hunting Hobby… Beware of Mist Nets, Birdlime, and Night Hunting
articles.body: A bird is freed from a mist net. Illegal methods — nets, birdlime, night shooting — destroy the hobby. Illegal hunting — mist nets, birdlime, electronic callers, and night shooting — is a major threat to migratory and endangered birds in Lebanon, and to the ethical sport of hunting itself. Illegal hunting (“poaching” / al-sayd al-ja’ir) is a major problem in Lebanon. Many migratory and threatened bird species — including raptors, the White Stork, Turtle Dove, and Golden Oriole — are killed during their annual passage through the country. Hunting often uses illegal methods such as mist nets, birdlime, and electronic bird callers, and is frequently carried out outside the hunting season and in spring, the birds’ breeding season. These methods serve both personal take and commercial ends, with small birds sold to restaurants and cage-bird shops. Sadly, over the past twenty years night hunting has appeared as a multi-method practice: besides electronic devices, the indiscriminate shooter lights a tree, paints a tree on a wall and lights it, or uses lasers and spotlights to kill birds at night — especially thrushes (samman) in large numbers — with a clear impact on their populations. Illegal hunting does not only threaten bird numbers; it also undermines the work of conservation advocates, ecologists, and the responsible hunter to protect these species — especially those at risk of extinction. Competent authorities have adopted laws and regulations against illegal hunting, but enforcement is often lax, particularly amid the crises the country faces. Irresponsible hunting also endangers people: hunting accidents and the use of shot are sources of concern. Environmental organisations therefore work to raise awareness and to call for stricter enforcement of land-hunting laws in Lebanon.

articles.title: Hunting in Jordan: Understanding Licences, Seasons and Species Protection
articles.body: Agriculture Law Article 56: licences, protected wildlife and prohibited methods, distinct from annual season decisions. Al Khazneh in Petra, Jordan Terrestrial hunting in Jordan is governed by a framework combining licences, species protection and restrictions on where and when hunting may take place. Agriculture Law No. 13 of 2015, as amended, is a central reference. Article 56 addresses wild birds and wild animals. This explainer concerns an established framework; it does not announce new legislation or the opening of a hunting season. The Ministry of Agriculture lists the law and its amendments in its official legislation catalogue. The law empowers the agriculture minister to issue instructions covering licensing, hunting areas, dates and protected species. The Royal Society for the Conservation of Nature (RSCN) states that the wildlife protection committee determines areas, seasons and permitted numbers annually, with announcements published through RSCN. Hunters therefore need to check the relevant species, day, location and quota alongside their licence. Last year's dates cannot establish permission for this year. RSCN hunting regulation. RSCN provides an online hunting-licence application service. The ministry's published 2015 service guide also identifies hunting-firearm documentation and Interior Ministry approval within the licensing process. This illustrates why firearm requirements need separate attention. Because that guide is historical, applicants should confirm current documents and charges with the responsible authority rather than treat it as a 2026 checklist. Historical 2015 agricultural service guide. Article 56 sets restrictions beyond licensing. Hunting is prohibited inside nature and grazing reserves and in specified inhabited areas. It also prohibits vehicles, spotlights and automatic weapons in hunting, alongside poisons, adhesives and certain capture methods. Nests, eggs and young animals receive protection, while hunting birds of prey and predatory wild animals requires ministerial approval. Protected species are classified into three lists according to their degree of protection. Agriculture Law, Article 56. Depending on the offence, consequences include fines, imprisonment and confiscation of wildlife, equipment and weapons. The law also provides for increased fines for repeat offences within the specified period. The practical starting point is a valid licence, followed by verification of the official seasonal announcement, species, location and firearm requirements. This article does not confirm that any season is open on its publication date. It is general legal information, not individual legal advice. Read the full legal texts Full original Jordanian Agriculture Law 13/2015 — FAOLEX (Arabic PDF; subsequent amendments must also be consulted)

articles.title: A Jurassic bird that could not fly broadens the story of avian evolution
articles.body: A peer-reviewed Nature fossil study identifies a striking early terrestrial branch of bird evolution. Min Wang / Chinese Academy of Sciences The early history of birds was not necessarily a straight path towards more powerful flight. A newly described Late Jurassic species from southeastern China provides evidence for a different ecological experiment around 150–148 million years ago. The fossil, Yuezhuornis yangyuanensis, comes from the Zhenghe Fauna of Fujian Province. In research published in Nature on 14 October 2026, scientists describe a mosaic of bird-like and dinosaur-like anatomical features. Most notably, the forelimbs were markedly short relative to the rest of the skeleton. Comparative analyses led the authors to infer that this bird lived on the ground and was flightless. Skull, dental and foot characteristics offer further evidence that the earliest avialans followed several anatomical and ecological pathways rather than one universal trajectory. The finding does not settle when flight first evolved, nor does it show that every early bird was flightless. Whether this particular lineage inherited or subsequently lost flight capabilities is part of the larger evolutionary discussion. The discovery matters because it expands the known diversity of Jurassic birds at a time when fossils remain exceptionally rare. Original research: Xu, Wang et al., Nature, 14 October 2026. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-10972-z. Original peer-reviewed research

articles.title: Among Cedar Peaks and Valley Shadows: Hiking and Camping in Lebanon
articles.body: Camping on a mountain route between Sannine and Aqoura —Source: Wikiloc. In Lebanon, the scenery changes quickly between the coast and the mountains: a village perched above a deep valley gives way to cedar woodland and cool air. Walkers, wildlife watchers and photographers can choose a day on the trail or a night at a suitable campsite. The Lebanon Mountain Trail, one section at a time The Lebanon Mountain Trail runs about 470 kilometres from Andqet in the north to Marjayoun in the south. Its 27 sections cross more than 75 towns and villages. You need not walk it end to end: choose a section that suits your time and fitness, then check an updated map or consult a local guide for the start, return route and water stops. The appeal extends beyond altitude. The trail passes farms, villages and mountain paths, offering encounters with the people and history of the land as well as its peaks. On the Lebanon Mountain Trail —Source: Wikimedia Commons. Qadisha, a valley of landscape and memory In the Qadisha Valley, steep cliffs rise above old monasteries and caves. Walks near Qannoubine and Qozhaya reveal different views with the season and the light. Some descents are demanding, so pick a marked route suited to your group and keep well back from exposed edges. The rocky walls of the Qadisha Valley —Source: Wikimedia Commons. Cedars and waterfalls The cedar landscapes of the Shouf, Tannourine, Ehden and Bentael offer walks, birdwatching and photography. Each protected area has its own trails and rules; ask its managers which routes are open and check conditions before setting out. Near Tannourine, the Baatara Gorge waterfall, also known as Balou Balaa, adds a striking geological sight. Its flow varies with rainfall and season, while wet rock and cliff edges demand care. Balou Balaa near Tannourine; flow changes with the season —Source: Wikimedia Commons. A night under the stars Choose an organised campsite with basic services, or a site where the landowner or responsible authority explicitly allows overnight stays. Wild camping is not a blanket permission. Overnight stays and fires are prohibited in protected places including the Shouf Cedar Nature Reserve under its published rules. Check the site’s conditions and access before travelling, and light a fire only where local rules expressly permit one. Mountain temperatures can fall quickly even in spring, summer or autumn. Carry enough water, warm layers, suitable footwear, a light and a charged phone; tell someone your route and expected return. Pack out every item of litter, stay on paths and respect farmland and wildlife. The best photograph is one you can take without leaving a trace behind. Plan with the Lebanon Mountain Trail Association, UNESCO’s Qadisha Valley listing and the relevant reserve managers.

articles.title: Lebanon's Hunting Law 580/2004: Why an open season does not authorize every hunt
articles.body: A statutory guide to permits, protected birds, prohibited methods and no-hunting areas. Raouche Rocks in Beirut, Lebanon An announcement opening a hunting season does not override the underlying legislation. Lebanon's Hunting Law 580, dated 25 February 2004 and published in the Official Gazette on 4 March 2004, establishes lasting rules on eligible species, licensing, prohibited methods and protected places. Article 4 treats wild resident and migratory birds and mammals as protected unless they are designated as permissible quarry under applicable conditions. The season dates are determined through a separate implementing measure; they are not a general permission to shoot any bird. Article 6 requires a hunting licence issued by the Ministry of Environment, supported by the relevant firearms authorization and third-party liability insurance. Article 8 prohibits hunting in cities, villages and nature reserves, and includes a buffer of at least 500 metres from dwellings, places of worship and public or private facilities. Article 9 prohibits trapping nets, birdlime, other indiscriminate devices, spotlights and recorded bird calls used to attract quarry, alongside additional restrictions. Article 10 protects wild nests, eggs and young throughout the year. Responsible hunting therefore involves more than observing a calendar. This article explains the original 2004 law, not a newly enacted 2026 law. For any specific legal action, consult subsequent amendments, regulations and current official decisions. Source: Lebanon's Ministry of Environment, Hunting Law 580/2004, Articles 3, 4, 6, 8, 9 and 10. Original statute at the official source

articles.title: Leen Araji: Equestrian Champion and Mental Math Champion
articles.body: Leen Araji — jumping champion and mental-math talent. Equestrian sport answers not to age but to the will to challenge. Sayd meets Leen Araji — a Lebanese jumping champion and a world-ranked mental math talent. Equestrian sport is not subject to the will of age, but to the will to challenge and to strong resolve. That is why it is a kind of special arithmetic, with special equations, that reaches its goals in a leap of light. Leen Araji is an equestrian champion with a Lebanese signature — and a mental math champion with a global one. Sayd held this conversation with her. She said in the interview: I was introduced to horses at the age of 10, trained by my cousin Sheikh Omran Araji, who was hard on me so I would achieve the best performance. The Araji family has long been known for loving and keeping horses. Horses give confidence and strengthen personal force. My first jump was in a Beirut competition. I felt no fear because I was determined not to fear; the feeling was beautiful, and I sensed I had to clear every fence the same way. We must calculate every step — in a horse jump or in a leap of life. That idea strengthened my mental math and my win in “Genius Map”: I ranked third in the Beqaa and fourth worldwide. I also want to become a world equestrian champion and to compete outside Lebanon. A horse feels the rider’s fear, and for that reason may turn against them and throw them. A rider should try several horses to understand their mistakes better and correct them through experience. Of course I would love to have a farm. I know enough about the horse world, but I do not enjoy training horses myself. In training we jump at heights of 100 cm; in competitions, between 60 and 90 cm. To date I have entered nine competitions and won seven of them. I do not have my own horse. I love “Doha” because she was the first mare I trained on and still do; if I had my own horse I would name him “Reem.” Outside equestrian sport my hobbies are swimming and boxing. If I marry one day, I will make my husband love horses. I could never eat horse meat — quite simply, I do not eat meat. I love competing in all Arab countries, but I lean toward Jordan. I have fallen from the horse more than once; once I broke my arm and stopped training for four months — but nothing keeps me from continuing, as the saying goes: “If we don’t fall, we don’t learn.” I love both: math and horses. A rider’s heart loves everything.

articles.title: Little Grebe: diving among reeds, where residents meet winter visitors
articles.body: Little Grebe A Little Grebe disappears below the surface and reappears away from the observer’s original view. Its small size conceals a busy life: diving for food, building among aquatic plants and sometimes carrying chicks on its back. An autumn sighting is not necessarily a migrant; in several Arab wetlands, residents meet winter visitors. [11] Identity Arabic name: الغطاس الصغير, documented in The Birds of Saudi Arabia. The scientific name is Tachybaptus ruficollis; the French name is Grèbe castagneux. It belongs to Podicipedidae, order Podicipediformes, not the duck family. AviList v2026 includes tricolor within the species while identifying a need for wider review of species limits in this complex. The listed global conservation category is Least Concern, LC. [1] [2] [8] Plumage, age and sex Breeding plumage combines a dark head with chestnut cheeks and foreneck and a pale patch at the bill base. Outside this plumage the face and neck become paler and less contrasting. Young birds retain pale and dark head and neck striping; chick markings should not be mistaken for another species. [6] The sexes look similar, and colour intensity alone cannot reliably sex a bird in an ordinary photograph. The ringing guide gives a length of about 25–29 cm and notes that ageing may require flight-feather examination. Field recognition therefore combines small size, head and bill shape and neck pattern rather than one colour. Several unobtrusive views are more useful than chasing the bird for a closer photograph. [7] Black-necked Grebe Podiceps nigricollis differs in breeding plumage through its black head and neck and golden feather tufts behind the eyes; these seasonal features must not be projected onto a pale winter bird. [14] Arab seasonality: residents and visitors In Saudi Arabia the reference describes a rare breeding resident and common winter visitor, distributed patchily, with winter occurrence from September to March. The UAE’s February 2026 checklist calls it a common resident and locally common migrant and winter visitor; the first confirmed breeding was at Kalba in April 1989. Neither statement means that all Gulf birds migrate or that abundance is uniform across countries. [2] [4] Lebanon has local resident and summer-breeding populations, including at Aammiq, Anjar and Oyun el Samak. The 2020 checklist records winter reinforcement chiefly in November–late February and passage in September–late November and mid-March–late April. The Tunisian study published in 2024 describes it as sedentary and records it during winter 2020–2021. An autumn increase therefore cannot automatically be assigned to arrival from abroad without tracking evidence. [3] [5] An original nesting study confirms breeding at Lake Tonga in northeast Algeria. The IUCN country list also includes Morocco, Egypt, Iraq, Oman, Yemen and Sudan; country inclusion establishes occurrence, not the residency or breeding calendar of every population. Its distribution extends beyond these examples, but local seasonality requires local evidence. [9] [10] In Egypt, the Lake Burullus KBA account lists Little Grebe among breeders, based on historical documentation and a latest assessment dated 2016, not a new count. Iraq’s Central Marsh surveys in October 2013–June 2014 classified it as resident and confirmed breeding through juvenile sightings. [12] [13] Habitat, food and behaviour It uses ponds, lakes, reservoirs and basins combining open water with emergent vegetation, sometimes entering brackish water. Food is mainly insects and larvae, supplemented by molluscs, crustaceans, amphibians and small fish, many caught by diving. An artificial pond can have ecological value, but the presence of a grebe alone does not prove clean water or a healthy ecosystem. [2] Its repeated, whinnying trill may be heard before the bird is seen among plants. Quiet waiting helps connect a call with its source; a sound recording still requires reliable comparison and does not establish a breeding pair or nest. A feeding bird should be distinguished from direct breeding evidence such as an occupied nest or dependent chicks. [11] Nesting and life cycle Both adults build with aquatic vegetation; the nest may float, anchored to plants. They share incubation and care, cover eggs when leaving and may carry chicks on their backs. Early swimming ability is not independence from parental care. [2] [6] BTO reports a typical clutch of 4–6 eggs, incubation of about 20–21 days and fledging at about 44–48 days. These are reference values, not fixed limits for every Arab population. A study published in Ardeola in 2015 followed nesting at Lake Tonga during 2010–2012, with egg laying from late March to late July. This is valuable local evidence, not a calendar for the Gulf or Nile Valley. [8] [9] Ecological importance and threats Its food web includes insects, other invertebrates and small fish, while marginal vegetation and suitable water conditions support nesting. At Lake Tonga, nest success varied with site conditions; predation and flooding were among recorded causes of failure. Site management needs this context before attributing change to a single cause. [2] [9] Least Concern does not mean that every local population is safe. Repeated surveys at the same sites are more informative than comparing two photographs or counts made with different effort. Responsible observers avoid cutting paths through reeds or approaching nests for photographs, record date, place and approximate age where possible, and leave sex undetermined when diagnostic evidence is absent. (2015), Nest-site selection and reproductive success in northeast Algeria, Ardeola 62:113–124 [10] IUCN: Tachybaptus ruficollis, assessment and country distribution [11] RSPB: Little Grebe [12] Key Biodiversity Areas: Lake Burullus, assessment 2016 [13] Fazaa, Dunn & Whittingham (2017), Iraq’s Central Marsh [14] RSPB: Black-necked Grebe identification Photo: © El Golli Mohamed, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0. articles.title: Al-Melwah closes with 60 winners and a wider field
articles.body: A falconer holds a falcon during the exhibition’s 2026 Al-Melwah activities, photographed before the final day. Al-Melwah racing concluded on 9 October 2026 at the International Saudi Falcons and Hunting Exhibition in Malham, north of Riyadh, with 60 winners recognised over six days. According to the Saudi Press Agency report carried by UrduPoint, SAR 723,000 in prizes covered the top five places in each of the twelve heats. Two winners lead the final day The closing day featured two heats for local owners and amateurs. In the Gyr-Shaheen heat, Ali Khalifa Al-Mansouri won with “8”, followed by Baddah Al-Dosari with “Hakem” and Rashed Al-Duaij with “018”. In Gyr-Taba, Majed Al-Qahtani took first place with “Ateem”. Fahad Hajras Al-Dosari with “Jabr” and Fahad Mohammed Al-Dosari with “378” finished second and third. Twice as many heats The programme expanded from six heats last year to twelve: six for owners and amateurs and six for professionals and elite competitors. The expansion creates two competitive pathways, with five prize-winning places in each heat. Across 200 metres from the starting point, known as the sanah, to the lure, or melwah, the race tests a falcon's speed and responsiveness. It also puts the falconer's training to a practical test, bringing a living heritage into a setting where performance and results can be followed. From breeding farms to competition Entry was restricted to young falcons purchased at the International Falcon Breeders Auction. This connection gives farm-bred falcons a direct place in competition: acquisition begins at the auction, training prepares the bird, and racing tests its abilities. Alongside its awards, the expanded Al-Melwah programme offers a window into the practical skills of falconry. Racing ended on 9 October, while the exhibition programme runs through 10 October.

articles.title: From Sayd’s Memory: A Journey of Awareness and Responsibility… Personalities and Voices in Nature’s Sanctuary (2016–2024)
articles.body: Prepared by: Editorial Board Hunter Rita Habib Al-Shaar — from Sayd magazine’s archive. Since its launch, Sayd magazine was never merely a platform for hobby details and equipment. It was a dialogue space that brought together artists, poets, businesspeople, and pioneering women of the outdoors under one ethical charter: respect for nature, compliance with the law, and opposition to random hunting. Here we revisit, in a documented chronological sequence, some of the most notable conversations Sayd’s pages carried that embody this long record: March 2016 | Businessman-hunter George Khashan: “Maturity leads us to protect nature” In early 2016, businessman George Khashan offered a responsible reading of the hunter’s relationship with the wild, explaining that protecting game begins with self-discipline before fear of enforcement. He said: “I do not hunt in large quantities out of fear of the law, but so that I can keep going hunting and so the next generation can go too… There is no written law in nature itself; we are the ones who set it through our ethics and upbringing.” September 2016 | Artist Nicola Al-Asta: “Hunting is a refined sport spoiled by selfishness” In autumn 2016, the magazine met Lebanese artist Nicola Al-Asta, who spoke of his long-standing love of the mountain and offered a model of an artist who sees the gun as a means of contemplation and calm, not of boasting about bags. With his characteristic candor he said: “My mother used to consider me a ‘hapless’ hunter… but for me hunting is art, patience, and a renewal of positive energy. Hunting is a refined school of ethics, and the worst thing in it is human greed and the selfishness of turning it into a slaughter.” August 2020 | Visual artist Mukhtar Hadi Yazbek: A brush that distinguishes the hunter from the “indiscriminate shooter” In summer 2020, the magazine recorded a distinctive artistic contribution by Mukhtar Hadi Yazbek, who designed two paintings adopted by the Society for the Protection of Nature in Lebanon (SPNL) and the Middle East Center for Sustainable Hunting for regional awareness work. He told the magazine: “The language of color crosses borders; with my brush I wanted to document the fundamental difference between a sustainable hunter who respects balance and an indiscriminate shooter who assaults wildlife.” November 2022 | Poet and journalist Hani Nadeem: “What spoils hunting is lack of awareness” In late 2022, poet Hani Nadeem spoke in depth, treating his going to the mountain as a return to humanity’s first roots before the falsehood of modernity. He said: “I return as a real human being without the cosmetics of city life… I am a son of the land and the soil. Hunting is a sport of nobles, and what spoils it is only lack of awareness and recklessness toward the environment—which requires firmness and strict application of the law.” February 2024 | Lebanese hunter Sarah Akiki: “Hunting is communion with the land and a challenge with elegance” In early 2024 the magazine devoted distinctive space to women’s presence, interviewing agricultural engineer Sarah Akiki, who trained in hunting from childhood. She pushed back against the traditional view of the woman hunter, affirming: “Abroad, a woman does not lose her femininity if she practices hunting, and woman has been a hunter since time immemorial. What matters to me is not the number of bags but the pleasure of walking and connecting with nature, and our care as women hunters for keeping the mountain clean and not leaving trash far exceeds that of others.” February 2024 | Hunter Rita Habib Al-Shaar: “Learn from the woman how to be a hunter, not a show-off” Hunter Rita Habib Al-Shaar — from Sayd magazine’s archive. In the same month, the magazine documented the experience of Rita Habib Al-Shaar, a Lebanese mother who combines family commitments with a passion for regulated hunting, raising a firm cry against chaos and night hunting: “Hunting is joy, calm, and adventure. The value of hunting is not in boasting by posting numbers of dead birds as a crime of extermination, but in preserving balance… And my constant message to the Ministry of Environment: no leniency with night hunting and violators.” In closing, this timeline shows that Sayd was never a fleeting publication, but a living record of shifts in environmental awareness in our community, and a platform where different groups—from stars, intellectuals, and businesspeople to women hunters and field pioneers—met to root an unchanging principle: hunting is an art, a responsibility, and a true partnership to protect the land.

articles.title: After the Bekaa: 24,750 square metres of illegal hunting nets removed in northern Lebanon in four hours
articles.body: The field team beside nets removed in northern Lebanon. Net removals in northern Bekaa and northern Lebanon have reached a combined 63,030 square metres. The Internal Security Forces’ Northern Investigation Detachment, working in the field and sharing information with the Anti-Poaching Unit’s joint operations team, removed 24,750 square metres of illegal hunting nets in northern Lebanon in just four hours. The operation follows the removal of 38,280 square metres of nets in northern Bekaa, bringing the combined total for northern Lebanon and the Bekaa to 63,030 square metres. Tall nets between orchard trees during the field operation. High nets among the orchards The density of the nets, their spread among orchards and their considerable height made removal a demanding field operation. The operation was coordinated with the head of the command and control room for northern Lebanon, the head of the Northern Investigation Detachment and officers from the detachment. It involved the joint operations team of the Anti-Poaching Unit (APU), affiliated with the Middle East Center for Sustainable Hunting and Anti-Poaching (MECSHAP) and the Committee Against Bird Slaughter (CABS). Field work on the nets between the trees. From the Bekaa to the north The earlier campaign in northern Bekaa was carried out with the Internal Security Forces’ Bekaa Investigation Detachment and resulted in the removal of 38,280 square metres of nets. The northern operation adds a further achievement to the cooperation between the Directorate General of the Internal Security Forces and the Anti-Poaching Unit team in protecting birds and nature in Lebanon. Nets collected after removal, with the Anti-Poaching Unit (APU) emblem visible. Sources: Internal Security Forces: northern operation; Internal Security Forces: Bekaa total

articles.title: Northern Bekaa: bird-net removals reach 38,280 m²
articles.body: Loading seized nets during the field operation in northern Bekaa. Field footage of operations to dismantle illegal bird-trapping nets in northern Bekaa. Watch this Short on Sayd’s YouTube channel The Bekaa Investigation Detachment of the Regional Gendarmerie Unit, under the Bekaa Area Command, carried out an exceptional field operation in cooperation on the ground and through information sharing with the joint Lebanese–international operations team of the Anti-Poaching Unit APU (MECSHAP–CABS). The operation resulted in the removal of an additional 17,640 square metres of bird-killing nets used for illegal hunting and the indiscriminate killing of birds, bringing the campaign’s overall total to 38,280 square metres. The missions, conducted over several days, covered Younine, Labweh, Arsal, Ras Baalbek, Mashari‘ al-Qaa, al-Kuwaitiya, Jabouleh, Jadidat al-Fakiha and the highlands of Nahleh. Numerous violation sites were identified and reached, and the seized nets were removed. After each mission, the seized material was handed over to the relevant units in accordance with established procedures. The operation was marked by a high level of professionalism, precise field coordination and rapid detection and intervention. The Bekaa Investigation Detachment also used a drone to survey the areas, spot nets from the air and locate them quickly and clearly, helping teams reach violation sites faster and carry out field interventions more efficiently. The mission was coordinated administratively and in media matters with the Bekaa Area Command, the Public Relations Division and the Gendarmerie Command operations room of the Internal Security Forces. Members of the Ras Baalbek police station also took part on the ground in removing some of the seized nets, as part of cooperation and coordination between the units concerned. A number of sustainable hunters in the Bekaa also contributed the field information needed to identify violation sites and locate the nets. This was not the first such cooperation. A similar operation last year resulted in the removal of approximately 8,000 square metres of nets. It was considered at the time the largest net-removal operation in Lebanon and the largest in the roughly fifty-year history of the international organisation CABS. The current operation, which removed an additional 17,640 square metres of nets over three days and brought the campaign’s overall total to 38,280 square metres, sets an exceptional new field record and underscores the importance of cooperation between security forces, specialist teams and sustainable hunters in confronting illegal hunting and protecting birds and wildlife in Lebanon. The total in the official bulletin In its bulletin of 8 October 2026, the Directorate General of the Internal Security Forces explained that the campaign’s overall total was 38,280 square metres: 20,640 square metres removed in the first phase, followed by an additional 17,640 square metres removed over three days. The bulletin reported the participation of APU (MECSHAP–CABS), the use of a drone and contributions of field information from sustainable hunters. articles.title: Northern Pintail: the long-necked duck linking Arab autumn to northern breeding grounds
articles.body: Northern Pintail Its name is not the Northern Pintail’s only distinguishing feature: among swimming ducks, a slender body, long neck and pointed tail reveal its shape. The adult male’s central tail feathers become particularly long in bright plumage. The Arabic name refers to a duck in the family Anatidae, not a singing bulbul. Its autumn return to Arab wetlands connects northern breeding grounds with winter waters where food remains available. Identity card Arabic: البلبول الشمالي; also shortened to البلبول English: Northern Pintail French: Canard pilet Scientific name: Anas acuta Order and family: Anseriformes; Anatidae Length: approximately 51–76 cm, depending on sex and tail length; wingspan approximately 86 cm Habitat: shallow fresh and brackish water, marshes and flooded fields Arab-world status: passage migrant and winter visitor, with abundance varying among countries and sites Global conservation category: Least Concern (LC); scientific name and taxonomy follow AviList v2026 [1] Autumn does not have one arrival date Autumn movements begin in northern breeding regions, with different routes linking Eurasia to North Africa, the Middle East and areas farther south. Not every Arab-world flock can be assigned the same origin. In Saudi Arabia, winter occurrence extends from October to March, making late October an appropriate time to search suitable habitat, but not a promise of birds on a particular lake. [6] [7] Where does it occur in the Arab world? In Tunisia, a winter 2020–2021 survey, published in 2024, confirms its presence. In Egypt, BirdLife and its partner Nature Conservation Egypt identify Lake Nasser as a stopover and wintering site. These are examples of documented winter occurrence, not evidence that every waterbody in these countries regularly hosts the species. [10] [11] In Palestine, the Wildlife Society describes it as common in winter and on passage. It is nationally uncommon and non-breeding in Saudi Arabia. Comparing checklists helps avoid applying one country’s status to another; abundance at a site also need not reflect distribution throughout a country. [9] [7] In the UAE: common on passage and in winter, with some summering individuals. This contrast between neighbouring countries illustrates why “Arab-world occurrence” cannot be reduced to one abundance category. A summer sighting alone also does not demonstrate a nest or successful breeding. [8] Males, females and immature birds An adult male in bright plumage has a dark brown head, a white breast with a white stripe extending up the side of the neck, a grey body and long central tail feathers. The slim neck and elongated shape strengthen identification. Tail length varies with sex, age and plumage condition, so a shorter tail should not automatically exclude the species. [2] The female is mottled brown, with a comparatively plain face and a rather dark grey bill. Immatures and males in eclipse plumage resemble her to varying degrees. Against a female Mallard or Wigeon, combine the long neck, slender body, bill and tail rather than relying on shared brown colouring. Precise ageing in autumn remains more demanding than identifying the species. [2] [5] How does it feed? In shallow water, Pintails lower the head and neck or tip up to reach food; on land they pick up grain and seeds. Their diet includes plant material and aquatic invertebrates, with insects particularly important to young birds and during the breeding season. They may feed or rest among other ducks, so a species count must not simply equal the total mixed flock. [5] Life cycle: from ground nest to winter quarters Breeding extends across large parts of Eurasia and North America, often in open landscapes near wetlands. Many pairs form during winter, but a pair together at an Arab wintering site need not nest there. The female makes a ground nest concealed in vegetation, sometimes some distance from water, and undertakes incubation and care of the ducklings. [3] A typical clutch contains 7–9 eggs, incubated for about 22–24 days. Ducklings leave the nest early and feed themselves under the female’s care, becoming able to fly at roughly 40–45 days. After breeding, the birds moult, including replacement of wing feathers and a temporary flightless period; autumn migration and winter settlement follow before the next breeding season. [4] Its value, and what needs protecting The Pintail’s journey connects distant places: safe breeding habitat is insufficient if feeding and resting sites disappear along the route. Recognised pressures include wetland loss, drought and damage to nests in farmland. A numerical trend documented in North America must not be transferred to all Arab populations without local evidence. [3] Global Least Concern status guarantees neither the stability of every population nor permission to hunt. Watch flocks from a distance, avoiding repeated flushing or approaches to a suspected nest. Dated observations and clear photographs can help track arrival times and changing use of sites, provided confirmed field evidence remains distinct from inference. articles.title: Northern Shoveler: a filtering bill and an autumn journey through Arab wetlands
articles.body: Northern Shoveler Among the ducks gathering beside autumn ponds, the Northern Shoveler often announces its identity before its colours are clear: a long bill widening into a spatula. Rather than simply digging into mud, it filters tiny food items from the water. Its seasonal return offers a way to understand the value of shallow wetlands, not just another name to add to a sightings list. Identity card Arabic: أبو مجرف; also مجرفي المنقار English: Northern Shoveler French: Canard souchet Scientific name: Spatula clypeata; older sources use Anas clypeata Order and family: Anseriformes; Anatidae Length: approximately 44–51 cm; wingspan approximately 69–84 cm Habitat: shallow freshwater or brackish ponds, marshes and lakes Arab-world status: chiefly passage migrant and winter visitor, with rare local breeding records Global conservation category: Least Concern (LC); scientific name and taxonomy follow AviList v2026 [1] Why it matters this season Arab wetlands gain importance as ducks move from northern breeding grounds towards their winter quarters. In Saudi Arabia, winter presence extends from October to March. On the western flyway, Danish ringing records document some birds reaching Morocco in October. These are examples of different migration routes, not a single arrival date for every Arab country. [6] [12] Different statuses across the Arab world In Tunisia, a winter 2020–2021 survey, published in 2024, confirms its presence. In Algeria, researchers published a June 2019 record from Sebkhet El-Mahmel of a pair accompanied by eight young. “Winter visitor” therefore describes the predominant pattern without excluding all local breeding; that record does not establish widespread residency either. [9] [10] In Egypt, historical assessments of Lake Nasser include the species among wintering ducks. This documents the site’s role, not a current population count. In Palestine, the Wildlife Society’s checklist describes it as very common in winter and on passage. Inclusion in a national list does not mean equal abundance at every pond, or that the species breeds there. [11] [8] Rare breeding has been recorded in Qatif, Saudi Arabia. In the UAE: locally common to very common on passage and in winter, occasionally in summer. An individual remaining through summer is not, by itself, evidence of nesting. [6] [7] The bill first, then the plumage A male in bright plumage has a dark green head, white breast and chestnut flanks. The wing shows a pale blue area and a green speculum. These colours are useful, but the bill’s widened tip remains the most dependable feature when poor light conceals the head’s sheen. [2] Females and immature birds are mottled brown; a moulting male may look more similar to them. Brown markings alone do not establish that a bird is female. When comparing it with a female Mallard, consider the conspicuously expanded bill together with head and wing structure. Colour or a distant photograph is not enough to assign sex and age confidently. [3] Small food, distinctive behaviour Fine plates along the bill edges form a filter for aquatic invertebrates and seeds. Birds sometimes swim in circles or sweep their bills from side to side while feeding. This specialisation helps explain their association with productive shallows. Finding one on a treatment pond or in turbid water does not establish that the water is clean or safe for people. [4] From nesting to the next migration Most breeding occurs in northern temperate Eurasia and North America. The female makes a ground nest concealed by vegetation, lines it with down, incubates the eggs and tends the young. BTO data give a typical clutch of 9–11 eggs, around 22–23 days of incubation and flight at roughly 40–45 days. These are approximate biological intervals, not a fixed calendar for every population. [5] Ducklings hatch covered in down and can swim soon afterwards, but still need cover and care. After breeding, plumage is renewed; males become temporarily flightless while their wing feathers are replaced. Birds subsequently gather and move towards wintering areas. A quiet bird seen in summer must therefore be distinguished from evidence of a nest or brood. [4] Its value, and responsible watching The Shoveler illustrates the diversity of feeding strategies within a wetland, linking tiny aquatic organisms with the bird food web. Its conservation requires connected feeding and resting places, rather than protection of an attractive image in isolation from habitat. Global Least Concern status does not guarantee that every local gathering is secure or that draining a small pond has no consequences. [13] Use binoculars from a fixed position and do not flush a flock for a photograph. Record the date, location, number and behaviour: these details help distinguish passage from repeated occupation. Hunting status depends on the rules applying to the country, site and season; it cannot be inferred from the conservation category or the label “wild duck”.
