articles.title: Northern Wheatear in the Arab world: an autumn traveller of open ground
articles.body: Northern Wheatear A small bird pauses on a stone, drops to the ground for prey and returns to a lookout. When it flies, white flashes across the rump and tail. This is a familiar Northern Wheatear scene during migration, when open ground across the Arab world becomes a stop along a much longer journey between breeding and wintering areas. Identification card Arabic name: الأبلق الشمالي English name: Northern Wheatear French name: Traquet motteux Scientific name: Oenanthe oenanthe Family: Muscicapidae Length: approximately 14–16 cm Habitat: bare ground, short grass, stony plains and sparsely vegetated slopes Arab-world occurrence: widespread passage migrant; breeds in parts of the Levant, with limited winter occurrence in some areas Global conservation status: Least Concern (LC) From the Maghreb to Arabia Ringing data in the Eurasian-African Migration Atlas connect April and September–October encounters in Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia with several European breeding regions. A passing wheatear cannot therefore simply be described as a bird from one particular country. A recovered ring establishes a connection between documented locations, rather than necessarily revealing every part of the journey. In the Levant, passage overlaps with local breeding. Lebanon's checklist documents summer breeding, especially at 1,500–2,500 metres, autumn passage from early August to late November, and smaller numbers in winter. In Saudi Arabia, Saudipedia describes a common passage migrant that does not breed in the country. The comparison matters: occurrence in an Arab country does not itself establish residency or wintering status. Most populations travel to wintering areas south of the Sahara. Tracking research on North American breeders has shown that even populations very far from Africa reach that continent by different routes. This does not make every wheatear seen in the Levant an Alaskan bird. An individual's origin needs its own evidence. Why autumn brings it into view Southward movement reaches North Africa from August and becomes conspicuous in September, while the last birds leave Europe during October. Local observations from Dhahran in eastern Saudi Arabia include September and October, as well as spring passage. These are regional seasonal windows, not fixed arrival dates for every country and year. A bird may pause in a short-grass field, on stony ground or beside a farm. A few days' presence does not show that its journey has ended. Recording the length of a stay, behaviour and observation date is more useful: passage, wintering and breeding are different situations that one photograph cannot establish. Recognising more than the spring male A breeding male usually has a grey back, black mask and dark wings. The female is browner and less contrasting, without the same bold black mask. In autumn, sandy or warm tones soften the appearance of many individuals, unlike the sharply patterned spring males familiar from illustrations. Assess the upright stance, legs, face and wing pattern, then the black-and-white tail when it becomes visible naturally. A white rump alone is insufficient because other wheatears share it. Nor does an overall brown colour in a distant photograph reliably establish sex or age. Document several features and leave uncertain identifications open. Small prey and a sheltered nest Its diet consists mainly of insects and other small invertebrates, with some berries. Sparse vegetation leaves room to locate and reach prey. Near a stone or low perch, the pauses and short movements to the ground can be watched without attracting the bird with food. In breeding areas, the nest is concealed in a cavity or rock crevice. BTO data give five to six eggs as a typical clutch; a British nesting calendar should not be transferred directly to Arab mountain habitats. A bird standing on a rock in October is not evidence of a nest beneath it. Conservation and responsible observation Least Concern describes global extinction risk and does not rule out local declines. European monitoring shows that a wide geographical range does not remove the need for habitat protection and continued surveys. The category also does not determine hunting law, which must be checked with the relevant national authority. Stay far enough away for the bird to keep feeding. Do not flush it to reveal the tail or follow it towards a nesting cavity. Record date, habitat, elevation and behaviour. Leaving a stopover undisturbed helps protect the journey briefly made visible by this small traveller. articles.title: Oman's 2003 wildlife law: Protected birds, permits and conservation beyond hunting seasons
articles.body: Royal Decree 6/2003 addresses reserves, protected species, permits, enforcement and confiscation. Nizwa Fort, Oman Oman's legal safeguards for wildlife go beyond opening and closing hunting seasons. The Nature Reserves and Wildlife Conservation Law issued by Royal Decree 6/2003 on 8 January 2003 provides a framework for protected species, nature reserves, permits and enforcement. The law defines hunting broadly to include deliberate capture, immobilisation, killing or attempted capture of wildlife. Under Article 14, a permit is required for hunting, keeping, breeding or transferring protected animals or their offspring inside or outside a nature reserve. Further permission requirements govern collecting specimens and possession of protected wildlife material. The first statutory schedule lists the houbara bustard among specially protected animals and birds. The second includes groups such as falcons, owls, eagles and vultures. Penalty provisions distinguish offences involving the protected schedules and provide for confiscation of wildlife, gear and vehicles used in violations. Article 13 also distinguishes zones within reserves: certain compatible recreational activities may be allowed in designated public areas, while access to stricter protection zones requires permission. The underlying law dates to 2003. This is a 2026 editorial explanation of that instrument, not a claim of new legislation. Readers should consult the responsible authorities for subsequent amendments and current implementing measures. articles.title: Peregrine Falcon — Falco peregrinus
articles.body: Peregrine falconPhoto: Sumeet Moghe — Wikimedia Commons — CC BY-SA 4.0. Range: One of the most widespread birds in the world: found on every continent except Antarctica. In Lebanon it is recorded year-round, and it is also among the raptors that pass with migration routes over the country. Life cycle and habitat: It nests on rock cliffs, and has often taken skyscrapers and bridges as nest sites in cities. It hunts medium-sized birds in the air: watching from a height or soaring, then stooping toward the prey in a rapid dive. It usually kills with a bite to the neck after the strike or the seize. Lifestyle: A flying hunter specialized in taking birds. Ordinary flight speed, according to the Cornell Lab, is about 40–55 km/h, and in a direct chase it may reach about 112 km/h. In a dive from great height, stoop speed may approach about 320 km/h (around 200 mph)—which is why it is counted among the fastest creatures on Earth in a dive. Its Latin name, Falco peregrinus, points to the “wanderer”: many individuals migrate long distances, and some nest sites have remained in use for successive generations. Hunting status: Across Arab countries the peregrine is treated as a protected bird of prey; hunting it as quarry is generally prohibited. In Lebanon, Wild Hunting Law No. 580/2004 limits hunting to quarry species set by the minister; everything else—including all birds of prey—is protected year-round and may not be hunted; the peregrine is not among the permitted quarry. Despite legal protection, it still faces illegal shooting in some seasons and along some flyways. Conservation status: Globally Least Concern with the International Union for Conservation of Nature. Its numbers collapsed in the mid-twentieth century because of pesticides such as DDT, then recovered after bans and captive-breeding and release programs; in the United States it was removed from the threatened-species list in 1999. Traits: Falconers have prized it among the finest hunting birds for more than a thousand years, and their techniques later helped breed it in captivity to rescue collapsed populations. The oldest ringed peregrine known lived more than 19 years. Today it is seen over coasts, cities, and cliffs alike.
articles.excerpt: One of the most widespread birds in the world: found on every continent except Antarctica. In Lebanon it is recorded year-round.

articles.title: Protecting Autumn Migratory Birds in Lebanon: A Field Partnership Since 2017, Al-Khatib Affirms the Sustainable Hunter’s Role
articles.body: Members of the Anti-Poaching Unit with birds rescued during a joint patrol — Middle East Center for Sustainable Hunting and Anti-Poaching Beirut — Sayd The Committee Against Bird Slaughter — known as CABS — announced the launch of its autumn campaign to protect migratory birds in Lebanon, in cooperation with its local partner the Middle East Center for Sustainable Hunting and Anti-Poaching — MECSHAP, with a focus on protecting migratory raptors and combating hunting with nets and birdlime (lime sticks / glue traps), according to its announcement published on 8 September 2026. In a statement to Sayd, Adonis Al-Khatib, head of the Middle East Center for Sustainable Hunting and Anti-Poaching, said: The Anti-Poaching Unit (APU) at MECSHAP, in cooperation with CABS, is preparing to carry out the autumn anti-poaching camp in Lebanon, as part of a field partnership ongoing since 2017, which began after CABS contacted MECSHAP through the Society for the Protection of Nature in Lebanon (SPNL). He added: “CABS works against illegal bird killing in a number of European countries, while its cooperation with APU has been a unique experience, as it was CABS’s first such experience with sustainable hunters taking part directly in anti-poaching. The experience has shown that the sustainable hunter is a true partner in protecting migratory birds and confronting violations in Lebanon.” From the daily field life of the Anti-Poaching Unit team: a break to prepare food outdoors. He continued: “Work during the spring and autumn camps focuses on monitoring and documenting violations involving birdlime, nets, night hunting, and indiscriminate killing of migratory birds, in coordination with the security agencies, the Lebanese Army, and the competent judiciary. The unit is entering this autumn’s camp at a high level of readiness, supported by a wide network of hunters and citizens who supply the operations team with reports, photos, and precise locations.” Source: Committee Against Bird Slaughter announcement — 8 September 2026, and Adonis Al-Khatib’s statement to Sayd.
articles.excerpt: An autumn campaign to protect migratory birds in Lebanon, and Adonis Al-Khatib tells Sayd: a field partnership since 2017 affirms the sustainable hunter’s role against illegal killing.

articles.title: Qatar's Law 4/2002: The statutory limits that apply beyond hunting seasons
articles.body: Six provisions address prohibited locations, times, nests, marine turtles, enforcement and penalties. Al Zubarah Fort, Qatar Qatar's seasonal hunting notices are implementing decisions, not the hunting law itself. The legal framework includes Law No. 4 of 2002, issued on 11 May and published on 20 May 2002, listed as in force by Qatar's official Al Meezan legal portal. Article 1 forbids hunting wild mammals, birds and reptiles in natural reserves, on islands, within cities and villages, within 500 metres of public roads and on private land without the relevant owners' consent. Article 2 permits hunting elsewhere only during specified seasons, between sunrise and sunset. Separate implementing decisions determine eligible quarry species and permitted hunting tools. Article 3 protects marine turtles and their eggs, bird eggs and nests, and wild flora. Article 4 provides for authorized enforcement officers to investigate offences. Article 5 provides, unless another law prescribes a more severe penalty, for imprisonment not exceeding one year or a fine up to QAR 10,000, or both. Equipment and weapons used in the offence are confiscated, and repeat offences attract the statutory increased punishment. These are provisions of a law enacted in 2002 and explained in 2026; they should not be confused with any new seasonal notice. articles.title: The Red-footed Falcon… Killed by the Ignorance of Indiscriminate Shooters
articles.body: Red-footed Falcon (Falco vespertinus) — not the Common Kestrel. While conservation science invests heavily in bird protection elsewhere, ignorance at home still kills protected raptors that are neither game nor food. This bird is the Red-footed Falcon (Falco vespertinus) — not the Common Kestrel. While the West undertakes painstaking studies, intensive workshops, long hours of monitoring, and heavy spending to preserve natural balance through bird conservation and sustainable living, the ignorant among us — whose minds have never been touched by the light of knowledge — kill any bird without knowing its role or ecological importance. They disregard every law, faith, and ethic, expressing sick psychologies that have not risen to the level of humanity but sink to brutal assault on God’s creatures… These killed birds are not hunting quarry and are not eaten. This is a falcon known locally as lazeeq or red uwaisaq; its scientific name is Falco vespertinus, in English the Red-footed Falcon. It is a falcon belonging to the falcon family Falconidae.

articles.title: Regulating Hunting Protects Wildlife… Banning It Worsens the Crisis
articles.body: Science-based regulation, with sustainable hunters as partners. Lebanon’s experience of blanket hunting bans showed they do not stop violations — they push them into more dangerous forms. Science-based regulation, with sustainable hunters as partners, is the balanced path. Lebanon’s experience of banning hunting in recent years has proven ineffective. It did not stop violations; it transformed them into more dangerous patterns. A wide segment of indiscriminate shooters (qawwasin) emerged who use cheap guns that are easy to replace when confiscated, while mist-netting and liming rose by more than 70% — methods far more lethal to birds and harder to detect than shotgun hunting. This reality weakened deterrence, opened the door to illegal hunting, and burned bridges with sustainable hunters who could have been partners in protection. A total ban also ignored the social and economic dimension of rural communities, increasing resistance to the law and deepening secret practices. Scientific regulation of hunting is the balanced solution: setting seasons that do not conflict with bird breeding; listing prohibited species on the basis of Red Lists and international agreements; banning abusive methods such as mist nets, birdlime, and electronic callers; and limiting take to traditional individual means. Cooperation with sustainable hunters has proven effective: most violations were detected thanks to their work with the Anti-Poaching Unit, composed of hunters who operate alongside the army and security forces in monitoring, documentation, and filing cases before the environmental public prosecutor. Field work has also documented wildlife and enriched scientific knowledge of bird status. The fundamental solution lies in establishing responsible hunting areas managed under the oversight of the relevant ministries, municipalities, and sustainable hunters — so that hunting shifts from a drain on nature to a genuine means of protecting it.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia's Environment Law: Hunting permits and wildlife safeguards
articles.body: A reference guide to the Environment Law, hunting permits, protected wildlife and seasonal implementing decisions. Qasr al-Farid in Hegra, Saudi Arabia A Saudi hunting-season announcement does not, by itself, establish what may be hunted, where or with which equipment. The legislative foundation is the Environment Law, issued by Royal Decree M/165 on 10 July 2020, alongside its terrestrial-wildlife hunting regulations. It replaced the previous Wild Animals and Birds Hunting Law of 1420 AH. Bureau of Experts: Environment Law. The regulations require a hunting licence and empower the National Center for Wildlife to set species, quotas, locations, dates and permitted methods. They protect endangered species, pregnant animals, young, nests, eggs and habitats. Protected areas have specific controls; a seasonal announcement does not automatically open them. Regulations, Articles 3–8. A weapon licence neither replaces a hunting permit nor establishes that the weapon may be used for every quarry species. NCW guidance requires permits through Fitri and compliance with approved species and methods, prohibiting mass-capture equipment and unauthorised attraction or calling methods. Check the applicable permit conditions and decision rather than a circulated image or an earlier season's announcement. NCW regulatory guidance. Article 7(2) prohibits hunting with firearms of any type, except within private hunting enclosures specifically licensed by NCW and subject to its conditions. Regulations, Article 7. The penalty schedule officially published in September 2024 lists first-offence fines of SAR 10,000 for hunting without a licence, and SAR 5,000 for hunting in a prohibited location or period. These examples do not exhaust potential penalties or compensation. Official penalty schedule. NCW's official FAQ also warns that displaying hunted wildlife outside vehicles, on roads or online is an offence. Publishing a souvenir photograph is therefore not outside the regulatory framework. NCW FAQ. This reference explainer was prepared on 15 October 2026. It announces neither new legislation nor a season opening and is not legal advice. Consult updated texts, seasonal decisions and permit conditions before travelling. articles.title: Saudi Falcons and Hunting Exhibition 2026: Al-Melwah, Auctions and Artificial Intelligence
articles.body: A falconer holds a falcon during Al-Melwah race activities at the Saudi Falcons and Hunting Exhibition 2026. The International Saudi Falcons and Hunting Exhibition 2026 in Malham, north of Riyadh, brings together falconry, competitions, auctions, hunting and shooting equipment and modern technologies. This year’s programme goes beyond a conventional exhibition to offer a broad view of hunting, falconry and related activities. Running from 1 to 10 October, the exhibition has seen several noteworthy developments in recent days, led by the start of Al-Melwah racing, Mongolian falcon auctions and the presentation of AI-enhanced technologies for monitoring, tracking and protection. Al-Melwah: 12 Heats and SAR 723,000 in Prizes Al-Melwah racing has begun at the exhibition, with falcons competing to cover 200 metres in the fastest possible time. This year’s edition comprises 12 heats divided between owners and amateurs, and elite and professional competitors. It includes six categories of young falcons: saker, peregrine, pure gyrfalcon, muthallath pure gyrfalcon, gyr-taba and gyr-peregrine. Total prize money reaches SAR 723,000. Participation is restricted to young falcons purchased at the International Falcon Breeders Auction, directly linking the competition to falcon breeding and production. Mongolian Falcons Attract Substantial Bids A falcon presented at the Mongolian falcon auction within the exhibition. Elsewhere at the exhibition, Mongolian falcons have attracted falconers and buyers to their dedicated auction. One auction night saw two falcons sell for a combined SAR 550,000: a young saker for SAR 150,000 and an adult saker for SAR 400,000. On another night, two young saker falcons sold for a total of SAR 350,000, one fetching SAR 250,000 and the other SAR 100,000. Mongolian saker falcons command particular interest among falconers for their size, endurance, long wings and varied plumage, characteristics that contribute to their value in the falcon market. Artificial Intelligence Enters Monitoring and Protection Visitors learn about displays at the Ministry of Interior pavilion. The developments at the exhibition extend beyond falcons and competitions. The Ministry of Interior pavilion presents digital solutions and AI-enhanced technologies used in monitoring, tracking and response, alongside technologies associated with environmental protection and the sustainability of marine resources. The pavilion also introduces visitors to regulations governing the possession and carrying of hunting firearms, as well as rules relating to sea fishing. This technological presence reflects a growing shift in the relationship between hunting and wildlife management, as monitoring, data analysis and tracking become an increasing part of protection and regulation. More Than 5,000 Products Traditional sea-fishing crafts feature in the exhibition’s 2026 edition. The exhibition also features a substantial area dedicated to firearms, ammunition and hunting and shooting equipment, displaying more than 5,000 products representing over 181 international brands. Exhibits include firearms and accessories, optics, equipment and products associated with hunting and outdoor travel. Sea fishing also features in the 2026 programme, with traditional tools and crafts relating to boats, nets and rope-making. This broadens the exhibition to encompass hunting on land and fishing at sea, alongside falconry and shooting. Between Al-Melwah races, auctions recording prices of hundreds of thousands of riyals and the expansion of equipment and modern technologies, the International Saudi Falcons and Hunting Exhibition 2026 offers a comprehensive picture of a sector combining heritage, industry, trade and technology.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia Launches the Sixth Hunting Season and Tightens the Rules: 5,000 Riyals Fine for Prohibited Places
articles.body: The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia launched the wild hunting season for 2026–2027, in an experience entering its sixth year and continuing to develop a model that organizes hunting practice and links it to wildlife protection and the sustainability of its resources. The National Center for Wildlife (NCW) announced that the season, which began on 1 September, runs until 31 January 2027 and is limited to the species, locations, and means allowed under approved regulations and controls. The current season sees a measured expansion compared with previous seasons: the number of species allowed for hunting rose to 30; the national hunting quota increased by 11%; and the number of licenses rose by 34%—adjustments the center says are based on monitoring results, studies, and evaluation of the previous five seasons. Holders of licensed hunting guns of the allowed types—air and gas guns that operate without gunpowder—as well as falconers registered with the Saudi Falcons Club, must obtain hunting permits electronically via the “Fitri” platform. Issuing licenses to hunt allowed species with falcons has also become linked to the existence of a falcon ownership certificate or passport. In parallel, the permanent ban on hunting endangered wildlife species continues, and hunting is prohibited inside cities, villages, farms, rest houses, and population gatherings, and inside protected areas and major projects—including NEOM, Qiddiya, and the Red Sea Project—in addition to a belt extending 20 kilometers inland from the Kingdom’s coasts. The regulations also ban hunting means that allow catching more than one animal at the same time, including shotguns and nets, as well as unauthorized attraction and calling methods. The National Center for Wildlife (NCW) considers that the previous five seasons made it possible to build a base of data and experience that helps set species, quotas, and licenses according to species’ status and capacity to renew. The center’s CEO, Dr. Mohammed Ali Qurban, affirmed that the lawful hunter is a partner in wildlife sustainability, stressing that regulating hunting allows the practice to continue, while random and excessive hunting depletes species and reduces their numbers. Tightening on prohibited places The Special Forces for Environmental Security renewed the warning against wild hunting in prohibited places, affirming that the violation carries a fine of 5,000 Saudi riyals, and calling for compliance with regulations and instructions on protecting the environment and wildlife. The tightening comes as the season continues until 31 January 2027, within a policy aimed at balancing regulated hunting with habitat conservation, especially during migration seasons. The Saudi experience holds particular importance in the Arab region, offering a model that combines the right to practice hunting with scientific regulation, monitoring, and species protection, at a time of growing need to develop the concept of responsible and sustainable hunting in the region.

articles.title: Sayd Returns… And This Is What We Want to Offer You
articles.body: Adonis Al-Khatib Adonis Al-Khatib, editor-in-chief of Sayd. When we founded Sayd, we set out from the conviction that hunting is responsibility, culture, and knowledge of nature and the principles of practice. A person who goes out into nature needs to know its birds and animals, understand its seasons and respect its limits, and grasp the effect of their practice on the life around them. Today, as we work on relaunching the magazine, we carry that conviction into a new stage. We want Sayd to become a trusted Arab reference for sustainable hunting and the world of nature, and a platform that joins scientific knowledge with human experience and responsible practice. What does that mean for the reader? And what will they find in Sayd in the coming stage? They will find, first, knowledge they can return to. We will work to present documented material on birds, wildlife, and biodiversity: How do we distinguish species? What do we know about their behavior and habitats? Why do they migrate, and what dangers do they face? And how do we enjoy watching and photographing them and contribute to protecting them? We want the image to help recognition, the fact to rest on a source, and the article to leave the reader with a deeper understanding of what they see in nature. When knowledge is unsettled, we will state its limits; when a fact needs correction or updating, we will review it. Hobbyists and professionals in these activities will also find a space that addresses their practical questions. Responsible hunting, shooting, equestrianism, falconry, and sea fishing have a place in this magazine, as do travel gear, safety, and good preparation. We will cover these fields with help from people of experience, in a way that joins practical benefit with respect for the law, the environment, and sound practice. Laws and seasons will have a clear presence, with a distinction between enforceable texts and demands and proposals. Our position is to support a clear legal season grounded in knowledge and accompanied by real enforcement and serious monitoring. We reject random and illegal hunting, the targeting of protected species, and practices that deplete wildlife. We want the responsible hunter to be a partner in protecting nature, and for that role to show in their behavior, knowledge, and stance. Our return comes as autumn and the bird migration season approach, with the opportunity they bring for knowledge, watching, and photography, and the responsibility toward birds on passage and their habitats. This season will be among the first gateways of our editorial work, alongside following developments in equestrianism, shooting, and nature issues. People and their stories have a fundamental place in Sayd. From the magazine’s beginnings, in-depth interviews were part of its character. In the coming stage, we want to continue dialogue with influential figures in Lebanon, the Arab world, and beyond: officials, businesspeople, artists, riders, and hunters, and with experts, researchers, photographers, and people of distinctive experience. What matters to us in these encounters is what experience reveals: How did their relationship with nature and this hobby begin? What did they learn? How did their view of nature and responsibility change? And what can they offer others? We aspire to build an Arab archive of testimonies and stories worth preserving and reading again. We will work, gradually, to expand Sayd’s presence at specialized championships, exhibitions, and festivals, from Lebanon to Arab countries—especially the Gulf—and to open space for international experiences that add knowledge and expertise. We also want to introduce readers to serious clubs, associations, initiatives, and projects, and to convey the questions and challenges of those working in these sectors. Although “Hunting and Equestrianism” is our main title, the world we belong to is wider. In ecotourism there is a chance to discover a place and respect it; in heritage, a memory of the human relationship with the land; in photography and art, other ways of seeing nature. “Your Health in Nature” and “The Kings’ Table” also have their place, treated with care for accuracy and linking knowledge to experience and local culture. We return with an archive that encourages this work. Older pieces on hunting, shooting, laws, and birds have kept receiving readers years after publication, even during periods of reduced activity. That stock places on us the responsibility of reviewing and renewing it, preserving its value, and adding what deserves to join it. This vision will not be complete in a single day. We will begin with selected pieces and coverages that can be delivered, and develop our presence and sections gradually, while improving the reading experience and access to content—especially on mobile. We will listen to readers and specialists, because their questions and notes are part of building a useful magazine close to its audience. And we want this return to last. Therefore we welcome cooperation with institutions, associations, and companies that share our respect for nature and value specialized media. Accuracy of information and independence of editorial decision will remain the basis of any sponsorship or partnership; the reader’s trust is what gives this work its worth. This is our invitation to our longtime and new readers, and to everyone who has knowledge, experience, or a story worth telling: share your questions and expertise with us, and help us widen this Arab space for sustainable hunting and the world of nature. Sayd returns to be closer to its readers, deeper in knowledge, and clearer in its responsibility toward nature and people.

articles.title: Shireen Bou Rafoul: From valley to valley, the hunters couldn’t stop her!
articles.body: Shireen Bou Rafoul monitoring hunting violations. She loves hunting and considers it part of her identity. But when the choice is between a hunting trip and a mission to rescue a bird, she chooses anti-poaching work. The director of the Anti-Poaching Unit (APU) tells Sayd about the moments from the field that stay with her: a wing trapped beneath a stone, a stork resting its head on her hand, and a kestrel that regained its sight and its freedom. One of the honey buzzard’s wings was injured; a stone pinned down the other, preventing it from escaping. When Shireen Bou Rafoul found it in the field, it was trying to pull its wing out from beneath the stone to free itself. That struggle stayed with her, becoming one of the scenes she recalls whenever she thinks back to her beginnings in bird protection. Shireen did not come to this work out of opposition to hunting. She was a hunter, and still says: “I really, really love hunting. It’s part of my identity.” But between the hunting she loves and a bird left injured and trapped, she found a line she chose to draw. She began taking part in the activities of the Middle East Center for Sustainable Hunting and Anti-Poaching (MECSHAP) and felt she belonged there. She volunteered to lead the Anti-Poaching Unit (APU). The work gradually took up more space in her life until it became, in her words, “an inseparable part” of it. From one valley to the next, Shireen travels on anti-poaching missions throughout Lebanon, without exception: from north to south, from the Bekaa to the mountains and the coast. While some hunting offenders complain about Shireen and her work in the field, many hunters committed to sustainable hunting support her, reporting violations or injured birds they find. Between the offenders’ complaints and these hunters’ support, she carries on with her missions, taking with her stories that do not end when the patrol is over. Shireen Bou Rafoul at work in the field. Shireen Bou Rafoul on a field mission to rescue a bird of prey. A stork’s head on her hand There is another encounter she cannot forget. The unit’s veterinarian was operating on a stork’s wing, which Shireen was holding steady. The bird turned its neck and rested its head on her hand. “It couldn’t do anything except rest its head on my hand,” she says, recalling the moment as she experienced it. She remembers the effect of that gesture: an injured bird, a wing in the veterinarian’s hands, and a head coming to rest on her own hand. Since then, the suffering of birds wounded by gunfire has felt closer to her. Protection was no longer an abstract idea; it became bound up with birds she had held and helped treat, and others the team could not save. A kestrel with its eyes sewn shut During a campaign this autumn, Shireen faced another scene of cruelty. According to her account, the team came across someone using a kestrel to lure a peregrine falcon. The kestrel’s eyes had been sewn shut. The kestrel was alive and flapping its wings, deprived of sight so it could be used as bait. Shireen can find no words to soften the brutality of what she saw: “Can you imagine someone sewing your eyes shut while you’re alive?” The team took the bird and removed the thread. As she recounts it, the kestrel needed some time to regain its sight before it was released and took flight again. This time, the story ended in freedom. But fieldwork does not offer those who do it the same ending every time. The kestrel. A peregrine they could not save While on patrol, her colleagues found a peregrine falcon in critical condition. To give it the most carefully informed treatment possible, Shireen says the team contacted a falcon hospital in the United Arab Emirates and sent X-rays. According to her account of the consultation, the fractures were severe, and the possibility of poisoning from lead in its body was also raised. Hope remained, and attempts to save it continued, but it died. “We were all upset,” she says. It was not the first time a bird had arrived with injuries beyond the ability of those trying to save it. Yet the loss did not make them give up. She says it strengthened their determination to protect whatever they could, before an injury became another story without a happy ending. When hunters and bird protectors work together Shireen Bou Rafoul, director of the Anti-Poaching Unit (APU). During hunting seasons especially, Shireen receives calls and complaints at all hours and sets off with her assistants on urgent missions to rescue injured birds or free captive birds of prey. She calls on the security forces for missions that require their presence. Many photographs document her alongside security personnel as they address hunting violations, draw up official reports and confiscate hunting guns. She accompanied them on the latest campaign, which included the removal of more than 38,000 square metres of nets used to kill birds. Shireen Bou Rafoul removing hunting nets in cooperation with the Internal Security Forces. From valley to valley.. with the CABS team Shireen praises the readiness and rapid response of Internal Security Forces personnel, considering their presence crucial to completing the missions. She also describes cooperation with the Committee Against Bird Slaughter (CABS) as one of the foundations of the work’s success. She finds particular significance in an organisation dedicated to combating the killing of birds working alongside a centre rooted in sustainable hunting. Shireen Bou Rafoul on a joint mission to address hunting violations. For her, this is not a confrontation between every hunter and every defender of birds. She sees proof in people who once committed serious violations and now help protect birds, report offences and raise awareness. These changes give her more hope than any general talk about the possibility of change. War and the hardest question The hardest thing she faced this year did not concern a bird alone. During the war, confronted with destroyed homes, families losing their loved ones and children dying, Shireen found herself questioning her ability to carry on with the work. How could she rush out into the field to protect birds while family and friends were suffering and she was unable to stop what was happening to them? She recounts how the team tried to help however it could. After conditions grew relatively calmer, she returned to her mission. This did not mean forgetting people’s suffering, but returning to what she could do: “If everyone does their part, everything falls into place.” Shireen does not sum up the reality of illegal hunting with a single verdict. She sees violations declining in some places and changing form in others, and observes that financial pressures are pushing some practices towards trade. She understands the difficult circumstances, but does not see them as a justification for poaching. Nor does the work end at nightfall. She speaks of patrols and joint missions to combat illegal night hunting, of awareness-raising and of offenders being arrested by the competent authorities. As for a hunting trip she might want to take herself, that remains possible when she is sure no other mission is waiting for her. When the two choices coincide, she does not hesitate: “I definitely prefer and choose anti-poaching work.” From the honey buzzard beneath the stone to the kestrel that could see and fly again, hunting has taken on another dimension in Shireen’s life: knowing when to go into the field, not to return with a bird, but to let it return to the sky. Photos: Anti-Poaching Unit (APU)

articles.title: The shrike: a bird that executes its prey on thorns
articles.body: A small bird turns thorns into tools for holding prey and storing food. How does it do it, and where can shrikes be seen in Arab countries? A thorny branch, an impaled mouse, and a small bird with a black mask standing nearby. The scene resembles a gallows in the wild, yet its maker needs neither an eagle’s bulk nor a falcon’s talons. This is the shrike, a bird that turns a thorn into a tool for securing its prey and a dining table. It may make the branches of a single shrub into a store of meals to return to later. From a distance, it looks like an unassuming grey bird on a high branch. But that perch is a lookout. Its eyes follow movement on the ground, its hooked bill ready to strike at a large insect, a lizard or a small rodent. Once the prey is in its hands—or rather, between its bill and its feet—the thorns enter the story. The thorn that stands in for a talon The shrike belongs to the passerines, but lives as a predator. Without the powerful talons of birds of prey, it uses what its surroundings provide: a sharp thorn, barbed wire or a crevice between two branches. It secures its prey, then uses its bill to tear off pieces to eat. The thorn becomes an extension of its natural equipment: it holds what is difficult to grip and helps the bird handle prey large in relation to its own size. Part of the prey may remain for another meal, or surplus catches may be impaled rather than eaten straight away. This harsh-looking spectacle therefore serves several purposes: controlling food, making it easier to eat and keeping it for later. Insects and small vertebrates on branches within a shrike’s territory can look like an open record of its hunting success. When a food store becomes an advertisement Another detail makes the story more remarkable. In a study of Great Grey Shrikes in Poland, researchers found that males selected more conspicuous places to impale prey during the mating season. This suggests that their stores may also serve a social purpose: food that can be seen may carry a message to a potential mate or a rival. It is an ingenious use of space. A shrub provides a lookout, a tool for securing prey, a food store and, sometimes, a display stand. Among the shrikes that practise this behaviour, the Great Grey Shrike occurs across substantial parts of the Arab world. Some populations are resident in particular countries; others arrive on migration or in winter. Identification Arabic name: الصرد الرمادي الكبير. English name: Great Grey Shrike. French name: Pie-grièche grise. Scientific name: Lanius excubitor. Family: Laniidae. Order: Passeriformes. Length: about 24–25 centimetres. Weight: around 48–81 grams according to The Birds of Saudi Arabia, with variation among populations. Key features: a grey back, a black mask through the eye, a long tail, black-and-white wings, and a bill with a hooked tip. Food: large insects, lizards, rodents and small birds. Global status: Least Concern, according to the global assessment cited in the references. This does not mean that its numbers cannot decline or that all its populations are equally abundant. Where can it be seen in Arab countries? — The Maghreb Local resident populations live in Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia, in northern habitats as well as deserts and oases. Libya also has resident populations. In suitable habitats, shrikes can therefore be encountered throughout the year, not only during a short passage season. Their plumage varies in shades of grey and white. Some older references placed these birds under Southern Grey Shrike, but their classification has since changed. This article follows AviList 2026, which includes the relevant North African and Arabian populations, as well as Steppe Grey Shrike, within Great Grey Shrike Lanius excubitor. Egypt Resident breeding populations are documented, including at Gebel Elba and in the Red Sea mountains. In the Western Desert, shrikes have been recorded securing prey on boxthorn spines and barbed wire. The striking ‘gallows’ scene is not remote from our own landscapes. Saudi Arabia and the Gulf In Saudi Arabia, the Great Grey Shrike is a widespread resident breeder, with additional passage and wintering populations. The Birds of Saudi Arabia describes its use of acacia thorns to impale prey in the central and western parts of the country. The United Arab Emirates, Qatar and Oman have resident breeding Arabian populations, joined by Steppe Grey Shrikes on passage or in winter. In the UAE specifically, autumn passage generally extends from August to October and spring passage from March to April, with some birds remaining over winter. Resident birds can be seen throughout the year. Kuwait is different: its checklist treats Steppe Grey Shrike as an uncommon passage migrant and winter visitor, while the Arabian population resident in neighbouring countries is a vagrant. There is no single calendar of occurrence for the entire Gulf. The Levant In Jordan, Great Grey Shrike is listed as resident. Its status in Syria varies with population and region, from rare local breeding to winter visits and passage. For Lebanon, the checklist published in 2020 records historical breeding, but found no conclusive recent evidence of it at the time of preparation. It documents scarce or rare passage in October to mid-November, and very rare passage from early March to early April. The bird should therefore not be presented as a common resident in Lebanon today. Where to look in the field Look for open country with scattered shrubs or trees: farmland, the edges of oases, semi-desert, or places with thorny vegetation and perches overlooking the ground. The first thing you notice is often its exposed position on a branch or wire, followed by the black mask and long tail. It can resemble other grey shrikes. A clear photograph of the head, wings and tail, together with the location and date, helps identification. Differences in colour do not necessarily indicate a different species: age and local population also play a part. Nest and family The shrike builds a cup-shaped nest in a tree or shrub, using twigs, grasses and rootlets, and lining it with softer material. The female does most of the incubation, and both parents care for the young. Saudi and Emirati references usually report 3–4 eggs, sometimes more. Incubation lasts about 15–17 days, and the young leave the nest after roughly two and a half weeks. Breeding timing varies geographically: March to May is prominent in the UAE, though activity may begin earlier. Scattered shrubs and trees remain an important part of its habitat. Photographers and birdwatchers should leave impaled prey where it is, keep away from nests and avoid rearranging a scene for a picture. You may leave while the mouse remains on its thorn. To a passer-by, it is a startling image; to the shrike, it is part of a way of life in which a small branch becomes a tool that gives it power beyond its size. References: The Birds of Saudi Arabia, vol. 2, p. 252; Antczak, Hromada & Tryjanowski (2012), study of shrike impaling behaviour; Hegazi (1981), wild-bird food in the Egyptian Western Desert; Goodman & Abdel Mowla Atta (1987), The Birds of Southeastern Egypt; Ramadan-Jaradi et al. (2020), Lebanon bird checklist; Aidek et al. (2025), Syria bird checklist; Jordan BirdWatch and Kuwait bird lists; UAE national assessment; AviList v2026. articles.title: From Sicily to Lebanon: The Battle to Save Migratory Birds from Illegal Hunting
articles.body: European Turtle Doves in Douz, Tunisia.Photo: Skander Zarrad. As autumn migration continues, efforts to protect birds are unfolding on several fronts around the Mediterranean: legal action in Sicily, the seizure of nets in Lebanon’s Bekaa Valley, a defence of field cooperation in Cyprus, and warnings about large hunting hauls in Libya. These different events share a common aim: safeguarding birds’ journeys between their breeding grounds and wintering areas. Sicily: A Court Halts Early Hunting of Turtle Doves In Sicily, nature conservation organisations have secured a legal advance for the European Turtle Dove. According to a statement published by LEAL on 4 September, the region’s Council of Administrative Justice upheld the suspension of hunting this species during the early opening of the season, following legal action led by LEAL and Pro Natura, with support from the Committee Against Bird Slaughter (CABS) and Green Impact. The decision concerns the early hunting of turtle doves specifically; it does not amount to a ban on all hunting on the island. Its significance lies in reducing pressure on the species at a sensitive stage of its seasonal journey. Lebanon: More Than 20,000 Square Metres of Nets In Lebanon’s Bekaa Valley, the Internal Security Forces announced the seizure of illegal hunting nets covering a total area of 20,640 square metres, during a campaign carried out by the Bekaa Investigation Detachment of the Regional Gendarmerie Unit. The campaign coincides with the autumn bird protection camp run in Lebanon by CABS in cooperation with the Middle East Center for Sustainable Hunting and Anti-Poaching (MECSHAP), amid daily field cooperation between the organisations participating in the camp and the security forces. CABS announced the launch of the camp on 8 September, despite tense regional conditions, to monitor migration routes and combat the trapping of birds with nets and limesticks. Hunting nets and poles seized during the security forces’ campaign in the Bekaa Valley. Cyprus: Defending Cooperation with the Authorities In Cyprus, the debate has reached parliament. Ahead of a meeting of the parliamentary environment committee in mid-September, CABS urged lawmakers to protect cooperation between civil society organisations, the police and the authorities responsible for combating illegal hunting, warning of attempts to disrupt it. The case shows that bird protection depends not only on fieldwork, but also on maintaining the institutional framework that enables violations to be detected and pursued. Libya: When Hunting Hauls Become a Competition On the African shore, Libya’s Al-Barari nature conservation organisation warned about circulating photographs of large hauls of European Turtle Doves. According to a report by Al-Wasat, the organisation said one of the photographs showed more than 700 birds. The organisation warned that displaying such hauls could turn into a competition that encourages further hunting, and called for the circumstances and legality of the hunting to be investigated. It also raised concerns about trade in the birds — a matter that requires investigation and cannot be established by photographs alone. A flock of migrating White Storks over Istanbul.Photo: Tema. Protection Beyond Borders The events, organisations and methods differ, but the issue extends beyond any one country. Birds travel along interconnected routes, and protection at one stop on their journey remains incomplete if nets or illegal hunting await them elsewhere. From courtrooms to field patrols, complementary forms of protection help safeguard migration and conserve nature. articles.excerpt: From Sicily to Lebanon, Cyprus and Libya, courts, field teams and cooperation with the authorities form different fronts in protecting migratory birds from illegal hunting.

articles.title: The planet’s skies are losing their balance: BirdLife sounds the alarm on global flyways
articles.body: A large flock of migratory birds crossing a wetland. BirdLife International — State of the World's Birds. Exclusive to Sayd Magazine | An editorial reading of the State of the World's Birds report Seasonal migration is no longer only a beautiful sight of flocks crossing the horizon as the seasons turn. It has become a precise vital sign of the planet’s pulse and the health of its ecosystems. In its latest edition, devoted entirely to intercontinental flyway networks, BirdLife International released its flagship report, revealing a dark and complex picture of what migratory birds are enduring. Their flocks face rising pressures that are redrawing the map of the world’s biodiversity. The bleed in numbers: 45% of species in continuous decline The report draws on a scientific database that assessed 1,843 migratory bird species worldwide. It finds that 45% of these species are recording a continuous numerical decline along their various routes, while only 14% are increasing, and 30% remain relatively stable. The data indicate that one in nine species (about 11%, or 200 species) is now globally threatened with extinction under the IUCN Red List. The degrees of risk break down as 32 species classified as Critically Endangered, 57 as Endangered, and 111 as Vulnerable, alongside dozens of other species close to the threat threshold — a sign that the crisis spans wide ecological groups. The most fragile groups: shorebirds and seabirds in the lead The report’s findings show that wetlands and marine environments are taking the hardest hit. Fifty-four percent of migratory shorebirds and waders are in sharp decline, as sabkhas are drained and coasts and tidal zones — vital refuelling stations before desert and sea crossings — are filled in. Forty-nine percent of seabird species face a similar drop because of bycatch in nets and fishing lines on the high seas, plus plastic pollution and the decline of fish stocks. Even birds once considered common in hunting and migration seasons, such as the European Turtle-dove and some ducks and coots, have suffered successive declines that have led to tighter international protections. Migratory European bee-eaters (Merops apiaster) on a thorny branch, one bird in flight — a colourful species of the Mediterranean flyways. Wikimedia Commons — CC BY-SA. Traps along the route: when wings meet infrastructure and human activity The report stresses that protecting a migratory bird in its breeding country alone does not guarantee its survival unless stopover sites and wintering grounds are equally safe. The main threats overlap along international routes: Habitat loss and degradation: more than 58% of 1,099 Key Biodiversity Areas (KBAs) are severely degraded by intensive agriculture, industry, and wetland drainage. Unregulated and illegal hunting: long coastal nets, electronic calling devices, and hunting outside permitted periods continue, especially at the Mediterranean and Middle East bottleneck, where estimates point to tens of millions of birds taken each year. Energy and wind corridors: wind farms and uninsulated high-voltage lines in narrow thermal corridors cause repeated collisions and electrocution of soaring birds such as eagles, storks, and falcons. Climate change and invasive species: the timing of food at arrival sites falls out of step, and rodents and other introduced animals prey on nests on remote islands. From diagnosis to rescue: a window of hope and the Nairobi Declaration The report does not stop at bleak numbers. It stresses that conservation science works when international efforts come together. The Global Flyways Summit adopted the Nairobi Flyways Declaration, under which governments and international development banks (including the World Bank) committed billions of dollars to protect wetland networks and restore safe routes. The clearest message BirdLife’s report sends to communities, people who love the wild, and hunters alike is that migratory birds cross political borders without passports. Keeping them requires moving from limited local protection to integrated, sustainable management along the entire flyway, so these flocks remain in our skies for generations to come.
articles.excerpt: An editorial reading of the State of the World's Birds: 45% of migratory species are in continuous decline, and one in nine is threatened with extinction.

articles.title: Widespread environmental destruction in southern Lebanon threatens one of the world’s key bird-migration flyways
articles.body: Thick white smoke over vegetation in the south — documentation linked to the use of white phosphorus munitions, according to reports by international organizations. Since October 2023, and through the escalation of March 2026, southern Lebanon has continued to see documented environmental destruction, recorded by several international and local bodies, that has hit forests, farmland, soil, and water. To this day (September 2026), and despite Lebanon and Israel signing a US-sponsored framework agreement on 26 June 2026, Israeli raids and explosions continue in southern border areas. White phosphorus: international documentation Human Rights Watch documented the Israeli army’s use of white phosphorus munitions in at least 17 towns in southern Lebanon. According to data gathered by the Lebanese researcher Ahmad Baydoun with the group “Al-Janoubiyyun al-Khudr” (the Southern Greens), more than 918 hectares were damaged in 191 documented white-phosphorus attacks between October 2023 and the ceasefire in November 2024. Amnesty International documented that Israel began using white phosphorus in Lebanon between 10 and 16 October 2023. Its use in populated areas violates Protocol III of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons. On the scientific side, the Lebanese National Council for Scientific Research estimated that at least 2,000 hectares of forest, olive and citrus groves, and farmland were partly destroyed by white phosphorus. Among the losses, the historic woodland “Horj al-Rahib” was destroyed — a 16-hectare oak forest on the edge of Aita al-Shaab. The Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS), in a detailed report, also recorded Israel’s use of white phosphorus munitions that set wide fires in farmland, killing vegetation and causing long-term degradation of soil and water. Fires consuming vegetation on a rocky hill near inhabited areas in southern Lebanon Migratory birds in the line of fire Lebanon lies on one of the world’s most important bird-migration corridors. It forms the second most important migration route for birds between Europe, the Middle East, Asia, and Africa, also known as the African–Eurasian flyway or the Eastern Mediterranean flyway. Millions of birds of more than 400 species cross it, between breeding sites in central and eastern Europe and wintering grounds in central and eastern Africa, among them the White Stork, the Lesser Spotted Eagle, and pelicans. A specialist study published in 2026 in the journal Environment and Security concluded that drone warfare generates “multi-layered environmental risks,” among them noise disturbance, pollution from electronic debris, and behavioural stress in wildlife, especially birds. The study indicates that birds may interpret the sound of drones as an aerial predator, which can drive panicked flight, disrupt feeding, or cause them to abandon nest sites. More serious still, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) confirmed in its 2025 assessment the global extinction of the Slender-billed Curlew (Numenius tenuirostris), one of the first officially recorded extinctions of a migratory bird species. This bird was among the species that relied specifically on the southern Lebanon corridor within their migration route. The IUCN warns that migratory birds already face accumulated pressures from habitat loss, urban expansion, pesticides, and climate change, in addition to the reality of conflict zones damaged by white-phosphorus pollution and heavy metals. In October 2025, during the IUCN World Conservation Congress in Abu Dhabi, members adopted a resolution calling for the rehabilitation of Lebanon’s damaged ecosystems, recognising wide environmental degradation that includes soil and water pollution, loss of vegetation cover, erosion, fire risk, and the threat to ecological connectivity between habitats.

articles.title: 80,000 Visitors and 158 Exhibitors from 15 Countries… Suhail 2026 Closes a Decade of Passion for Hunting and Falconry
articles.body: Doha — Sayd See the Suhail 2026 photo album: falcons, visitors, and faces of the fair → The Katara International Hunting and Falcons Exhibition “Suhail 2026” concluded its tenth edition in Doha after five days that saw attendance exceeding 80,000 visitors and broad participation by specialized companies and entities, completing the exhibition’s first decade as it has become one of the region’s foremost appointments for hunting, falconry, maqnas (desert hunting trips), and overland travel enthusiasts. This year’s edition ran from 8 to 12 September under the slogan “A Decade of Passion and Heritage.” At its opening, the exhibitor list comprised 158 entities and companies from 15 countries, spanning fields from falcons and their equipment and hunting gear to camping, vehicle outfitting, modern technologies, and logistics services. Suhail’s identity is no longer limited to being a fair for selling hunting supplies. The tenth edition showcased more than 20 innovations and inventions related to hunting, shooting, and travel—an indicator of a specialized market in which modern technologies intersect with heritage practices. Falcons at the heart of the event The Suhail falcons auction remained one of the fair’s biggest draws for the public and falconers, with a selection of distinctive and rare falcons on offer and competition to acquire them. Mohammed bin Abdulatif Al-Misnad, vice-chair of the organizing supreme committee, described the auction as one of Suhail’s most prominent activities, and noted that this year’s edition coincided with the start of a new season for falconry and maqnas. Falcons topped the interest of visitors to Suhail 2026 and its specialized auction. Source: QNA The exhibition halls presented a broad picture of contemporary hunting: falcons and training and care equipment; gear for trips and outdoor camps (kashtat); vehicle fittings; products for hunters and falconers; and traditional crafts and arts inspired by the desert and hunting. At the same time, the environmental dimension appeared in a number of participations and experiences, including sustainable hunting, alongside entities such as the Department of Antiquities at Qatar Museums, which used the presence of desert-goers to raise awareness about protecting archaeological sites while practicing outdoor hobbies. From hobby to a specialized market Suhail’s figures point to the expansion of the economy surrounding hunting and falconry in the region. Exhibition director Abdulaziz Al-Bu Hashem Al-Sayed spoke of strong purchasing activity in the halls, considering that the goal is no longer merely to hold a commercial fair, but to consolidate a specialized gathering that brings together hobbyists, companies, and interested parties from different countries. A scene from falcon activities at Suhail 2026. Source: QNA This expansion is also visible in the nature of the participants themselves. Alongside specialized companies, institutions offering shipping and storage services took part—including Qatar Post—while the fair included vehicle-outfitting and camping sectors and services linked to falcons and hunting. The edition also enjoyed support from the “Daem” fund for the ninth consecutive year. At the close of the exhibition, DTS won the Best Stand award, while the Best Garage award went to “Al-Muharrik Al-Sahrawi” (The Desert Engine), alongside specialized competitions in making falcon hoods (baraqi‘) and other elements tied to falconry culture. Media as a partner in Suhail At the close of the edition, Malaka Mohammed Al-Shreem, member and secretary of the organizing supreme committee, stressed the importance of local, Arab, and international media in conveying the image of the exhibition, and considered the media a strategic partner in strengthening Suhail’s presence and introducing Qatari heritage worldwide. After ten editions, the road appears open to a new stage for the fair. The supreme committee has already begun thinking about the next edition, with a drive to keep developing the event and consolidating its place as an international gathering for falconers, hunting and maqnas enthusiasts, and specialized companies. Thus Suhail 2026 closes its first decade—but the figures and the breadth seen this year suggest that the first ten years may be only the beginning. Source: Qatar News Agency (QNA).

articles.title: Syrian Hunter Amani Al-Homsi: I Oppose Illegal Hunting… I Hope Syria Enacts a Hunting Law Fair to Nature and to the Hunter
articles.body: Amani Al-Homsi, hunter from Aleppo. Syria’s best-known woman hunter speaks to Sayd about passion without bloodlust, sexist comments, the need for a seasonal hunting law, and ethical practice that protects both hobby and nature. Syria’s most famous woman hunter embraces nature with a mother’s love and takes her quarry with a falcon’s skill — without hesitation. It is the balance of spirit and body, skill and knowledge: harmony between nature and the responsible human being. Amani, a daughter of Aleppo, whose children take pride in her in hunting clothes because they feel her strength and capability — and who has never disappointed them with a delicious meal prepared by her skilled hands. She said in the interview: The direct reasons that drew me into hunting were contact with hunters, my passion, and watching nature — not a love of killing any living creature. The most positive press comment that affected me was: “A queen from my country who managed to balance her household duties and her hobby, and was creative and distinctive.” Of course there are negative comments too, including: “A woman’s place is the kitchen.” I have only outperformed men at shooting fixed targets — which embarrasses some of them. In the Salamiyah area during the season for the zar‘i bird, men always lead. I keep my children away from hunting guns for their safety. The obsession with boasting and attracting attention is a social blight amplified by social media. Issuing a new, organised hunting law that respects seasons in Syria is a core concern for hunters there. Several meetings have taken place between international associations and official bodies to draft a new hunting law that considers both the environment and the hunter… and we wait. Hunting kit is essential for survival: water, food, a knife, and emergency gear. In dangerous areas such as deserts and forests, extra equipment is needed — a whistle, a flare, plus a mobile phone or radio. Most important: trips to such areas should be in a group, not alone. On one bird-hunting trip along a riverbank in Tartous Governorate I ended up fishing: I left my companions, swam, and caught fish — which made them laugh. Once I climbed a mountain in Tartous, slipped, and rolled five metres down over stones, leaves, and thorns. I had some bruises, but I will certainly repeat that trip later. Yes, a woman hunter’s presence among hunters helps curb illegal hunting. I have felt that in meetings and hunting lectures I joined: everyone tries to present a respectable image of themselves and of their knowledge of the difference between random shooting and responsible hunting that protects the hobby — and that is good. The only time I hunted outside Syria was in the Qaa area of Lebanon. I love hunting very much in my country. Syria is a hunting country par excellence, and I hope laws are issued soon that allow me to move and hunt in all regions as in other countries. My preferred game… thrush (samman) and duck. I call on hunters to practise ethical, humane hunting that does not harm nature and does not drive birds toward extinction. I hope that in our countries, as in many others, the hunter will also hunt with the lens — so that the relationship with nature is not only a relationship with the gun.

articles.title: Mashhoor Wins the Saudi National Day Cup as Taif Closes Its Racing Season
articles.body: On the track at King Khalid Racecourse in Taif The 2026 Taif racing season concluded at King Khalid Racecourse on Saturday, 26 September, following two evenings with a combined SAR 6.2 million in prize money and victories in the season’s leading cups. Mashhoor and Wootton Sun Take the Honours Mashhoor, representing Saud Mohammed Saud Al Ali Stable, won the Saudi National Day Cup over 2,400 metres. The race carried a prize fund of SAR 450,000. Wootton Sun, racing in the colours of Prince Faisal bin Khalid bin Abdulaziz, won the Okaz Cup in two minutes and 16.93 seconds. Sahab Alriyadh and Hanouf Athbah Win Major Cups Sahab Alriyadh won the King Faisal Cup, while Hanouf Athbah claimed the Prince Abdullah Al Faisal Cup. Winners on the Final Evening Saturday’s other cup winners included Jabkhan in the Jockey Club Challenge Cup, Bushra in the King Khalid Racecourse Arabian championship, and Double Talk in the fillies and mares championship. Power of Beauty won the open-class cup.

articles.title: The awsaj thornbush: reading the land, and the wild’s old pharmacy under the spines
articles.body: Dense green Arabian boxthorn (Lycium shawii) in the Negev.Photo: Krzysztof Ziarnek, Kenraiz — Wikimedia Commons — CC BY-SA 4.0. A knowing hunter does not walk the open country blind, waiting for a bird to pass by chance. He reads the scrub, feels the soil, and often senses where game may drop before he sees it. In our Arabian deserts and wadis, few shrubs tell the place as clearly as awsaj (Lycium shawii). You find it in the belly of a shuʿayb — tangled, sharp with thorns — a small fortress against summer drought, waiting for the first hint of rain. A migrant’s inn and fuel stop A green, living awsaj in bare ground is a meaningful drop point. A tired migrant — a small warbler-type dukhaykhla, a shrike, or a dove that has flown hundreds of kilometres — finds here what many other bushes lack: Cover: The woven spines shelter small birds from many raptors, including peregrines, and make it harder for ground predators such as foxes to push into the heart of the shrub. Inside, small birds rest and roost. Energy fruit (“wolf grapes”): Small round red berries, known locally as ʿinab al-dhiʾb or awsaj berries, offer moisture and natural sugars a spent bird can use before the next leg. That is why many hunters sweep awsaj first at dawn for a flicker of feathers deep inside. Red berry of Arabian boxthorn (Lycium shawii) on a leafy branch, Aqaba.Photo: Krzysztof Ziarnek, Kenraiz — Wikimedia Commons — CC BY-SA 4.0. From the folk field pharmacy Elders did not pass awsaj lightly; it belongs to long-standing Arabian folk medicine. What follows is heritage as told in the field, not modern medical advice, and it does not replace clean water, proper dressings, or care when needed: Cuts and scratches: Folk telling has it that if someone took a nick from sharp stone or thorn and feared contamination, they would take a handful of tender awsaj leaves, rub and crush them between two clean stones, and set the juice as a dressing straight on the wound. The astringents in the leaves, the story goes, stop light bleeding and act as a natural disinfectant against infection. Sand in the eyes: It is told that in sudden sandstorms the Bedouin used to boil awsaj leaves in a little clean water, leave it to cool fully, then use it as a wash for irritated eyes — to cool them and clear sand grains. Camp stomach upset: Folk accounts also say that for a sudden camp cramp, or after drinking water that sat badly, boiling a few awsaj leaves and sipping the bitter water slowly works as a natural soother and anti-spasmodic. Nature is not an enemy to defy, but an open book; those who learn the language of its shrubs lose their way less often.

articles.title: The Silence Horses Speak
articles.body: A bay horse rearing in a green pasture. On those who ride not to arrive, but to remain An hour before the sun finds the stable, someone is already there—a man or a woman who has beaten the light to the door. No cameras. No crowd. No cups lined up on a shelf. Only the smell of hay and damp sand, warm breath rising in the last cool of dawn before the day’s heat, and a hoof that strikes the ground once, as if to say: You’re late. This is the world newspapers rarely show. The world of people who truly love horses—who know a mare is not possessed but companioned, and that trust built over years can collapse in a moment of neglect. In the barns they say horses read their people before their people read them. They catch the tightness in a shoulder, the hesitation in a hand, whatever sits unspoken in the chest. That is why no one lies in front of a horse. Dawn Rituals And this world has its quiet rites. Cleaning a hoof is less a chore than a habit of attention; long grooming is a conversation without words; a leather saddle that softens with the years carries its rider’s memory the way an old notebook does. The rider who starts the day already cantering—before pausing once at the horse’s head to breathe with her—misses half of what he came for. There is elegance in this life that has nothing to do with extravagance. It is the elegance of what lasts: riding boots you care for over ten years until they grow more beautiful; a light linen shirt that takes in morning sweat and the scent of horses together; a simple stable kept as ordered as a reception room. Luxury, here, is having time—and spending a full hour on a creature that thanks you only with a look. A white horse galloping across open pasture. Heat as Teacher In our countries, heat governs the stable. People who truly love horses do not fight the heat; they make peace with it and learn its rhythm: When to ride: Early dawn and late afternoon belong to horse and rider. The hours between are for shade and rest. Water first: A horse drinks tens of liters a day—more in hot weather. Water should be clean, as cool as practical, and always available. On long, hard work, salts (electrolytes) are added under a veterinarian’s guidance; sweat takes more from the body than water alone. Cooling after work: Do not leave a horse suddenly after effort. Walk until the breathing settles, then wet the body and legs with lukewarm or cool water and scrape the excess so heat does not stay trapped against the skin. Warning signs: Breathing that stays rapid, sweat that suddenly stops, or unusual lethargy. These can signal heat stress; calling the vet then is not something to postpone. When to call the vet Rapid breathing that will not settle, sweat that suddenly stops, or unusual lethargy can signal heat stress. Do not postpone the call to your veterinarian. General practical guidance — not a diagnosis. Sand and its risks: Sandy ground looks soft, but a horse that eats feed off the ground may swallow sand with it and develop what is called sand colic. Better to offer feed in raised mangers or on mats, and keep fiber intake regular. Soft sand is not always harmless A horse eating feed off sandy ground may swallow sand with it. Offer feed in raised mangers or on mats, and keep fiber intake regular. Any suspected colic = veterinarian at once. No DIY electrolytes without guidance. The hoof: Severe dryness makes the hoof brittle. It needs balanced moisture and regular farrier care—not an excess of products. This is knowledge horse people learn by living with animals—knowledge our ancestors mastered in the desert long before it was written down. Arabian horses, long known for patience and for enduring hard ground, answer care with a loyalty few other creatures match. People of the Land, People of the Sky Those who know horses know the land as well: which pastures ripen first, which tracks soften under a hoof, which way the wind arrives. Very often a lover of horses is also a lover of birds—from the falconer with a bird on the forearm to the rider who stops to watch a flock cross at sunset—because both have learned to listen: to a distant neigh, or to a wing cutting the air so that the mare turns her ears before anyone has seen it. Some say horses teach patience. More truly, they teach presence. When you ride a mare across open ground at the golden hour, and the sun descends in honey light over the dunes, there is no inbox left in your head, no appointments—only the rhythm of four hooves, the warmth of a body beneath you, and a horizon that approaches without hurry. That is what it means to belong to horses: to know that the finest part of riding is the stretch of time when you do not seem to be going anywhere at all.

articles.title: Touqi Season highlights wildlife and birds at King Abdulaziz Royal Reserve
articles.body: Gazelles at King Abdulaziz Royal Reserve, in an archival image. The King Abdulaziz Royal Reserve Development Authority inaugurated the second Touqi tourism season on 8 October 2026. Running through April 2027, it forms part of Saudi efforts to develop ecotourism while protecting wildlife and natural habitats. The new season builds on its first edition, which welcomed more than 20,000 visitors over 78 days, and expands nature, adventure and heritage experiences as well as opportunities for local communities. Nine bird species added to the reserve records Last summer, the authority also announced a scientific milestone: nine bird species had been documented within the reserve for the first time. The findings were based on a year-long field survey and published in the peer-reviewed journal Check List in June 2026. Researchers from the authority and King Saud University surveyed terrestrial, aquatic and migratory birds, including occasional visitors outside their usual migration routes. The species included the lanner falcon, long-eared owl, rosy starling, yellow-throated sparrow, black-headed bunting, slender-billed gull, Eurasian dotterel, spur-winged lapwing and greater flamingo. A wadi and watercourse in King Abdulaziz Royal Reserve, in an archival image. Photo source: Saudi Press Agency (SPA) / King Abdulaziz Royal Reserve. Covering more than 28,000 square kilometres, the reserve has vegetated valleys, wetlands and reservoirs behind dams that provide habitat for wildlife and migrating birds. Together, scientific monitoring, conservation and regulated ecotourism illustrate how protected areas can help sustain biodiversity while allowing visitors to discover it. articles.title: Tracking turtle-doves from Azerbaijan to the Nile exposes a difficult migration route
articles.body: GPS data reveal sea and desert crossings, critical stopovers and substantial gaps in knowledge. Perlman et al. / Bird Conservation International (CC BY 4.0) A migratory route is more than a line across a map. For the European Turtle-dove (Streptopelia turtur), it is a chain of habitats where birds must find food and rest while crossing seas, deserts and human-altered landscapes. A peer-reviewed study published online in Bird Conservation International on 8 October 2026 describes GPS tracking of 26 turtle-doves tagged in Azerbaijan and the eastern Mediterranean. Sixteen were recorded beginning southward migration; two provided particularly extensive tracks reaching Sudan and South Sudan. During active migration, the tracked turtle-doves covered up to 752 kilometres in a day. Among birds with sufficiently detailed tracking data, the longest measured continuous flight covered 719 kilometres in 13 hours. Their routes included crossings of the Red Sea and desert. Farmland along the Nile emerged as an important stopover environment, particularly in Egypt and Sudan. The conservation implication is regional: protecting breeding grounds cannot substitute for maintaining stopover habitats along an entire flyway. Hunting pressure and habitat change must be considered across borders. These tracks are not a definitive map for the species. The sample is limited and most tagged birds did not yield complete migration records. The researchers therefore identify promising areas for further study rather than claiming comprehensive coverage. Original research: Perlman et al., Bird Conservation International, 8 October 2026. DOI: 10.1017/S0959270926100860. Open access under CC BY 4.0. Original peer-reviewed research
