articles.title: Turtle Doves Cross Hunting Borders: One European Flyway Recovers, Another Remains Under Pressure
articles.body: European Turtle Dove in Algeria.Photo: Mourad Harzallah / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 4.0. European countries have cut Turtle Dove hunting by about 90% across the two main flyways they manage. Yet the bird's breeding population has followed different paths: growth in the west, and a continued decline with signs of stabilisation in the central and eastern flyway. What does that divergence tell us about managing a bird whose journey crosses borders? A July 2026 report from the European Federation for Hunting and Conservation (FACE) paints a mixed picture for the European Turtle Dove (Streptopelia turtur). The population breeding on the western flyway has continued to increase: its spring 2025 index was the highest since 2009. On the central and eastern flyway, the long-term trend is still downward, though the index has shown signs of stabilising since 2021. Hunting has fallen by about 90% on both flyways compared with the respective baselines used by the management programme. In 2025, western flyway countries reopened hunting under small quotas after a four-year moratorium; quotas on the central and eastern flyway remained low. Countries require hunters to report their take, with several using digital systems to track quotas. FACE argues that the continuing decline in the central and eastern flyway, despite the large reduction in hunting, warrants closer study of other pressures, especially the habitats Turtle Doves need to breed and feed. This finding does not mean hunting has no effect. It means reducing it alone has not yet produced a recovery comparable to the one observed in the west. Where do Arab countries enter the story? The bird's migration extends beyond the European scope of the FACE report. The western route crosses the Iberian Peninsula, Morocco and Mauritania towards Africa. Other routes pass through Italy, Malta and Tunisia, or through Greece, Egypt and the Levant, including Lebanon. Breeding grounds in Europe, stopover sites and wintering grounds in Africa are therefore parts of the same story. For Arab hunters, the report points to a practical question: how many Turtle Doves pass through each season, how many are hunted, and what is changing in farmland and resting habitats? The European experience demonstrates the value of regular counts, trackable quotas and measuring the results of management decisions year by year. Assessing the species in our countries requires local data and cooperation among the countries on its routes. Sources: FACE Turtle Dove Report 2026; Bird Migration Atlas; International Single Species Action Plan.

articles.title: Hunting law in the UAE: federal protection and local falconry rules
articles.body: Federal wildlife protection and Abu Dhabi’s local falconry rules, with the limits of local permits explained. Al Jahili Fort in Al Ain, United Arab Emirates Terrestrial hunting in the United Arab Emirates sits within federal wildlife legislation and emirate-level rules. Understanding whether an activity is permitted requires checking the species, location, method, season and licence together. Abu Dhabi’s falconry arrangements should never be presented as permission to hunt throughout the country. A foundational instrument is Federal Decree-Law No. 9 of 1983 regulating the hunting of birds and animals. It prohibits hunting specified animals, including gazelles, hares and spiny-tailed lizards. The protection attached to a species therefore matters before any hunting trip is considered. Federal legislation. Federal Law No. 24 of 1999 on environmental protection and development, amended by Law No. 11 of 2006, provides further safeguards. Article 12 prohibits hunting, killing or capturing listed birds and animals, protects nests and eggs, and requires authorisation for their possession, transport or sale as specified in the legislation. Environmental law and amendment. Within Abu Dhabi, Local Law No. 22 of 2005 regulates wild hunting. Its implementing regulations were issued under Resolution No. 69 of 2015 and amended by Resolution No. 5 of 2021. Environment Agency – Abu Dhabi licences specify the relevant seasons, areas and authorised species. Local regulatory amendment. Official open-area falconry rules restrict the quarry to captive-bred houbara bustards. Eligible licence applicants are UAE citizens aged at least 18, using registered falcons. Protected and restricted areas and prescribed separation distances must be respected. Damaging vegetation and transferring a licence to another person are prohibited. Agency falconry guidance. Weapons are separately regulated. Federal Decree-Law No. 17 of 2019 requires licences or permits for activities involving weapons. The legality of the proposed hunting activity and its method must therefore each be established. Official UAE government guidance. This is an explainer of established legislation, not a hunting-season announcement or legal advice. Before travelling, consult the relevant emirate authority, the latest seasonal decision and the actual licence conditions. A local permit has a defined scope; it does not create a nationwide hunting entitlement. articles.title: Vultures talk before they hatch
articles.body: From egg to nest: photographs of recording work in the Netherlands during the 2024–2025 study period. Soft calls from inside the egg reveal the beginnings of a rich vocal world in Rüppell’s vultures—and could open a new avenue for conservation. The sound comes first, from inside the egg; the chick’s arrival follows. That is how the story begins for Rüppell’s vultures, whose vocal lives appear far richer than their supposedly silent image suggests. Researchers documented soft calls produced before hatching in a study published in PLOS One on 21 October 2026. According to Utrecht University, the chicks begin making these sounds about two days before they emerge. Original recording of a Rüppell’s vulture egg before hatching Download recording Video S2 from the study’s supplementary material, approximately 18 seconds. Increase the volume or use headphones for this quiet recording. A single call from inside the egg Download recording Audio S1 is a very short sample of one call from inside the egg, lasting approximately 0.22 seconds. A voice before emergence The study describes soft, tonal calls beginning after the chick breaks into the egg’s air chamber and starts breathing with its lungs. The calls continue through hatching and appear to develop into the chick’s post-hatching sounds, becoming more variable. Artificial incubation at Rotterdam’s Diergaarde Blijdorp offered an opportunity to record this stage. Whether parents answer their chick’s calls while it is still inside the egg could not be determined by the study. A society with calls of its own The team, led by Connor Proudfoot, studied two groups of Rüppell’s vultures in the Netherlands, comprising 35 birds, and analysed 2,500 calls. Recordings collected between September 2024 and May 2025 covered feeding, competition, reproduction and care of young. The researchers distinguished 16 call types: some clearly differentiated, others graded and overlapping. This vocal world includes food-begging calls, calls associated with resource defence or receiving aggression, and sounds accompanying the feeding of chicks. Its diversity offers a window into the social life of a bird often described as quiet. Could sound help conserve the species? Rüppell’s vulture, Gyps rueppelli, is critically endangered. The significance of the research therefore extends beyond the surprising sound inside an egg to a practical question: could hearing these calls help parents prepare for their chick’s arrival? In artificial-incubation programmes, a model may replace the real egg, and chicks return to the nest only several days after hatching. The researchers propose testing the role of pre-hatching calls and their potential future use in improving chick acceptance and breeding success. This remains a proposed research step; the study has not tested that effect. The beginning of a fuller picture The study provides a quantitative description of the species’ vocal repertoire, rather than the final word on it. The work took place in captivity: wild populations may use calls or encounter contexts not represented in the recordings, including interactions during soaring flight. Behind the silent bird of popular imagination is a world worth listening to. Photographs: Connor Proudfoot; recordings: Proudfoot et al. © 2026 Proudfoot et al. articles.title: Wanaameen wins Prince Mohammed bin Saud Al Kabeer Cup prep by 15 lengths
articles.body: Archive photograph. The Saudi-bred horse dominates the 2,000-metre finale as Camilio Ospina completes a treble at King Abdulaziz Racecourse. Wanaameen won the Prince Mohammed bin Saud Al Kabeer Cup preparatory race by 15 lengths at King Abdulaziz Racecourse in Riyadh on Saturday, 24 October 2026, covering 2,000 metres in 2:10.649 in the evening’s finale. Camilio Ospina rode the four-year-old Saudi-bred horse for trainer Bader Rizaiq and the sons of King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz. Shadow finished second and Kaflahom third, according to the Jockey Club of Saudi Arabia’s official results. The race offered SAR 120,000 in total prize money, including SAR 60,000 for the winner. It was a preparation for the cup, not the cup race itself, and concluded a 12-race dirt card. A treble for Ospina The victory completed a treble for Ospina, who had earlier won race five over 1,400 metres on Allah Yahyiha and race nine over 1,800 metres on Majaal. All three horses are owned by the sons of King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz; Hesham Abdulwahed trained the winners of races five and nine. In race eight, an open race, Ya Dar won under Ricardo Ferreira for trainer Abdullah Alsidrani, completing 1,600 metres in 1:43.864. The race carried a SAR 120,000 purse, with SAR 60,000 going to the winner. Arabian and locally bred winners Baseq And Bake opened the meeting with victory in the 1,200-metre open Arabian race, ridden by Ricardo Ferreira and trained by Bassim Almousa, in 1:22.630. In race ten, for Arabians over 2,000 metres, Algheed won in 2:23.044 under Fawaz Alshammari for trainer Reyaan Alibrahim. Among the locally bred runners, Dahmat Alwadi won race six, an open contest for two-year-olds over 1,600 metres, under Eddie Castro for trainer Abdulaziz Alhzabi. Ghala Wateen took race eleven, a 2,000-metre maiden for locally bred horses, in 2:14.040 with Mohammad Alyami riding for trainer Mana Saleh Alzamanan. The meeting continued the 2026–2027 Riyadh racing season, which opened at the same racecourse on 16 October. articles.title: When Autumn Becomes a Season for Hunting Images
articles.body: Source: Mecshap From the rifle to the lens: how journalism can help protect migratory birds and change the culture of displaying kills. Golden leaves are not the only things that fall in Lebanon’s autumn. Birds that should be crossing its skies on their way to Africa sometimes fall too, discovering that a stopover has become an ambush. Storks and birds of prey arrive along their migration routes, only to be met by some people with a rifle and a phone: the first to bring down the bird, the second to immortalise a false feat of heroism. As though hitting a creature exhausted by its journey required an applauding audience. This is precisely where the philosophy promoted by Sayd Magazine comes into focus: ‘hunting the image instead of the bird’. It does not extinguish the passion for pursuit and challenge, but gives it a nobler spirit, replacing the rifle with a lens and camouflage for killing with camouflage for documenting. It allows the bird to live and continue its journey. Lebanon is an important passage for migratory birds travelling between Europe, Asia and Africa. Flocks gather along corridors that make them more vulnerable to being targeted. Protecting them goes beyond compassion for a broken wing: depending on their species, birds help control pests, disperse seeds and maintain ecological balance. Their repeated loss is therefore a loss for nature and agriculture alike. Everyone has a part to play in the cycle of protection that allows birds to pass safely, and the media must provide a broad platform for that effort. Through reporting, broadcasting and public awareness, they can make this loss understandable, moving birds beyond the category of beautiful scenery and showing how their lives serve a function in nature. Coverage that stops at a photograph of a slaughtered flock before moving to the next story may create a passing shock, while leaving the culture that produced the scene comfortably in place. The image itself carries a striking paradox. A study published by André Raine and colleagues in Oryx in February 2025 analysed approximately 1,844 photographs posted on Facebook and Instagram between 2011 and 2023. Researchers identified 212 species of hunted birds, 94% of which were legally protected in Lebanon. Photographs intended for boasting thus became evidence documenting violations: the irresponsible hunter displays an achievement, while the researcher reads a record of an offence. One article will not stop every rifle. But the media can withdraw the applause surrounding it. From awareness to follow-up Such coverage has value in building knowledge, but statements need more follow-up on the ground: where are the nets set? How are birds sold? And what happens after a violation is detected? Media follow-up in Lebanon could improve through regular coverage that begins before autumn migration, explains protected species and hunting rules in clear language, and includes experts and law-abiding hunters. Television and digital platforms can tell stories of rescue and birdwatching, while avoiding precise disclosure of sensitive species’ locations or presenting killing footage as entertainment. The media can thus play a vital and influential role in protecting migratory birds in Lebanon. One initiative would be to challenge ‘hunting for engagement’ through parallel campaigns that present wildlife documentarians and environmental advocates as the real heroes, highlighting images of birds flying free as a constructive alternative to photographs of killing and abuse. It is important to move beyond emotional awareness towards economic and agricultural understanding, producing investigative reports and accessible media material about migratory birds’ ecological roles. Explaining how birds of prey and storks help control rodents and agricultural pests, for example, can show citizens and farmers that killing these birds causes direct material and economic losses for the country. Developing environmental investigative journalism and field monitoring could be a particularly important initiative. Investigations could use open-source tools to trace videos and leaked material documenting the mass killing of migratory birds, and hold social media platforms and the relevant authorities to account for shortcomings in enforcing the law and restricting this content. Media partnerships with schools and field organisations may also be among the most effective long-term initiatives. Interactive content for young people—short stories, interactive documentaries and programmes on TikTok and Instagram—could be created with environmental experts and civil society organisations, spreading a culture of birdwatching tourism as a promising source of economic and tourism activity for Lebanon. One article will not stop every rifle. But the media can withdraw the applause surrounding it and turn a violation into an issue that persists after the video disappears. Autumn can then become a season for watching the travellers in our skies, and birds can stop paying the price for a human desire to be seen.

articles.title: When the coast changes… where do birds rest?
articles.body: Batroun’s pelican at the edge of the Mediterranean. Amira Rajab / dpa The Lebanon–Cyprus–Egypt triangle: estuaries, salt pans, lakes and harbours in the protection of bird habitats. In 2026, reports on managing Lebanon’s Damour basin, a new study of Egypt’s Lake Manzala and the debate over expanding Latchi harbour in Cyprus reopen one question: where do birds rest when the coast changes? At the water’s edge, they need an estuary that still receives river water, a shallow bank rich in food, sheltering reeds or a quiet rock after diving. These features make a place valuable as habitat and deserve a place in development plans from the outset. Lebanon | From the Damour estuary to Anfeh’s salt pans Anfeh’s salt pans beside the Mediterranean. EPA / The National In 2026, the integrated management plan for Damour brings the relationship between river and coast back into focus. Reports reveal the pressures on the area: around 200.7 hectares of agricultural land were converted to built-up uses between 2014 and 2024 within the basin study area, alongside water abstraction, pollution and construction along riverbanks. These pressures are particularly important at the estuary and its surroundings, where freshwater meets the sea and the river connects with farmland and coastal vegetation. This area provides habitat for migratory birds in Lebanon. Surveys of the lower Damour have recorded migratory and resident species, including White Pelican and Common Crane. Protecting the estuary therefore means preserving a space used by birds and its connections with water and surrounding vegetation. Recent reports identify the flow of water reaching the estuary as a management priority, alongside restoring riverbanks and regulating land use. Protecting the coast is tied to what happens upstream: abstraction, pollution and encroachment have consequences along the river all the way to the sea. On the northern coast, Anfeh’s salt pans reveal another aspect of this relationship. Between sea and rock lie shallow basins created by the craft of salt harvesting, bringing together work, heritage and nature. Sources document their role as resting and feeding sites for migratory birds, while some abandoned pools have become refuges. Areas that may appear unused thus retain a living function along birds’ journeys. The salt pans face pressure from changes in coastal land use and tourism development, making their protection about more than preserving a traditional occupation. Safeguarding the basins, their connection to the sea and their open character can allow salt production to continue while retaining feeding and resting sites for birds. On Batroun’s beach, the famous ‘Bajou3a’ gives the relationship between birds and the coast a familiar face. Her image beside the sea brings the question closer to people: where do birds find rest and food, and how can we preserve these spaces as the shoreline changes? Egypt | Manzala: more open water… different habitats A wader at the water’s edge in Port Said. اليوم السابع A scientific study published in 2026 places Lake Manzala before a precise question: how does bird life change when open water expands at the expense of reeds and shallow margins? The study compared twenty sites within Ashtoum El Gamil Protectorate, in the lake’s north-eastern area, before and after dredging and vegetation removal. It found declines in vegetation cover, bird diversity and abundance within the study area, with different responses among bird groups depending on the habitats they use. A wader searches for food in shallow water and mud, while other birds benefit from open water. When water depth changes or vegetation disappears, the opportunities available to each group change too. A lake can therefore appear larger and more open while losing some of the habitats that give it its diversity. The study recommends allowing reeds to recolonise and restoring shallow, muddy areas along the margins. These recommendations connect lake rehabilitation with birds’ needs: open water for diving and swimming, vegetation for shelter and nesting, and banks for feeding and resting. This diversity is especially important at Ashtoum El Gamil, where the lake environment meets the Mediterranean. Differences in water, vegetation and margins create a series of habitats that birds use in different ways. Successful rehabilitation is also measured by the diversity a place retains. Cleaning water and improving circulation can go hand in hand with protecting reeds, shallow areas and islands. When these elements remain, the lake can accommodate birds with varied needs and retain its role as a living coastal environment. Cyprus | Latchi: the harbour on the birds’ map Latchi harbour at the centre of the debate over expansion and protection of the bay. BirdLife Cyprus In October 2026, BirdLife Cyprus renewed the debate over the limits of development through the proposed expansion of Latchi harbour in the island’s north-west. The organisation said the proposal would increase recreational boat capacity from 200 to 384 in Chrysochous Bay, which is surrounded by protected areas and supports seabirds, turtles and the Mediterranean monk seal, alongside Posidonia seagrass meadows. The new element in the debate is what birds’ movements reveal. According to the organisation, data from the Pandoteira project show regular use of the Akamas coast and the bay by the Mediterranean subspecies of European Shag, with young birds frequently visiting the harbour’s surroundings. A space for mooring and navigation on an engineering plan appears on a bird’s map as a place to feed and rest. Tracking devices help explain this relationship: they reveal where birds travel after leaving their nests and which parts of the coast they use during the day. Shags nesting on rocks and coastal islets also need waters in which to find food and places to perch quietly after diving. The organisation warns of increased noise, lighting, pollution and human presence as boat numbers rise, and calls for assessment of cumulative effects across the whole bay. Marine habitats are interconnected, and birds’ movements extend beyond the project boundaries drawn on paper. The significance of the Cypriot case lies in bringing feeding and resting sites into the expansion decision and its conditions, and considering the harbour within its wider environment. Knowing where the nest is does not suffice; the protection map must accommodate the bird’s daily life. What remains at the water’s edge? From Damour and Anfeh to Manzala and Latchi, interventions and birds differ, but the question remains: what do we preserve for them when the coast changes? An estuary that receives water, quiet rocks, reeds and shallow banks deserve to appear in development plans alongside quays and roads. A coast that makes room for people’s lives can also leave birds a place to rest.

articles.title: Where Do Birds Rest?
articles.body: Flamingos at Ras Al Khor against Dubai’s skyline: a bird refuge beside the city. WWF Major migration refuges in the Mashreq and Arabian Peninsula The greater spotted eagle has returned to Kuwait’s Jahra Reserve with the autumn migration season of 2026. Its arrival signals more than the start of a season: a bird travelling long distances has found water, food and somewhere to spend the winter. From Jahra to the wetlands of the Bekaa, Iraq’s marshes and the Arabian coast, these places help make migration possible. World Migratory Bird Day highlights this journey and its need for safe habitats. From the Mashreq to the Arabian Peninsula, we explore some of the major refuges: some provide brief stops to replenish energy; others accommodate birds for months. Routes vary between species: shorebirds need productive shores, ducks suitable waters, and raptors areas offering prey and quiet. Kuwait | Jahra: winter among water and reeds The Kuwait Environment Protection Society’s bird team recorded the first greater spotted eagle at Jahra Reserve this season. This raptor uses wetlands during winter, benefiting from food and resting places. Jahra combines shallow waters, reeds and open ground, attracting birds of different sizes and feeding habits. Its value extends beyond the sight of a rare bird: it illustrates the need for a complete habitat usable throughout the season, supported by continued monitoring and protection. Lebanon | Aammiq: a pause in the Bekaa A glossy ibis forages in shallow water at Aammiq wetlands. Reuters — Ali Hashisho In the Bekaa Valley, Aammiq provides migrating birds with water, reeds and meadows within a broad agricultural landscape. Lebanon’s largest natural freshwater wetland is an important site for passage, feeding and roosting. Ducks, herons and other waterbirds find different resources within this diversity, while other birds use the surrounding land. The glossy ibis, searching shallow water with its curved bill, illustrates the relationship between bird and habitat. Protecting this refuge means caring for water, vegetation and surrounding farmland, and preventing poaching and disturbance at gathering sites. Jordan | Azraq and Aqaba: an oasis and a seaside stop A bluethroat at Azraq: part of the bird diversity associated with the oasis and its surroundings. Birdingplaces Azraq Oasis, in the eastern desert, attracts birds seeking water. Its pools and vegetation offer waterbirds and passing migrants opportunities to feed and rest; maintaining water is central to its ecological role. Further south, Aqaba Bird Observatory provides another stop where desert meets sea. An agreement between the Royal Society for the Conservation of Nature and UNDP at the start of October supports the sustainability of its habitats. Together, the two sites illustrate natural habitat protection and restoration in a region where every wetland matters. Syria | Jabbul: refuge in shallow waters East of Aleppo, Sabkhat al-Jabbul is one of Syria’s major wetlands. The shallow saline lake, its margins and islands provide waterbirds with places for passage and wintering, including flamingos and duck species. Different depths and margins allow birds to stand, forage and find quiet. Protecting Jabbul therefore requires maintaining its water and ecological characteristics, together with the surrounding areas used by birds. Iraq | The marshes: reeds and open water In southern Iraq, Hawizeh, Hammar and the Central Marshes offer extensive reeds, open water and shallow wetlands. They form an important part of the network used by waterbirds during migration and winter. This diversity provides feeding, shelter and roosting sites for ducks and other waterbirds. Marsh life depends on water flows and quality, and on surrounding communities. Protection involves managing resources, responsible hunting, and preserving the extent and connections of wetland habitats. Saudi Arabia | Farasan: stops on the Red Sea Pelicans over the waters of Farasan, where shores meet mangroves. Saudi Press Agency (SPA) Off Jazan, the Farasan Islands combine mangroves, sandy and muddy shores, and coastal salt flats. These habitats offer waterbirds and shorebirds several places to feed and rest along the Red Sea routes they use. Winter counts demonstrate the importance of field monitoring. Birds seen above the coast also depend on food in mud and shallow water, and on quiet shores. Protecting Farasan means preserving these details, from mangroves to gathering and roosting areas. Oman | Barr al Hikman: a table revealed by the tide Shorebirds at Barr al Hikman, where shallow water and falling tides reveal feeding areas. Times of Oman In Al Wusta Governorate, Barr al Hikman’s mudflats extend along coasts rich in life. Receding tides reveal broad feeding areas, making the site a major winter refuge for shorebirds in the region. These birds depend on the tidal cycle: they feed on exposed mud and gather on higher ground as water rises. Feeding areas and nearby resting sites therefore need protection together. Disturbance that repeatedly forces flocks into flight consumes energy needed for their stay and onward journey. United Arab Emirates | Ras Al Khor: refuge beside the city In Dubai, Ras Al Khor offers a striking view of birds against the city. Its wetlands and shallow waters host flamingos feeding on small organisms in habitat providing food and rest. Ras Al Khor illustrates the importance of retaining space for nature within cities. Water alone is insufficient: birds need healthy habitat, quiet areas and managed viewing that allows visitors to enjoy the flocks without disturbing them. Every observation helps These sites are examples within a wider network supporting migration. This year’s occasion stresses the importance of every bird and observation. Birdwatchers, photographers and responsible hunters can contribute by recording species, location and date, keeping their distance and reporting violations. Protecting the journey begins with knowing where birds stop, then keeping those places safe.

articles.title: White Stork — Ciconia ciconia
articles.body: White storkSayd Magazine archive Range: A large bird with white wings tipped black, and red bill and legs. It breeds across Europe, North Africa, and western Asia, and winters mainly in sub-Saharan Africa. Its eastern flyway runs through Turkey, the Levant, and the Nile Valley; Lebanon is part of the Levantine bottleneck for soaring migrants between Europe and Africa. It is told from the black stork Ciconia nigra by its mostly white plumage and red bill. Life cycle and habitat: Socially monogamous in the season; the male arrives early and chooses the bulky stick nest, often reused for years on trees, rooftops, or platforms. The female typically lays about four eggs; incubation lasts roughly 33–34 days with both parents sharing; hatching is asynchronous. The parents feed the young; fledging follows after about 58–64 days. It forages in damp meadows, shallow farmland, and pools: insects, worms, amphibians, small reptiles, rodents, and sometimes fish or nestling birds. Lifestyle: Gregarious on migration and in winter gatherings; more territorial at the nest. The famous bill-clattering, amplified by the throat pouch, is its social signal. It climbs on warm air then glides long distances, saving energy against continuous flapping; it avoids long Mediterranean sea crossings because thermals form poorly over water. Hence the preference for land bridges and bottlenecks—among them Lebanese skies at peak seasons. White storkSayd Magazine archive Hunting status: Across Arab countries, hunting white stork is generally prohibited unless a specific state issues an official seasonal decree that expressly lists it. In Lebanon, Wild Hunting Law No. 580/2004 limits hunting to quarry species set by the minister; everything else is protected year-round; white stork is not among the permitted quarry in the absence of a current open-season decision. Conservation status: Globally Least Concern with the International Union for Conservation of Nature, with an increasing trend in parts of Europe thanks to protection programs. It remains exposed to wetland loss, power lines, and illegal shooting on some flyways. Traits: A lesson in flight economy. Its massive nest can become a living structure that sometimes hosts smaller birds. Bill-clattering is a clear social message without complex song. Over Lebanon it passes as an emblem of the eastern–African migration corridor.

articles.title: White Wagtail in the Arab World During Migration and Winter
articles.body: White Wagtail From riverbanks and lakeshores to fields and gardens, the White Wagtail draws attention with its long tail and constant movement. Its Arab-world range stretches from Morocco to Egypt, the Levant, Iraq and the Arabian Peninsula, with different patterns of occurrence: passage and wintering in many countries, and local breeding in parts of the range. October offers an opportunity to follow this seasonal presence, whose timing varies between countries. Identification card Arabic name: الذعرة البيضاء English name: White Wagtail French name: Bergeronnette grise Scientific name: Motacilla alba Family: Motacillidae, the wagtails and pipits Length: approximately 18 centimetres, including the tail Arab-world occurrence: passage migrant and winter visitor across extensive areas, with local breeding populations, including the resident Moroccan subspecies Global conservation status: Least Concern (LC) Legal status: the relevant country’s laws and current decisions; global conservation status does not determine whether hunting is permitted When movement provides the first clue A White Wagtail may attract your attention before its colours become clear: quick steps, a short pause, then a long tail moving up and down. This is a useful starting point for identification, provided it is not your only clue. Look at its body shape, colour pattern and movements together; field identification improves when several features are considered rather than a fleeting impression alone. It has a slender body. In the widespread alba subspecies, the back is grey, the underparts white, and parts of the head and breast black. White stands out on the face and along the sides of the dark tail, with white markings also visible on the wings. Its flight follows an undulating path, accompanied by clear, short calls that may alert you to the bird before you see it. Its appearance changes with age and season. In winter plumage, the throat becomes white while a dark mark remains on the breast. Juveniles look duller, with some brownish-grey tones. A broad black breast patch, as shown in breeding-plumage photographs, should therefore not be a requirement before considering White Wagtail as a possibility. Different patterns from Morocco to Oman In Morocco, two patterns overlap: the Moroccan subspecies Motacilla alba subpersonata is a resident breeder, alongside birds arriving on passage and for winter. A wagtail seen there in autumn may therefore belong to the local population or be a seasonal visitor. Winter occurrence is also documented in Tunisia, including sites in the south. Egypt is a country of regular passage and wintering, with field studies documenting the species in the Nile Delta’s agricultural habitats. Farther east, the 2026 Birds of Lebanon guide describes White Wagtail as a common passage migrant and winter visitor, and as a relatively scarce migrant breeder. Regional references also record breeding in northern Iraq. These differences matter: finding a bird in an Arab country during winter does not establish that it breeds there. In the Arabian Peninsula, Saudi surveys confirm winter occurrence, while the Oman Bird List describes it as abundant on passage and in winter. In the UAE, white-faced birds are very common passage migrants and winter visitors from mid-September, mainly October, to April. White Wagtail abundance also varies within a country according to habitat and season; birds may be numerous at one site and absent from another. Interpreting an October sighting October falls within the White Wagtail’s season of occurrence in many parts of the Arab world, but there is no single arrival date that applies throughout. For Egypt, a study published in 2019 places passage and winter occurrence between late September and early May. Lebanon’s passage-and-winter window is wider, from late August to late May, while Morocco’s resident birds must be distinguished from seasonal visitors. An October record should therefore be read with its country, site and date. The wagtail may be passing through, settling for the winter, or a local bird where breeding occurs. One observation cannot reliably distinguish these possibilities; repeated visits and comparison with a local guide are useful. Where to look, and what might cause confusion? White Wagtails use open spaces with short grass or bare ground, including watersides, fields, gardens and areas near buildings. They can appear in places people use every day. An open patch near water is therefore worth a few minutes of quiet watching, without entering private property or approaching sensitive locations. Watch for confusion with Grey Wagtail, Motacilla cinerea, which shows conspicuous yellow beneath its tail despite its name. Yellow colouring can also cause confusion with Yellow Wagtail and closely related species. Do not let a single colour settle the identification, particularly in young birds. Compare the head, breast and tail, and consult a clear photograph or a reliable guide when uncertain. Small prey and a place in the food web Its diet consists mainly of insects and spiders. It picks up prey while walking, makes short dashes after it, and may snatch an insect during a brief flight. Food includes flies, beetles and larvae, including prey associated with water. This diet illustrates its connection to conditions on the ground and along the water’s edge, where its food resources occur. From a habitat-conservation perspective, keeping shores clean and reducing pollution and disturbance benefit the places where birds feed. The presence of one wagtail is not enough to establish water quality scientifically, nor does it allow an estimate of the species’ numbers across an entire area. Its first value is as an observation that can be documented and contribute to systematic monitoring. A wide range and cavity nesting Its Arab-world occurrence is part of a wider range extending across most of Europe and large parts of Asia, with breeding in parts of North Africa and at the margins in Greenland and western Alaska. Migration patterns differ between populations. Geographical forms also vary within the species, so head markings in a Moroccan photograph may differ from those of a wintering bird in the Gulf. It builds its nest in a sheltered place, such as a wall crevice, a cavity or a suitable space in a building. A clutch usually contains four to six eggs. Incubation takes about two weeks, followed by a similar period for the chicks in the nest, and both parents feed them. The nesting season varies by region and population. Global conservation and responsible observation The White Wagtail is classified globally as Least Concern (LC). This assesses extinction risk at species level and does not necessarily describe the condition of every local population. Protecting feeding and nesting places and reducing pollution and disturbance remain important even for a widespread bird. Whether hunting is permitted cannot be inferred from that category. To establish the legal position, consult the relevant country’s laws and decisions in force on the date of the activity, including provisions concerning species, seasons and protected areas. A hunting rule or exception in one country cannot be applied to another. For responsible observation, record the date, place and approximate number, with a photograph showing the identifying features, and let the bird continue feeding. Avoid chasing it for a closer shot. The simple sight of a tail wagging on an autumn shore deserves to be recorded as it is, accurately and quietly. Photo credit: Charles J. Sharp — Wikimedia Commons — CC BY-SA 4.0.

articles.title: Wings reclaim the sky… Tamara El Zein visits Zgharta’s bird rescue centre
articles.body: White storks at the Lebanese Association for Migratory Birds’ site, where injured birds receive care and rehabilitation before returning to the wild when their condition allows. Environment Minister Dr Tamara El Zein visited the Lebanese Association for Migratory Birds’ centre in Jerjour, in the district of Zgharta, to learn about efforts to rescue, care for and rehabilitate injured birds for their return to the wild. The visit included the release of treated and rehabilitated birds in Horsh Ehden Nature Reserve to mark World Migratory Bird Day. The programme also included an environmental tour of the reserve to explore its biodiversity and natural riches, before concluding with the opening of an insect exhibition. Environment Minister Tamara El Zein taking part in the release of birds following treatment and rehabilitation, during her visit to the association and Horsh Ehden Nature Reserve. From injury to another chance to fly The visit highlights work that extends beyond the moment of release: receiving an injured bird, providing appropriate care and monitoring its recovery until it can return to the wild. The association’s centre, headed by Dr Michel Sawan, receives wild birds of different species, including raptors and storks. Care involves isolating cases when necessary, treating wounds and fractures, and rehabilitation. Injuries that cause permanent disability may prevent a bird’s release, in which case its care continues within the association’s facilities. Images from the site show a group of white storks in a fenced care area — a scene that captures the centre’s role as a place to regain strength before a possible return to the sky. Storks and raptors return to the wild During 2025 and 2026, the association’s activities documented other milestones in returning birds to nature. On 5 April 2025, it organised a release with the Polish Embassy in Beirut, including storks that had undergone lengthy rehabilitation after being rescued from illegal hunting. In June 2026, the release of a honey buzzard was announced in cooperation with the municipality of Metrit in Koura, after the bird received care at the association’s shelter and recovered from its injury. The event conveyed a message about protecting raptors and their role in agricultural ecosystems, while connecting bird rescue with local community participation. Feliks… a rescue journey across borders Among the most striking stories to emerge in 2026 was that of Feliks, an eastern imperial eagle that set off from Serbia and reached Syria, where it fell into the hands of illegal hunters. The Lebanese Association for Migratory Birds helped rescue him. He spent more than six months at a shelter in northern Lebanon before returning to Serbia. There, a specialist team continued his care and flight training until he was released near Subotica on 6 August 2026. Tracking showed that within days he had reached the Slovak–Polish border. This story illustrates how protecting a migratory bird may require cooperation across countries: its route connects regions and nations that share responsibility for keeping it safe. Protection continues after release Alongside rescue, the association raises awareness of the value of wildlife. In July 2025, it worked with the North Lebanon Agriculture Department on a seminar in Danniyeh about the role of birds and wild animals in protecting crops and forests. The environment minister’s visit brings these elements together: care within the centre, a return to nature and attention to reserves and biodiversity. Yet the rescue journey does not end when a bird spreads its wings. Its safety still depends on protecting habitats and migration routes, respecting hunting laws and preventing attacks on protected species. Images: stills from a video published on the Lebanon Heaven page.
